Franziska Herbert and four coauthors teach robots task structure from human demos. Their 2026 preprint builds semantic-geometric task graphs from demonstrations. Long-horizon manipulation is hard for robots to learn raw. Bimanual tasks add two hands whose moves must be ordered.

A good task record must hold two kinds of structure. One is the discrete semantic side: steps and objects used. The other is how object geometry shifts over time. Both sides can vary much from demo to demo. The team's graphs join meaning and geometry in one form. That form supports reasoning about how a task unfolds. Robots can then plan long tasks with clearer steps.
arxiv-2601-11560:
Zifeng Wang and seven coauthors launch DeepEvidence for biomedical discovery. Their 2026 preprint builds on biomedical knowledge graphs. Such graphs encode vast, mixed data for the life sciences. Literature, genes, pathways, drugs, diseases, and trials all sit inside.

Using those graphs jointly for discovery stays hard today. Their structures differ from one resource to the next. They evolve over time as new studies land. Cross-resource alignment is limited and needs manual work. That hand work caps the depth and scale of exploration. DeepEvidence aims at deep graph research with less friction. Better tooling could speed drug and disease insight.
arxiv-2601-11660:
Chunshu Wu and four coauthors argue that zeros can be informative. Their 2026 preprint gives a masked binary U-Net for segmentation. Real-time segmentation enables AR, VR, robots, and drones. Tight budgets bind accuracy, latency, and energy on edge devices.

U-Net balances accuracy and efficiency better than big transformers. High-resolution input still strains compute, memory, and power. Binary networks cut weights to one bit for speed. Masking turns many values to zero in the network. Those zeros, the team shows, still carry useful signal. Running on Tensor Cores targets the hardware in edge chips. The aim is real-time masks within strict budgets.
arxiv-2601-11860:
Xin Xiong, Zijian Guo, Haobo Zhu, and a cross-lab team tackle decay in clinical AI over time. Tools that work well at launch often fade as data shift. Causes span new patient mixes, code updates such as ICD-9 to ICD-10, and shocks such as the COVID-19 pandemic.

Full retraining is often too costly or blocked by privacy rules. Their frame aims for durable AI that adapts as it moves to new sites and times. It treats drift as a fact to plan for, not a surprise. Sound drift tools could keep care AI safe for longer.
arxiv-2601-12160:
Y. Shen, W. He, J. Sears, and a large team report the first watch of plasmons in low-valence nickelates. Nickelate superconductors opened a new field for the study of electron fluids that pair in odd ways. Plasmons are joint waves of the electron gas, and they hold key facts on charge dynamics.

Such waves had not been seen in nickelates before this work. Their data add a new probe of how charge moves in these materials. That probe can test theories of their odd superconductivity. The team span labs in the US and abroad.
arxiv-2601-12860:
Youngmin Lee, Subong Lim, and Wissam Raji study the Rankin Cohen bracket for vector valued modular forms. Modular forms are functions with rich symmetry, central to number theory. The Rankin Cohen bracket combines two such forms into a new one. For vector valued forms, the bracket carries extra structure worth mapping.

The team explore how this bracket relates to Petersson inner products. They derive an explicit description of the adjoint map for the bracket operator. The study extends to Jacobi forms and skew holomorphic Jacobi forms. An isomorphism connects their brackets with the vector valued case. Adjoint maps for the extended operators are examined as well.
arxiv-2601-13260:
Sawsan Alqahtani and co-authors argue that tokenizers are core design picks, not mere prep steps. A tokenizer cuts text into bits that a large language model reads. The go to cut is byte pair encoding, which joins the most common pairs step by step. It scales well, but the cuts can clash with true word parts.

That clash can waste model room and can grow bias. It hits tongues and fields far from the train mix the most. The team reframes the cut as a model pick in its own right. They urge that it be judged with the same care as net shape or train data. For model builders, the piece is a call to own the first step of the chain.
arxiv-2601-13660:
Aiko Miyamoto and co-authors hunt for changing iron light from the heart of the Circinus galaxy in 2026. They used eight sets of Chandra X-ray data taken over about twenty-two years. Their target is neutral iron-K alpha emission, a sharp X-ray glow from iron atoms. The glow comes from the region near the galaxy's core, about ten to a hundred parsecs out.

Maps and spectra split by place let them track the glow spot by spot. They search for time variability, shifts in brightness over the years. Changes would hint at how light and gas move near a giant black hole. Long records like this are rare and prized.
arxiv-2601-14160:
Ali Hamza Bashir and co-authors adapt language models to German law with synthetic data in 2026. Large language models often struggle in specialized domains like legal reasoning. Limited expert knowledge leads to factually incorrect outputs or hallucinations. German legal question answering is the target task here.

Their method fine-tunes advanced models on novel synthetic data. A generation approach creates training cases in the legal style. Domain adaptation through synthetic data avoids costly expert labeling at scale. Reliable legal assistants could help citizens and junior lawyers find rules fast. The dip was brief, so fast alerts from sky watchers were key. Their quick word let big scopes join in time to catch it.
arxiv-2601-14260:
Xiaoxuan Yang, Peilin Chen, Tergel Molom-Ochir, and Yiran Chen tackle a hardware problem in this 2026 paper. Transformers run most large language models, but they are costly to run at scale. The authors name three main challenges. One is the attention step, which needs huge matrix work.

Attention also forces much data movement. Intermediate results shuttle back and forth between memory and compute units. That traffic drives up both delay and energy use. The team's answer sits in processing-in-memory designs. Such designs place compute inside or near memory chips. The paper works on end-to-end speed-up for transformers on that kind of hardware.
arxiv-2601-15160:
Yuval Kansal and Niraj K. Jha argue that a knowledge graph can quietly act as a reward model. Their 2026 arXiv paper deals with the reasoning of large language models. The models shine at math and code, but multi-hop reasoning in specialist science stays weak.

The authors propose a bottom-up route. A model first learns firm domain facts, stated like axioms. Signals derived from paths in a knowledge graph then reward good steps. From those facts the model composes answers to complex new tasks that it has never once seen before.
arxiv-2601-15360:
Eichi Uehara repairs a popular estimator for treatment effects that vary by person. His 2026 arXiv paper deals with heterogeneous treatment effects in fields like ad tech and health care. Two problems strike at once: extreme class imbalance and heavy-tailed outcomes.

The X-Learner handles imbalance by cross-imputation. But the author shows it breaks under outlier smearing when squared error rules the fit. A few wild outcomes can poison the estimates. Robust X-Learner swaps in robust methods to stop that smearing. The repair keeps the cross-imputation strength while taming the heavy tails.
arxiv-2601-15760:
Shubham Patel and Utkarsh Mishra squeeze more from a quantum optimizer in a 2026 arXiv paper. The algorithm is QAOA, built for combinatorial optimization. They test it on MaxCut, a classic graph problem. Three graph families serve as testbeds: 3-regular graphs, Erdős-Rényi graphs, and Barabási-Albert graphs. Their recipe starts with parameter transfer initialization. Good parameters from earlier runs seed the new one.

Targeted single-layer optimization then refines the result. Regularization keeps the search focused, per the title. The abstract reports a mean approximation ratio of 0.9443 for the transfer approach, before the record cuts off. Parameter tuning is QAOA's practical bottleneck. Cheaper tuning widens the problems users can afford to try.
arxiv-2601-15860:
Shui-Hsiang Hsu, Tsung-Hsiang Chou, Chen-Jui Yu, and Yao-Chung Fan build a table representation in a 2026 arXiv paper. Table retrieval finds the most relevant tables for a natural-language query. The search runs over large corpora. Structured tables and unstructured questions differ in form and meaning. That gap makes embedding alignment hard. Recent methods enrich tables with synthetic queries. Many still sample partial tables coarsely and fuse signals simply.

Their method is STAR, a semantic table representation. It uses header-aware clustering and adaptive weighted fusion. Headers carry much of a table's meaning, so the method leans on them. Adaptive fusion weighs parts by their value per query. For search over data lakes, such gains decide whether the right table surfaces at all.
arxiv-2601-15960:
Zihao Wu and a large team report a possible galaxy cluster from the dawn of time in a 2026 arXiv paper. The candidate sits at redshift about 10.5. That distance places it within the first 500 million years, per the title. It contains 18 galaxies with consistent photometric redshifts. They show robust F115W dropouts, the color signature of very distant sources. The group spans 8 comoving megaparsecs in projection.

The data come from the JADES survey with JWST. An overdensity this early is a strong claim. Structure needs time to grow, and 500 million years is little time. A confirmed cluster that young would strain formation models. The authors present it as a candidate, inviting the spectroscopic checks that can settle it.
arxiv-2601-16360:
Tom Moshaiov and Shaul Zemel give curve forms for group marks on cycles. Their 2026 preprint deals with the symmetric group and its marks. Past work by Cohen and Zemel showed a key size is a curve in n. That size is the span of a group form tied to a set split. The split has a fixed small part and a part that grows with n.

The pair now give like curve forms for marks on cycles. Marks and sizes both turn out as curves of set grade. Curve forms let teams work values for big n at once. No step by step sum is then needed for each n. The work adds firm forms to group maths.
arxiv-2601-16560:
Ruisheng Shi and coauthors test eclipse hits on the Ethereum peer net. Their 2026 preprint deals with hits that cut a node off from true peers. A hit node sees just foe peers and their false tale. Past hits were well read in Bitcoin and Monero nets. How they fare on Ethereum post Merge was far less known.

The team tests if the same tricks can take Ethereum nodes. Post Merge shifts in the peer rules may block or aid hits. Clear risk maps help node hosts set peer guards. Such guards keep the chain tale true for all users. The work brings a known hit to a new net.
arxiv-2601-16960:
Olivia Pal, Veda Duddu, Agam Goyal, Drishti Goel, and Koustuv Saha study student trust in AI answers. Trust and use are oft read as one linked pair. Tune trust right, and fit use should follow, folks say. Their 2026 preprint doubts that link in school work. Students now ask bots for help on a daily basis.

The team frames the doubt as shared mind-read skill. Each side models what the next side knows. Misfit models can leave trust high but use poor. Or trust low while use stays fit. Their work can guide school tools that earn apt trust. It warns grades based on trust polls alone.
arxiv-2601-18260:
Eytan Kats and co-authors teach a model to locate organs inside the body from a photo of its surface. Their 2026 preprint deals with depth images of the patient's outside. Automated patient positioning matters in medical scanning. A well-placed patient shortens the scan and improves throughput and comfort. If a system can infer where organs sit from the surface shape, the scanner can be set up before any imaging dose is spent.

Learning that inside-outside map is the paper's core task. Surface depth is cheap and safe to capture. Organ position varies with body shape, so the map must be learned, not ruled. The work joins computer vision with radiology workflow.
arxiv-2601-18360:
Weikang Qian and three colleagues study the shape of a set of plans that show up in hard choice tasks. The sets pair a kind of curved cost rule with caps on how much of each group can be picked. Such sets sit inside tasks in ports, power grids, and work plans. The shape of the set tells a solver which cuts will trim the search with no loss.

The team find a new class of sharp cuts for two such sets. They build the cuts by a step trick that lifts a small true claim to a large one. Sharp cuts can cut run time a lot on real tasks. Their work gives solver teams new tools to add to the kit. It also maps the form of these sets with more care than past work did.
arxiv-2601-18460:
Francisco Gancedo and four colleagues study what can go wrong where two fluids of unlike weight meet and move. The heavy fluid sits on top of the light one in their setup. That stack is not calm: the edge between the fluids tends to grow wild with time. Thick rules of flow, with drag, set how the edge moves.

The team prove that the wild growth does not stop. In their setup the edge grows in length or in curl for all time, with no cap. A proof of that kind rules out hopes that drag alone would calm the stack. It also maps a hard case for teams who model oil, water, or air in tanks. Such proofs keep models honest about what they can and cannot tame.
arxiv-2601-18660:
Jaume de Haro gives a fresh, clear path to a set of marks used to chart a fall into a black hole. The marks are named for Novikov. They ride with bits that fall in a straight line toward the hole. In the chart, time and place are set by those falls, so the chart fits how a fall feels from in-side. Past paths to the marks were long and hard to read.

De Haro starts from falls with a twist: the bits bear a kind of charge that past work tags as less than none. Those falls form a full set that spans the whole of the hole's world, in-side and out. From them the marks drop out in a short, plain way. A clear path could help teach the chart and use it in new work on how holes grow and fade.
arxiv-2601-18760:
Henry Bell and three colleagues argue that the rules used to train language models should rest on why people hold their views, not just on which reply they pick. In the main path now, a model is taught to match a set of writ rules. Those rules are set by a small team. It is not clear how the rules could be set in a fair way with wide voice from all who are touched by the tools.

Picks alone hide the grounds of a view. Two folk may pick the same reply for quite unlike grounds. A rule built on picks may thus miss what folk prize most. The team set out a path that learns rules from grounds and worths. Such rules could claim a fairer base. They could also be checked in the open, ground by ground.
arxiv-2601-18960:
Sofia Cocciaretto and Vittorio Giovannetti study how much quantum data a lossy channel can carry. Most quantum link work rests on qubits, units with two states. Higher level units, called qudits, may carry more and compute better, a point fresh results stress.

They study a family of channels that model energy decay for such multi level signals. The work asks what the quantum capacity of these channels is, that is, how much quantum data can pass safely. Knowing the cap for real loss shapes helps plan links that use bigger units, not just qubits.
arxiv-2601-19060:
Jeonghwan Kim and ten co-authors teach a visual model to fetch facts tied to the exact spot in a photo. Answering questions about images often needs both sharp sight and outside facts. Past systems that fetch facts lack an inner rule for when to fetch and how to aim the search.

Their model, PixSearch, joins region level sight with fetch based reasoning in one end to end system. It can point at the part of the image the question is about, then pull facts for that part. Grounded fetching could cut the made up answers that plague visual question answering today.
arxiv-2601-19360:
Diego Rossini and Lonneke van der Plas find multiword expressions in text with a light, language aware model. Multiword expressions, like idioms, act as one unit of meaning spread over several words. Spotting all their types is a known hard step for language tools.

Their method labels each token as inside or outside an expression, adds linguistic features, and grows the training data by augmentation. Their model tops the prior best on its test set, ahead of far larger systems. A light model that wins on skill, not size, suits real pipelines that process text at scale.
arxiv-2601-19760:
Yuya Koshiba and colleagues report a laser that fires short, strong pulses in the infrared. The device uses a thin disk of holmium-doped YAG crystal, pumped by laser diodes. It was run in two modes: Q-switching and cavity dumping, two standard ways to store and release light in bursts. The output wavelength sits near two micrometres.

The pulses carry more than six millijoules of energy and last only a few nanoseconds. That combination gives a peak power above a megawatt. The beam quality is near the diffraction limit, meaning it stays tight and clean. Such sources serve in materials processing, sensing, and further laser stages. The work shows what thin-disk designs can reach in this wavelength range.
arxiv-2601-20260:
Xingxin Xu and four colleagues present a diffusion method for fusing images from different sensors into one picture. Fusion aims to keep fine detail and high visual quality while joining the strengths of each source image. Diffusion models generate sharp images, but they often lose detail when used for fusion.

The authors design a reversible, efficient diffusion process to cut that loss. Their goal is a fused image that keeps the texture of the inputs, not a smoothed version of them. Better fusion supports night vision, medical scans, and remote sensing, where each sensor alone sees only part of the scene.
arxiv-2601-20760:
Sarvesh Shashidhar, Abhishek Mishra, and Madhav Kotecha question a basic assumption in how AI models learn from human feedback. Their 2026 paper is about RLHF, the method that trains models with human ratings. RLHF has been effective for AI alignment, the task of making models act as people wish. But it treats all raters as if they respond in the same way.

Real users differ, and the authors put that heterogeneity at the center. If raters want different things, one reward signal may fit no one well. The paper explores what changes when feedback comes from a mixed crowd. It asks how training should handle clashing tastes and values. The work speaks to builders who want models that serve varied users, not an average one.
arxiv-2601-20860:
Babak Vakili asks whether quantum teleportation still works in a universe that expands. The 2026 paper studies teleportation in Friedmann-Robertson-Walker spacetime, the standard model of an expanding cosmos. Two scenarios take center stage. One is a power-law expansion, steady and simple. The other is the de Sitter universe, which expands at an ever-quickening rate. The approach is field-theoretical.

Two comoving observers share an entangled mode of a scalar field. Comoving means they drift along with the expansion. Vakili analyzes the quantum correlations between them. Expansion can stretch and weaken those correlations. The study asks how much fidelity teleportation keeps under such strain. The results matter for quantum information in curved spacetime, a field that joins gravity with quantum rules.
arxiv-2601-21060:
Zhuoyan Li and a large team of co-authors put humans and language models on the same feature-building team. Their 2026 paper studies feature engineering for tabular learning. Feature engineering turns raw columns into inputs a model can use well. Large language models are increasingly used to automate that craft. Given task details, an LLM can propose diverse transformations. Those proposals aim to enhance downstream performance.

The paper's twist is collaboration. Humans and models each bring strengths to the table. Models offer breadth and speed; humans offer judgment and context. The study examines how the pair should work together. Good features often decide whether a tabular model succeeds. This human-LLM workflow could make that step faster and better. The work serves data teams that live in spreadsheets and databases.
arxiv-2601-21160:
Michael Ibrahim, Nagi Gebraeel, and Weijun Xie study clustering when data stays split across many separate clients. No one knows in advance how many groups exist across all clients. Each client also holds its own mix, and the mixes can overlap or differ.

The authors build a shared learning method that works without pooling the raw data. It extends a classic expectation and maximization routine to the split-data setting. The method has to guess the total number of groups while it learns them. That makes it useful for settings where data must stay local, such as hospitals or banks that cannot share records.
arxiv-2601-21660:
Jingyang Zhao and Mingyu Xiao improve approximation algorithms for vehicle routing with capacity limits. In this classic problem, vans leave a depot to serve customers who each demand some load. Every van has a fixed capacity, and routes should be as short as possible.

The unsplittable version bars splitting one customer's demand across vans, which matches real practice. The authors give better guarantees on how close their routes come to optimal. Routing sits under delivery, repair, and transit services everywhere. Even small gains in the guarantee translate into large savings when the method runs at city scale every day.
arxiv-2601-21760:
Ruian Tie, Wenbo Xiong, and five co-authors downscale climate data to fine grids without any paired training examples. Supervised downscaling learns from matched coarse and fine data, which ties it to the models it trained on. New climate models break that pairing and expose domain gaps.

Zero-shot methods exist but can violate physics or lose their gradient signal at large scale factors. The authors use diffusion posterior sampling to stay both physical and stable. Fine local detail is what impact studies need, from flood risk to heat planning. A method that transfers across climate models saves retraining for every new release.
arxiv-2601-21960:
Aref Farhadipour and a large team lay out the rules for a shared contest in speaker verification. Systems that confirm a speaker's identity degrade badly when the language changes between enrollment and testing. The field's reliance on English-centered data makes that weakness worse.

The TidyVoice 2026 Challenge, described in this evaluation plan, is designed to confront the language mismatch problem head-on. The plan spells out how systems will be tested so results can be compared fairly. Challenges like this matter because voice verification guards bank accounts and devices worldwide. And a system that fails on non-English speakers fails a large part of the world.
arxiv-2601-22260:
Tom Gajecki, Jonas Althoff, and Waldo Nogueira work on a clear need: help cochlear implant users pick out one voice in noise. Their 2026 preprint uses brain wave cues to learn which speaker the user wants to hear. An implant turns sound into small electric pulses for the ear.

Their network joins the mixed sound with the brain wave cues in one light step. It then builds a pulse pattern for the wanted voice alone. The method also solves a mix-up that pure sound tools face. It points to implants that track the mind, not just the ear.
arxiv-2601-22360:
B. J. P. Jones works out how light hydrogen atoms bounce off helium at near-freezing cold. His 2026 preprint covers all three forms of hydrogen: plain, heavy, and the rare radioactive form. Both light forms of helium serve as targets.

The rates span a vast range, from near absolute zero up to room heat. The work is driven by a real need: sources of cold tritium for tests of the neutrino's mass. At such cold, each bounce can shift the atoms' paths and spins. Firm rates help teams design those sources with care.
arxiv-2601-22660:
Evan Gibson Smith and Bashima Islam train deep binary networks by freezing layers in stages, with no gradient shortcut. Binary networks use one-bit weights and activations, which makes them tiny and fast. Their 2026 preprint tests progressive freezing in place of the straight-through estimator, the usual trick that fakes a gradient.

Plain global freezing works for binary weights, they find, but fails for full binary nets. Blocked gradients through activations are the cause. The find maps where the trick can and cannot go. Tiny nets matter for phones and sensors. Honest limits guide the design.
arxiv-2601-23060:
Luo-Jia Kang builds a complete operator basis for the Standard Model Effective Field Theory with modular flavor symmetry. The effective theory extends the Standard Model with higher-dimensional operators that capture unknown heavy physics. Modular symmetries organize the flavor patterns of quarks and leptons.

The setup uses two copies of an A4 flavor group, one for quarks and one for leptons, with separate moduli. Right-handed quarks carry the simplest modular weights. A complete basis tells model builders exactly which operators the symmetry allows. Distinct moduli for the quark and lepton sectors let the symmetry treat the two flavor puzzles separately.
arxiv-2603-01360:
Gong Chen and Yingmo Zhang study long waves with a strong nonlinear term in this 2026 math work. Their equation, a quintic form of the Benjamin-Bona-Mahony model, tracks how such waves evolve over time. The main question is whether small, smooth waves settle down and act like simple linear waves in the long run.

Using a space-time resonance method, they prove that small smooth solutions do scatter to the linear flow. The strong term makes some parts of the proof easier than in a weaker quartic case. Other parts grow harder, since key patterns that held before fail at some resonance points. Careful estimates near those points close the proof, which adds a firm case to the study of wave decay.
arxiv-2603-02060:
Stefano Burrello, Carmelo Piazza, Rui Wang, and Maria Colonna test the stability of warm, dilute nuclear matter with light clusters present. Their 2026 work uses a generalized mean-field framework at finite temperature and symmetric isospin. Clusters like light nuclei count as degrees of freedom beside single nucleons here.

Free-energy curvature decides where the matter turns mechanically unstable, the spinodal region. An infrared momentum cutoff models Pauli blocking, which thins low-momentum states inside the medium. When that cutoff depends on density, thermodynamic consistency forces extra terms in chemical potentials and hydrodynamics. Those terms shift the spinodal boundary and reshape the unstable modes themselves. With a stiff enough cutoff, clusters can fluctuate out of phase with nucleons, a reversal of the pattern found when medium effects are ignored.
arxiv-2603-02260:
Ethan Chu, Yiyang Guo, and Jan Hoffmann extend automatic cost analysis to programs that jump around in this 2026 paper. Many tools can read code and derive bounds on time or memory use. They struggle when control jumps far, as with exceptions or effect handlers. A handler can catch a thrown effect from deep inside a program.

Their analysis is the first to bound costs across such jumps. It extends a type-based method built on amortized analysis, where costs are prepaid by data. New type rules cover exceptions and handlers, and a soundness proof checks them against a stack machine. Tests show the method handles programs older tools cannot. Overhead from supporting handlers stays low in their trials.
arxiv-2603-02360:
Edsel Peña, Dip Das, and Yuexuan Wu use tennis scoring to teach probability in this 2026 paper. Tennis has a nested scoring system of points, games, tiebreaks, sets, and matches. Their simple model gives each player a fixed chance to win each service point. Points are treated as independent across the whole match.

From those serve chances, they derive win chances at every level of the system. Big problems split into small ones, then recombine into full answers. The method showcases total probability and iterated rules for means and spreads. Fun questions include whether matches surely end and whether serving first helps equal players. Scoring systems act as decision tools that can crown the weaker player. The paper compares systems on that error risk as well.
arxiv-2603-02460:
Gabriel Melo, Thibaut de Saivre, Anna Calissano, and Florence d'Alché-Buc add error bounds to graph prediction in this 2026 paper. Some tasks output whole graphs, not single numbers. Honest error ranges for such outputs have been scarce. Their method gives coverage promises that need no assumptions about the data spread.

A distance between graphs anchors the method's mismatch score. That distance compares graphs no matter how their nodes are ordered. A quantile method then adapts the prediction set to each input's difficulty. Graphs are kept or dropped by their distance to the predicted one. The authors test the approach on a synthetic task. Such promises for structured outputs could matter wherever graph forecasts guide real choices.
arxiv-2603-02860:
Fermín Moscoso del Prado Martín and Suchir Salhan explain the pattern of sound frequencies across the world's languages. Every language uses its phonemes, its basic speech sounds, at uneven rates. Their 2026 paper models that uneven spread at two scales, using information theory.

At the large scale, rank-frequency curves match a simple random model whose single setting grows steadily with the size of a language's sound inventory. Larger inventories show lower relative entropy, a balancing effect the model captures. At the small scale, a maximum-entropy model using articulation, sound-combination, and word-structure rules predicts each language's exact sound rates well. Together the two views give one account of a pattern found in every spoken language.
arxiv-2603-02960:
Nahema Marchal, Stephanie Chan, Matija Franklin, and colleagues argue that AI systems have become knowledge agents and must be governed as such. Large language models now curate what people read, answer specialized questions, and shape shared knowledge. Their 2026 paper warns that badly calibrated agents could dull human skills and slowly drift public knowledge off course.

The authors propose a trust framework with three parts: build agents that are genuinely trustworthy, align them with human knowledge goals, and strengthen the surrounding knowledge infrastructure. Trustworthy agents should show competence, openness to being proven wrong, and honest habits, backed by provenance tracking and protected knowledge sanctuaries. The roadmap aims at a human-AI ecosystem where machine help sharpens, rather than replaces, collective judgment.
arxiv-2603-03260:
Wanqi Liu and Rong Zhao test whether a new café lifts the value of homes around it, or merely follows rising neighborhoods. Restaurants and cafés visibly mark gentrification, but cause and effect are tangled. Their 2026 study exploits the staggered timing of over twenty-one thousand openings across nearly five thousand small London areas.

An event study with area-specific trends, which passes pre-trend checks, tracks prices around each opening. Prices rose steadily afterward, reaching about four percent higher after four years. Matching openings to price-tier data shows the effect comes from upmarket arrivals, not budget ones, whose patterns look unreliable. The quality of commercial clustering, not its mere presence, drives the neighborhood premium.
arxiv-2603-03660:
Hai-Long Zhen and three colleagues ask how a quantum-gravity correction would repaint a black hole's portrait. The extended uncertainty principle modifies quantum mechanics at large scales. Their 2026 paper first builds an explicit bridge between that principle and spacetime geometry. It converts the principle's modified temperature function into a modified metric for the Schwarzschild black hole, then derives its thermodynamics from that metric.

One quantity refuses to move: the event horizon sits exactly where Einstein put it. The photon sphere, where light orbits, grows as the correction parameter rises, while the visible shadow shrinks, an optical shift with no change in the horizon itself. Comparing the predicted shadow with Event Horizon Telescope observations of the galactic center black hole, Sagittarius A-star, sets fresh constraints on how large the correction can be.
arxiv-2603-03760:
Seungha Hong and five others compress time series datasets in the frequency domain, where their rhythm lives. Forecasting trains on terabytes of sensor data, and dataset distillation, synthesizing a tiny dataset that trains like the huge one, promises relief. Generic distillation, though, overfits one architecture and scales badly on sequences. Their 2026 method, HDT, is built for time series from the start.

Each series is decomposed into sinusoidal components by the fast Fourier transform. A step called Harmonic Matching aligns the core periodic structure between the synthetic and real data. Because updates happen in the frequency domain, they apply globally across the whole series at once, never tearing the temporal dependencies that forecasting depends on. Extensive tests show strong generalization across architectures the distillation never saw, plus the scalability real deployments need.
arxiv-2603-03860:
Jiansheng Yao and Yingkui Zhao present a particle-grid simulation method for inviscid compressible flows with shocks and strong vortices. Such flows are hard for particle-grid methods because moving discontinuities, cell-crossing noise, and quadrature damage under deformation all cause trouble. Working from a combined FLIP and APIC framework with vorticity-aware artificial viscosity, the authors identify a long-time failure in Rayleigh-Taylor instability tests. Particles drain from spike heads, quadrature degrades, and nonphysical void-like dents appear.

Their fix adds conservative split resampling, which replenishes depleted cells while exactly conserving mass, momentum, and internal energy. It also adds a soft switch that weakens only the affine part of the update where particle support is thin. Tests on the Sod shock tube and Rayleigh-Taylor cases remove the voids while preserving vortex roll-up and matching reference growth measures.
arxiv-2605-00560:
V Venktesh, Mandeep Rathee, and Avishek Anand argue that in modern search, the costly problem is not inventing extra versions of a query but choosing among them. Reformulating a query many ways can raise recall sharply. Yet merging and reranking everything is prohibitively expensive, and stray reformulations drag results off topic, a failure called query drift. Their framework, ReformIR, is built around a strict inference budget.

ReformIR treats each reformulation as a first-class feature and builds one large candidate pool from all of them. A light surrogate model, taught online by a strong reranker, estimates each document's utility from reformulation-specific signals. Under the budget, the system spends teacher reranking where it pays most, anchored to the original query to suppress drift. On standard passage and deep-learning benchmarks it beat existing reformulation strategies, with the gap growing as reformulations multiply and rivals degrade.
arxiv-2605-00660:
SangHyun Park proves that a directed seven-dimensional torus, a grid of points on a seven-dimensional doughnut with wraparound edges, can be decomposed into directed Hamiltonian cycles for every odd side length. A Hamilton decomposition splits all the directed edges into cycles that each visit every vertex exactly once. Such decompositions are prized in network design, giving balanced routing patterns.

Park's proof has two engines. The first is a root-flat certificate: three local conditions on one flat slice, Latinness of rows, bijectivity between layers, and primitivity of return maps, which together guarantee a full decomposition. The second is a uniform construction for all larger odd moduli, using prefix coordinates and explicit count matrices to produce all seven Hamiltonian factors with no search. The two smallest moduli defeat that construction provably, so they are settled by finite certificates checked in the Lean proof assistant, inside one formal development.
arxiv-2605-00960:
Chirag Shinde introduces energy-based constraint networks, an architecture that learns structural coherence across modalities and assigns it a scalar energy. Frozen encoder embeddings pass through a state-space model with dual-head attention, producing one energy for overall consistency and per-position scores that localize violations. Independently trained branches detect different violation types and can be combined at inference without interference.

In text, the system scores well on both trained and unseen corruption types using a frozen BERT encoder. In vision, the same design gives strong deepfake detection without training data from one test set. Changing domain requires only new corruption strategies. Changing encoder requires only a new input layer, which supports flexible reuse.
arxiv-2605-01160:
Sabry E. Farrag argues that AI coding assistants create a Productivity-Reliability Paradox in software development. Trials report large output gains on well-scoped tasks, while a careful randomized trial records a slowdown for experienced coders. Large telemetry shows many more pull requests but much longer review times with flat delivery. Farrag defines the paradox in formal terms through a multivocal review of dozens of sources.

Three moderating variables and two amplifying mechanisms structure it. A scheme sorts six methodologies under three AI adoption tiers, and a Specification Governance Model grounded in transaction cost economics offers a practical decision guide. Two tools are tested as model examples in a four-month pilot. Specification discipline, not model capability, is named the binding constraint.
arxiv-2605-01260:
Xin Liang and six co-authors survey write-read decoupling in modern large-scale search engines. Frequent index updates keep results fresh, yet in the dominant Lucene-based architecture, segment merges triggered by writes compete with queries for CPU, disk, and cache, inflating latency. The survey systematically examines architectural solutions developed across industry and academia to separate write pressure from read latency.

Five principal patterns are identified, from node-level separation and compute-storage separation to full in-memory indexing, log-structured write paths, and in-place partial updates. Representative systems from major companies are surveyed. An emerging synthesis architecture combines several patterns with per-field update routing, sending simple fields through fast in-place updates while full-text fields follow a segment path. Open challenges include hybrid retrieval and serverless deployment.
arxiv-2605-01760:
Sebastian M Cioabă, Lele Liu, and Yi Wang close a conjecture about how a graph's Laplacian spectrum can shift when edges change. The Laplacian matching roots of a graph blend two spectra. Earlier work had defined the integral variation of those roots and shown a one-place change to be impossible. The two-place case was ruled out only for graphs whose cycles are sparse relative to their girth.

Wang, Cui, and Cioabă had conjectured the two-place variation never happens in any connected graph. This paper confirms that conjecture in full. The proof joins a structural relation from the earlier work to two new power-sum identities for Laplacian matching roots. Results of this stamp matter because spectral fingerprints are used to tell graphs apart and to certify network traits; knowing which variations cannot occur tightens every argument built on them.
arxiv-2605-01960:
Pranay Mundra, Adam Sealfon, Ziteng Sun, and Quanquan Liu consider answering database queries privately when the queries arrive as a stream. Real workloads are predictable, with recurring jobs and templates, even if their order is unknown. The authors ask whether predictions about future queries can improve accuracy under one shared privacy budget, without failing badly when predictions are wrong.

Their system, LAPRAS, uses a predicted query set to guide spending. Predicted queries get the best offline method, while the rest are answered online from what budget remains. A smooth allocation rule paces spending across an unknown number of surprise queries. The design aims to gain from good forecasts while staying robust to bad ones.
arxiv-2605-02060:
Maksim Kazanskii extends stochastic neighbor embedding, a method that maps high-dimensional data to a low-dimensional picture while keeping neighbours close. Such maps can badly distort how dense points are in a local area. Kazanskii adds a regulariser that aligns a profile of local concentration, based on inverse neighbourhood scale, between the source and the map.

The new method, DR-SNE, keeps that relative concentration while staying unchanged under global rescaling of the map. Across real and synthetic data, it generally improved concentration preservation with controlled loss of neighbourhood fidelity. Tests show a steady trade-off as the regulariser grows stronger. The work suits cases where local density itself carries meaning.
arxiv-2605-02160:
Xueyin Wang proves a continuity result for the Lyapunov exponent of quasi-periodic cocycles in a Gevrey class. The Lyapunov exponent measures the average growth rate of products of matrices that vary in a quasi-periodic way. Whether that rate varies continuously with the system is a basic question, and Gevrey regularity, which sits between smooth and analytic, sets the setting here.

Wang works with frequencies in a subexponential Brjuno class. Under a numeric condition linking the Gevrey index and the frequency parameter, the sum of the two lying between one and two, the Lyapunov exponent is continuous. The note is short and states the result with its precise assumptions, adding a case to the known continuity theory.
arxiv-2605-02660:
Dasari Naga Raju tests whether biological knowledge about tumor geography can help a model read a genetic trait from routine cancer slides. The trait is microsatellite instability in colorectal cancer, normally found by molecular testing. Models that read stained slide images often fail at a new hospital, because slides carry site-specific texture along with real biology.

Raju builds priors from known patterns: immune reaction at the tumor's invasive edge, and the local ratio of immune cells to tumor cells near each tile. These priors enter a transformer aggregator before attention, over features from large foundation models. Six reference combinations of model and aggregator set the baseline. The study asks whether steering features toward known biology yields signs that travel better across sites.
arxiv-2605-02860:
Mohamad Khajezade, Fatemeh H. Fard, and Mohamed Sami Shehata distill a large reasoning model into small open models that can detect code clones across programming languages. Equivalent programs in different languages often look nothing alike, so surface matching fails. Large models reason well about such pairs, but black-box use raises cost, privacy, and format problems, and small models often fumble reasoning-style prompts.

Training pairs come from a public multilingual code archive, with reasoning-style synthetic data built for teaching. Two compact students are fine-tuned with low-rank adapters. Stabilization tricks include forced-conclusion prompts and added classification heads that map output cleanly to a clone verdict. Across several language pairs, distillation consistently helped, and both raw accuracy and response reliability were tracked.
arxiv-2605-03060:
Andrea Panarotto, Riccardo De Santis, and Livio Finos build confidence intervals for generalized linear models that stay valid when the variance model is wrong. Standard intervals trust the mean-variance link, yet excess spread and uneven variability in biomedical data often break that trust and shrink coverage.

Their method flips the signs of single score parts to form tests, then inverts them with a bisection search to find interval bounds. Theory gives broad validity, and simulations show reliable coverage where Wald intervals fail. An RNA sequencing cancer study shows the method at work.
arxiv-2605-03160:
Michael A. Riegler and Birk Sebastian Frostelid Torpmann-Hagen warn that labeling sparse autoencoder features from top contexts alone can misname what a feature does. Standard checks steer one feature at one strength, which samples just one cell of a wider steering grid.

On three instruction-tuned models, features labeled as AI self-disclaimers switched voice form under steering, so the label named a regime, not a causal axis. Three near-orthogonal features proved jointly needed for grounded work, and matched random controls showed the damage came from direction, not size. The study urges grid-wide checks before trusting feature labels.
arxiv-2605-03260:
Shugen Song, Wenjie Mei, and Chengyan Zhao improve path tracking for vehicles by pairing sampling-based predictive control with continuous-time residual learning. The Model Predictive Path Integral method is strong for nonlinear systems, but its results hinge on how accurate the built-in dynamics model is.

Their ICODE-MPPI framework learns the missing dynamics with neural ordinary differential equations that respect time continuity across the prediction window. In high-fidelity simulations on complex paths, tracking error under steady disturbances fell by up to about two thirds versus standard control. Steering also grew smoother, with far less chattering in the commands.
arxiv-2605-03560:
Zijiang Yang shows that free-text medical notes carry strong signal for predicting death after hospital discharge, despite their messy, repetitive quality. Electronic health records hold vast unstructured notes that many models ignore in favor of clean coded fields.

Across prediction windows from fifteen days to a year, models using note information scored well above those without it. A deep network with a pooling mechanism that learns from the most informative notes beat traditional tree-based models by clear margins at every horizon. The models also surface keyword and document patterns linked to patient severity, consistent with prior clinical findings.
arxiv-2605-04660:
Xiaoteng Zhang and three co-authors present a high-order numerical scheme for simulating compressible fluid flow in two dimensions in a Lagrangian frame, where the computational mesh moves with the fluid. Accurate, robust schemes of this kind underpin simulations of shocks and extreme flows.

Their method combines a multi-moment finite volume approach, which evolves both point values at cell corners and cell averages to guarantee conservation, with a new two-dimensional nodal Riemann solver. The solver's fresh jump and balance conditions connect surface pressures to mesh motion in a way that stays compatible with the numerical fluxes. The result keeps third-order accuracy while inheriting the nodal solver's robustness.

The 2026 paper offers a new route to learning from distributed data that never leaves home.
arxiv-2605-08860: Constantino Tsallis's nonadditive entropy generalizes the classic Boltzmann formula for systems with long-range quirks. Leandro Lyra Braga Dognini and Tsallis take a closer look at how constraints shape the optimization of the S_q functional — which distributions maximize it under which rules. The 2026 paper is statistical-mechanics foundations.
arxiv-2605-08960: Designing new crystals atom by atom is a creative-mapping dream, but the models need bodily common sense. Chengqian Zhang, Yucheng Jin, Duo Zhang, and others transfer bodily priors from universal machine-learned interatomic potentials into crystal creative models with CrystalREPA. The 2026 paper grounds crystal making in real physics.
arxiv-2605-09060: Pointing at the thing a sentence describes — visual grounding — mostly works in English. J. de Curtò, Mauro Liz, and I. de Zarzà extend it with multilingual CLIP, grounding descriptions written in many languages. The 2026 paper brings visual grounding to the world's tongues.
arxiv-2605-09460: Generating images that preserve a person's identity usually takes many slow spread steps, pricing out real-time use. Dongqi Zheng shows when few steps are enough, accelerating identity-preserved making without any training at all. The 2026 paper makes personalized image making fast, free, and practical.

arxiv-2606-04060:
Zhonggai Wang, Kai Fang, and Guangyu Gao present in 2026 a method for teaching image segmentation systems new classes step by step when only weak labels are available. The known failure is drift: noisy labels slowly corrupt what the model remembers, so new classes overwrite old ones.

Their system, SASA, fights drift on two fronts. Learnable anchor tokens pin down each class's identity over time, while a flexible adjustment layer still lets the model adapt to each image. A spatial arbitration rule then filters unreliable label signals and enforces one class per object. Across standard benchmarks, the method beat prior approaches, with the clearest gains in long, multi-step learning sequences where drift usually hurts most.
arxiv-2606-04160:
Anna Marbut, Travis Wheeler, and Daniel Olson dissect in 2026 how refusal behavior, the trained habit of declining harmful requests, is distributed inside mixture-of-experts language models. In these models, each input is routed to a few specialized sub-networks called experts.

A steering vector can suppress refusal in ordinary dense models; the team extended the technique to three open mixture-of-experts systems. Steering worked just as well despite the routing complexity. A single expert, free to choose its location, recovered over three quarters of the full steering effect on average, but barely half when forced to the location full-layer steering uses. The refusal signals also differed from the signals that drive routing. Refusal, they conclude, is spread unevenly rather than run by one switch.
arxiv-2606-04260:
Šimon Schierreich and Ildikó Schlotter study in 2026 the majority illusion, a social network trap where a minority opinion looks dominant because the minority happens to hold the best-connected seats. Agents then misread their community and may act on the false picture.

Their question is detection: given a network, can some labeling of opinions produce the illusion for a chosen fraction of agents? They map how the network's structural properties move this decision problem between tractable and intractable. The result is a detailed complexity map for the parameterized problem, showing which structural restrictions make detection efficient and which leave it hard. Such maps matter because a platform that cannot even detect an illusion-prone network cannot hope to correct one.
arxiv-2606-04560:
Yoo and colleagues recycle the practice runs that reinforcement learning usually throws away, in a 2026 arXiv paper on training reasoning models. GRPO is a standard method for post-training with verifiable rewards. It uses each rollout for one gradient update and discards it. That is sample inefficient. Naive replay fails because the policy drifts quickly. Stored rollouts go stale and destabilize training. Their buffer stores and samples individual rollouts rather than whole groups. It adds safeguards against staleness.

Rollouts older than a fixed age are evicted. Each training batch anchors on fresh on-policy rollouts. It then adds replayed ones, prioritized by the size of each rollout's advantage. The team tested three Qwen3-Base scales on five math benchmarks. The method beat GRPO and naive replay baselines. Gains appeared at every scale and grew with model size. The largest gain was 4.35 percentage points on the five-benchmark average at 4B.
arxiv-2606-04960:
Chen and Jin prove that a charged gas in a bounded container settles into a unique steady state and returns to it after small disturbances, in a 2026 arXiv analysis paper. The Vlasov-Poisson-Boltzmann system couples particle transport, a self-consistent electric field, and Boltzmann collisions. For the stationary problem in a bounded convex domain, they construct a unique stationary solution. The key difficulty is regularity, because the electric field and collision operator are coupled.

They overcome it with a bootstrap framework. For the dynamical system near the stationary solution, they prove global existence and uniqueness for small perturbations, plus exponential convergence back to the steady state.
arxiv-2606-05060:
Genyue Liu and colleagues demonstrate high-fidelity neutral atom gates calibrated by low-rank Hessian optimization in this 2026 arXiv paper. Quantum optimal control can design fast, robust multi-qubit gates, but the resulting high-dimensional waveforms are hard to calibrate in the lab because direct searches converge slowly. The team exploits the low-rank structure of quantum control landscapes, where only a few waveform directions strongly affect fidelity.

Their method finds those sensitive directions, whose number is set by the accessible leakage and error channels, and optimizes only within that small space using closed-loop experimental feedback. Applied to an amplitude-robust controlled-Z gate on metastable ytterbium-171 nuclear-spin qubits, the optimized gate reached a raw fidelity of 0.9959, rising to 0.99902 after postselection on no detected loss, and performance barely changed under laser-power swings of up to 20 percent. The same directions could also correct certain Hamiltonian parameter errors.
arxiv-2606-05360:
Dmitrii Kolotkov, Sergey Belov, and Mohamed Sherif hunt for observable fingerprints of the entropy mode in the solar corona in this 2026 arXiv paper. Magnetohydrodynamic waves in coronal loops are prized seismological tools, and the fast and slow magnetoacoustic modes are exploited. The entropy mode, the third eigenmode of the system, has stayed inaccessible because it neither propagates nor oscillates.

Working in the corona's non-adiabatic conditions, where the entropy mode couples closely to the compressive slow mode, the authors model a one-dimensional coronal loop. The entropy mode decays faster than the slow mode, and that superposition of two exponential decays leaves distinct marks. The marks are a non-exponential damping profile during the first oscillation cycles, and an asymmetry between the upper and lower envelopes of the temperature and density swings. There are also deviations from the canonical quarter-period phase shift between temperature and velocity perturbations.
arxiv-2606-05460:
Lavsen Dahal and colleagues present ORACLE-CT in this 2026 arXiv paper, an anatomy-aware method for classifying diseases in abdominal CT scans. Most classifiers pool features from the whole volume. That lets evidence for a liver label leak in from anywhere and breaks the link between a prediction and its basis.

ORACLE-CT uses multi-organ segmentation to define an anatomical support for each label, the region where evidence for that disease may live, and restricts attention pooling to it. The framework is encoder-agnostic and was tested with three representation families: a vision transformer, a 3D convolutional network, and a radiology foundation encoder. It was trained on one dataset and checked on two external ones. Support-masked pooling improved discrimination on the benchmark and transferred better externally. It lifted one encoder's external scores on both test sets, while keeping every prediction traceable to its evidence.
arxiv-2606-05560:
Takuo Matsubara and co-authors extend a classic forecasting tool to streams of distributions in a 2026 arXiv paper. Exponential smoothing blends past values with fading weights and often beats fancier forecast tools. It was built for plain numbers, though. Some modern series record a whole distribution at each step, like the spread of returns within an hour. The team rebuilds smoothing inside Wasserstein space, where distance measures how much mass must move to turn one distribution into another.

The generalized method keeps the old tool's prized simplicity, with a single smoothing parameter. The authors show that parameter can be estimated consistently by minimizing a Wasserstein distance to the data. Theory backs the claim, and practice confirms it. Tests on high-frequency financial returns and household electricity demand showed the method works well. The paper gives distribution-valued series a forecaster as light as the classic one.
arxiv-2606-05860:
Poikarayil and colleagues let a language model design time-series networks on demand in a 2026 arXiv paper. Forecasting and anomaly detection models are usually hand-built per dataset. Classic AutoML searches fixed menus that fit varied data poorly. GenAutoML turns user requirements in plain words into runnable PyTorch code. A sandboxed loop runs the code, reads the errors, and repairs it alone.

A signature-aware runtime keeps generated models within promised shapes. A normalization wrapper guards against drifting, non-stationary inputs. Tests on transformer temperature and weather datasets showed the agent inventing fresh layouts per dataset. One generated model, WaveInterferenceNet, answered in under a hundredth of a millisecond per sample. That latency set a state-of-the-art mark while giant foundation models lagged on speed. The framework trades their brute accuracy for tailored, deployable speed. Industrial monitoring, where milliseconds matter, is the stated target.
arxiv-2606-06460:
Thamilvendhan Munirathinam proposes a polite way to bar AI agents from servers in this 2026 arXiv paper. Autonomous agents now hold real credentials and run infrastructure unsupervised. Access control today is binary: the agent gets in, or it is hard blocked like any intruder. There is no standard way to say this resource is off limits to agents, please leave. His Recuse Signal is that message, sent through channels the protocol already has.

He defines the signal as an open mini standard and built adapters for SSH banners, a PostgreSQL proxy, and a Kubernetes webhook, deployed on a live host. Fresh agents given a benign task were then watched. In the SSH pilot with GPT 4o models and Claude Code, the signal produced one hundred percent recusal, against full task completion with no signal. It stayed a cooperative signal, though: an explicit operator authorization framing flipped the strongest model to proceed.
arxiv-2606-06660:
Long robot tasks often fail slowly, with one bad move making the next ones worse. Chen proposes a safety switch for that problem in this 2026 arXiv paper. The system, called AEGIS, watches the inner signals of a working robot policy, the rules the robot uses to pick actions. A cheap probe reads those signals and warns that failure is likely soon.

When the probe flags a risky step, control passes to a stronger backup policy for just those steps. On the LIBERO-Spatial test suite, AEGIS rescued about ten percent of the runs the weak policy lost, roughly double the rescue rate of blind switching at the same cost. The backup was active on only thirty eight percent of steps, and the warning probe scored well within the first third of each run, before any switch took place.
arxiv-2606-06760:
A medical AI that chats about a scan but cannot point at the problem is half useful. Aofei Chang and co-authors close that gap with MedSIGHT in this 2026 arXiv paper. Their system joins a large vision language model, which reads images and text together, to pixel level segmentation, the outlining of exact regions in an image, inside one unified design.

A new part called the Region Perceiver turns areas of the image into region tokens the language model can reason over. A medical codebook adds region codes to the model's vocabulary, so it can name a body part or a lesion as a symbol and later decode that symbol back into an outline. Training proceeds in stages so the parts align stably. Using only seventy two thousand instruction examples, MedSIGHT reached state of the art results on medical question answering and segmentation across many imaging types.
arxiv-2606-07360:
Bayard solves a geometric boundary-value problem inside anti-de Sitter space in this 2026 arXiv paper. Anti-de Sitter space is a universe with constant negative curvature, central to geometry and theoretical physics. The question concerns spacelike hypersurfaces, slices that behave like space at an instant, whose scalar curvature is prescribed. The Dirichlet problem asks whether a surface exists matching the value and boundary data, expressed through a nonlinear equation.

Bayard proves the problem has a solution when the data are convex. That convexity condition, requiring boundary and target data to bend outward together, gives the estimates needed to control the equation. The result adds to the theory of prescribed-curvature problems, which extend classical questions about which shapes can realize a given function. Such problems connect differential geometry with the study of initial data in general relativity, where spacelike slices with controlled shape model space at a moment.
arxiv-2606-07560:
Wang shows that attention heads in language models contain two opposing factions, in this 2026 arXiv paper. Function-vector heads are the parts credited with carrying out rules learned from examples, and researchers identify them by their causal contribution, treating the set as one class. Using a sign-preserving attribution method, Wang finds the population splits. Writers push the correct answer's score up, while cancellers push it down, and removing both shifts the output less than either group alone would suggest.

The split proved causal and reproducible across model-task pairs spanning 3 architectures and 6 model sizes. A shuffled null test rejected the single-class story. Size-only ranking cannot see the split, so function vectors average a promoter with a suppressor. Ablating the cancellers improved the correct label's score in every test cell and raised accuracy. Cancellers matched none of the head types, making them a characterized mechanism.
arxiv-2606-07760:
Andersson and a large team introduce scCBGM, a generative model that edits single cells in ways biologists can read and steer, in this 2026 arXiv paper. Single-cell RNA sequencing profiles each cell's active genes, but the space of drug and genetic perturbations is too large to test exhaustively. A useful model must predict how a cell would look under untried conditions, and explain itself in named concepts.

The design routes generation through a concept bottleneck, a layer of interpretable concepts, with skip connections and a penalty that keeps the concepts disentangled. A flow-matching version extends the idea from editing measured cells to generating new ones. To judge counterfactual edits fairly, the team built a synthetic benchmark where the true edited cells are known by construction. Across real datasets the model led in combinatorial generalisation, predicting responses to unseen condition combinations, and in counterfactual accuracy at cell and population level.
arxiv-2606-08060:
Toshiharu Harada, Tetsuo Handa, Masaki Hashimoto, and Hidehiko Tanaka present TOMOYO Linux, a security system that judges access requests by what a program has been doing, in this 2026 arXiv paper. Conventional access control looks only at the pair asking: which application, which file. It ignores the application's intent and history, so a compromised or misused program inherits its full permissions.

Their mandatory access control keys decisions to the application's execution state: the chain of programs that led to this request. A request that fits the program's history can be allowed, while the same request arriving through an abnormal path can be denied. Administrators thus reduce damage from malicious attempts and mistakes without hand-writing rules for every file. The paper covers the concept, the Linux implementation design, and a brief evaluation. It is an English translation of the authors' earlier Japanese journal paper.
arxiv-2606-08260:
Qi Liu and colleagues present a single model that both edits and generates video in this 2026 arXiv paper. Video diffusion models, which build footage by gradually removing noise, have advanced quickly, yet editing and generation usually live in separate task-specific models. A unified framework is hard because tasks feed the model different mixes of inputs: a source video, reference images, or text instructions. Earlier unified attempts needed extra encoders or could not tell these conditioning tokens apart reliably.

Their framework, TIDE, integrates instruction-based editing, reference-guided editing, and multi-reference generation in one system. Its core device is the per-token task embedding, a small learned tag attached to every input token stating which task role it plays. With each token labeled, the model can explicitly tell apart target, source, and reference material even as their number and type vary across tasks.
arxiv-2606-08360:
Lingkai Kong and colleagues tackle a planning problem in public health outreach, in this 2026 arXiv paper. Peer-referral recruitment is key for studying and reaching hidden populations hit by infectious diseases. Agencies must allocate limited referral resources adaptively across many rounds. Each round's decisions shape both how many people arrive next and who they are. Prior work simplified this by assuming recruits are drawn independently from a uniform population.

That assumption ignores homophily, the tendency of people to refer others like themselves. The authors instead condition arrivals on the observable traits of current recruits. They build a generative frontier planning approach that looks ahead under this dependence. Planning must balance reaching more people against learning the population's structure, since today's referrals determine tomorrow's pool. The method is meant for field teams that must act fast with small budgets and hard limits.
arxiv-2606-08460:
Xunye Tian and colleagues turn a statistical weakness, having very few test samples, into a strength, in this 2026 arXiv paper. Two-sample testing asks whether two samples come from the same distribution. Data-adaptive versions learn a discrepancy measure from the data itself. Such methods usually split data to keep learning separate from testing. That suits few-shot settings poorly, where imbalance is severe: abundant reference samples on one side, a handful of query samples on the other. Their method, LOTTERY, exploits the imbalance constructively.

Using the abundant reference data, the method learns representations that summarize the salient structure of the reference distribution, giving signals for detecting departures with very few query points. Families of representations capture global and local structure, weighted adaptively using only reference samples. They prove control of the type I error rate, the probability of a false alarm, plus consistency guarantees.
arxiv-2606-08760:
Alejandro Mata Ali presents software for seeing the structure of quantum and tensor-network computations, in this 2026 arXiv paper. Tensor networks and quantum circuits are structural objects whose meaning depends on connectivity and contraction order. They are easier to reason about visually than as code. Yet in Python they are commonly built through backend-specific objects, making structural mistakes hard to notice.

One package supports visual debugging and structural inspection of tensor networks and traced contraction workflows. A second provides visual-to-code authoring, generating backend code from diagrams while preserving designs as data. A third renders quantum circuits clearly for inspection and side-by-side comparison. The packages are deliberately not simulators. They sit between the researcher and the simulation libraries, catching wiring errors that numerical output cannot reveal.
arxiv-2606-08960:
Zhong and colleagues automate the arms race between cheating agents and their checkers, in this 2026 arXiv paper. Agent benchmarks grade work with outcome verifiers, programs checking whether a task was done. Hand-written verifiers are brittle, so agents reward-hack them with shortcuts like deleting failing tests. Auditing 1,968 tasks across 5 terminal-agent benchmarks, the authors found 323, or 16 percent, hackable by frontier models given the task description.

Their hacker-fixer loop sets three language-model agents against each other. A hacker tries to pass without solving the task. A fixer patches the verifier against each exploit, and a solver confirms solutions still pass. On KernelBench the loop drove attack success from 62 percent to zero on held-out exploits. Weaker defenders sufficed: a loop run by Gemini 3 Flash cut Gemini 3.1 Pro's attack success from 76 percent to zero. The team releases the 323 hackable environments as the Terminal Wrench dataset.
arxiv-2606-09160:
Thapa and Pandyea build a phone-based farming advisor for Nepal that forecasts weather, recommends crops, and answers farmers' questions, in this 2026 arXiv paper. About two-thirds of Nepal's population farms, mostly at subsistence level, and planting still rests on experience and coarse forecasts. The system predicts weather 30 days ahead for 1,359 locations using two graph neural network models, which learn from places as a graph, capturing variation across space and time.

The spatio-temporal graph convolutional model beat the transformer-based model, its mean squared error near 0.011 against 0.013. Forecasts combine with soil properties, pH, moisture, and organic content, in a scoring algorithm matching crops to their preferred conditions. A retrieval-augmented chatbot, mixing SPLADE sparse retrieval with dense vectors, answers farming questions from domain documents. The system ships as a mobile app giving real-time suggestions. User feedback confirmed its relevance in rural settings, where personalized guidance is scarce.
arxiv-2606-09760:
Dushmanta Sahu and Captain Singh study how a magnetic field can set the hottest matter in the lab spinning in this 2026 arXiv paper. The matter is quark-gluon plasma, the melted state made in heavy-ion crashes. The effect is the Einstein-de Haas effect: when spins line up in a field, the whole body turns to keep total spin balanced. It is known in solids, less so in plasma.

The pair use a quasiparticle model of the expanding fireball. The induced spin rate grows with proper time, the clock of the fireball itself. Hotter plasma damps the effect, since heat fights alignment. Near the crossover heat, where plasma turns to normal matter, the rate grows large enough to matter. Curves for strong and weak fields cross at one heat. That cross splits a spin-led regime from an inertia-led one.
arxiv-2606-09960:
Vila-Cruz and colleagues design a continual learning system for small devices, in a 2026 arXiv paper on efficient machine learning. Class-incremental learning teaches a model new categories over time without forgetting old ones. Most methods need powerful hardware and long retraining cycles. Robots and edge devices, by contrast, must adapt quickly with limited energy and memory, which motivates a lighter design.

Their system, HydraCIL, freezes the feature-extraction backbone and creates a small task-specific classifier head for each new task, avoiding costly retraining. Features are extracted once, and prototype matching, which compares inputs against stored class averages, selects the right head at prediction time. On CIFAR-100, ImageNet-100, CoRe50, and Flowers102, HydraCIL matched or beat leading class-incremental methods. It also cut training time and carbon footprint sharply, suiting embedded settings where rapid adaptation matters most.
arxiv-2606-10160:
Matsuoka and colleagues use the James Webb telescope to check whether six distant galaxies hide active black holes, in a 2026 arXiv paper on astronomy. The galaxies, at redshift near six, came from the SHELLQs survey as candidate obscured quasars: they shine brightly in narrow hydrogen emission but lack the broad lines typical of quasars. Two objects show a broad component in their Balmer lines, direct evidence of active galactic nuclei.

The remaining four show similar profiles in permitted and forbidden lines, arguing against hidden broad-line regions. Combining these with similar objects reported earlier, broad lines correlate strongly with hydrogen luminosity. The inferred active fraction exceeds seventy-seven percent above a luminosity threshold and falls below fifteen percent beneath it, figures the authors report from the combined sample. Dust corrections from the Balmer decrement would imply unrealistically high hydrogen luminosities, suggesting the emitting gas has multiple zones.
arxiv-2606-10360:
Khanh and his team present a pretrained speech model built just for Vietnamese, in a 2026 arXiv paper on speech technology. Vietnamese is under-served by speech models trained mainly on English, so they pretrain on seventeen thousand hours of unlabeled Vietnamese speech. Their model, ViP-VL, uses vector-quantization learning within a ChunkFormer design, adding acoustic stacking and receptive field matching to enable an eightfold subsampling rate that keeps processing fast.

The released model sets new state-of-the-art results across four downstream tasks in their tests: automatic speech recognition, speech emotion recognition, dialect sorting, and speaker checks. Pretraining weights and the code are released to support future Vietnamese speech research. The work shows that language-specific self-supervised pretraining, with design changes tuned for speed, can beat general multilingual models on a mid-resource language. That pattern is useful for many languages still poorly served by speech tech.

asher-henry-hudson-navigator-1860:
George M. Asher put the journals of Henry Hudson in print for the Hakluyt Society in 1860. Hudson was the English sea captain who sought a north route to Asia. The journals cover his four voyages, the last of which cost him his life.

On June 15, 1608, off Novaya Zemlya, two of his men swore they saw a mermaid. Thomas Hilles and Robert Rayner told of her hair, her tail, and her fall back in the sea. The sober log book tone makes the tale the classic Arctic mermaid report of its age.
averroes-colliget-1560:
The Colliget is the medical summa of Averroes, the Kulliyat, his book of the general rules of healing. The text here is the ninth volume of the Venice edition of 1560, in the Latin of Joannes Bruyerinus Campegius. With it stand his exposition of the Cantica of Avicenna and three shorter sections gathered by the editors.

Seven books move from anatomy and health to sickness, signs, drugs, foods, and the keeping of health. Averroes writes as both philosopher and court doctor, keen on clear rules drawn from Galen and tested by reason. No English version in the public domain exists. The Colliget was a school book of medicine across Europe for centuries.
averroes-commentaria-metaphysicam-1560:
Averroes of Córdoba spent his life explaining Aristotle, and his long commentaries on the Metaphysics are the summit of that work. The text here is the eighth volume of the Venice Aristotle of 1560, in Latin. It holds the commentaries on books one through thirteen, with his short epitome of the same work.

Averroes reads Aristotle line by line on being, substance, form, and the first cause that moves all things. His readings taught the Latin schools so deeply that they called him simply the Commentator. No English version in the public domain exists. This is the book that set the terms of debate on God and being for three centuries.
averroes-destructio-destructionum-1560:
Averroes, the great judge and philosopher of Córdoba, wrote the Tahafut al-Tahafut to answer al-Ghazali's attack on the philosophers. Its Latin name means the Destruction of the Destruction. The text here is the Venice printing of 1560, in the Latin of Calo Calonymos, with the exposition of Agostino Nifo. Two shorter works on the soul travel with it. The book is in Latin throughout.

Point by point, Averroes defends reason against the claim that philosophy breaks faith. He argues for the eternity of the world, the order of causes, and the bliss of the knowing soul. No English version in the public domain exists. The volume is the Latin West's own copy of Islam's greatest debate.

Four tomes in, the tale of Egypt's place midst the lands of the old world stands full. Wars, trade, faith, and the fall of the pharaohs fill these last parts of the main tale in rich, grave prose.

burton-lake-regions-central-africa-1860:
Richard Burton led a Royal Geographical Society expedition into East Africa in 1857 to 1859, with John Speke as his second. The Lake Regions of Central Africa, from 1860, is Burton's own account. The goal was the great lakes and the source of the Nile.

Burton reached Lake Tanganyika, while Speke, traveling apart, found Lake Victoria and claimed the prize. Fever, desertion, and quarrels plague the march from the coast. Burton's eye for peoples, tongues, and trade is unmatched, even when his temper shows. The feud born on this trip shaped African exploration for a decade. His appendices on trade goods and routes served later travelers well.
childrey-britannia-baconica-1660:
Joshua Childrey was a Hampshire clergyman and naturalist whose Britannia Baconica appeared in 1660. The book catalogs the natural rarities of England, Scotland, and Wales, county by county. Its title honors Bacon, whose call for a natural history of wonders Childrey took up.

Giants' bones, strange springs, fiery exhalations, monstrous births, and echoes in old churches fill his lists with Baconian care. He records what local people reported, sorting the credible prodigies from tales he cannot credit. The book is the Restoration catalogue of prodigies and wonders, a snapshot of a land still marvelous to its own scholars.
