Xinni Lin, Fernando Antoneli, and Yangyang Wang present a 2026 mathematical methods study automating the classification of homeostasis in biological networks. Homeostasis means keeping an output nearly constant despite outside disturbances. In network models, rare points where the output stops changing can be identified from network structure alone using advanced graph theory. Doing that by hand becomes impractical as networks grow, and the concepts involved are hard for biologists to use.

The team built a Python algorithm that takes only a network's connections and its input and output nodes. It finds the relevant structures and lists all homeostatic mechanisms automatically. They demonstrate it on small and large networks, with single and multiple inputs, and cases where input and output coincide. An extension lets the method handle several input nodes by converting them into one combined input.
pmc-13260960:
Sari H Goossens and colleagues present a 2026 cross-sectional study asking whether a concise symptom history can separate two rare causes of exercise leg pain in young people. One is functional popliteal artery entrapment, where an artery behind the knee is squeezed. The other is deep posterior chronic exertional compartment syndrome, where pressure builds in a leg compartment. Both cause pain, tightness, and cramps, and neither has a gold-standard test, so diagnosis is often delayed.

Data came from sixty-nine successfully treated patients, twenty-four with the artery condition and forty-five with the compartment condition. Pain, cramp, and weakness scores did not differ between groups. High foot tingling scores, at rest and during exercise, were associated with the artery condition. High tightness scores at rest pointed toward the compartment condition. The authors say these symptom clues can aid diagnosis.
pmc-13261560: Corey Ratcliffe and co-authors publish a 2026 correction to their paper on machine learning reconstruction of 2D MRI for gauging brain shape in epilepsy. A review of stored data showed the patient subgroup labels were assigned wrongly early in the study. The group called drug-resistant idiopathic generalized epilepsy was in fact 42 people with drug-resistant focal epilepsy. The drug-sensitive group was 31 people with idiopathic generalized epilepsy, 11 of them drug-sensitive. Revised tables and a renamed figure are given.
pmc-13262560:
Boon Tat Yeap and colleagues survey how lockdown life treated university staff on Borneo. Malaysia's Movement Control Order forced academics and support staff into remote work almost overnight. Their cross-sectional study collected four hundred twenty-seven responses during the order's first phase.

A standard questionnaire scored physical, psychological, social, and environmental quality of life. Scores spread widest on the environmental side, covering money, safety, and home conditions. Gender made no difference, but education, years employed, marriage, and family income all shifted results. Better-educated and longer-serving staff coped measurably better, pointing to where support should aim in future disruptions.
pmc-13263160:
Omar Lopez and colleagues present a difficult case of lung disease returning after transplant in a 2026 case report. The disease, pulmonary alveolar proteinosis, fills the air sacs with fatty protein material because cleaning cells fail. A 73-year-old man developed it again more than three years after receiving two new lungs, but early tests were puzzling.

Scans showed a patchy pattern typical of the disease, and antibody tests were positive, yet washings and biopsies first came back negative. Three infections at the same time mimicked the relapse and breathing measures shifted oddly. A later washing found the telltale material. Inhaled treatment plus two whole-lung washings cleared the scans largely and eased symptoms, with partial breathing recovery.
pmc-13263760:
Tan Van Nguyen and colleagues explore whether frailty hits older Vietnamese women and men with diabetes differently. Six hundred forty-four clinic patients aged sixty and up were graded by Fried's frailty criteria across two hospitals. Their 2026 observational study then tracks six months of hospitalizations.

Three in ten participants qualified as frail, with women modestly ahead of men. Frailty raised hospitalization risk in both sexes, but the link ran stronger in women. The authors read this as grounds for sex-aware diabetes care in aging patients. Screening grandmothers and grandfathers by the same cutoffs may miss unequal danger, they suggest.
pmc-13264860:
Jose Arturo Pineda and a large team wrote a 2026 study protocol for the EIDAR study, which tests ultrasound as an early warning for swallowing problems in intensive care patients. Swallowing faults after a breathing tube comes out can cause lung infection and death. The best checks need the tube out, so a bedside scan before removal could flag risk sooner.

The study will enroll 100 adults at Dijon University Hospital who were on a ventilator for at least 48 hours. Within three hours before tube removal, staff will scan the neck to measure tongue and throat muscle size and lift. A scope check after removal, read by a blinded specialist, gives the true result. The team will judge how well the scan sorts patients and how feasible it is in the unit.
pmc-13268260:
Marina B Wasilewski and colleagues present a 2026 interview study of a hybrid stroke rehabilitation program in Toronto. The program mixes in-person and video sessions for outpatients, aiming to deliver therapy doses that clinics rarely sustain. The team interviewed 14 health care providers who deliver it, framing questions with an implementation science model.

Four themes emerged. Providers valued the model's flexibility. Fit with patient needs and resources mattered greatly. Hospital resources and infrastructure shaped what was possible. And confidence in video care varied widely between providers. The authors conclude that fixing virtual care processes and resources could protect access and quality. Providers wanted video care kept as a permanent part of stroke rehabilitation, with its drawbacks actively managed.
pmc-13268360:
Lucas Alves da Mota Santana and colleagues wrote a 2026 letter alerting readers to a new bat coronavirus in South America. The virus, found in a Neotropical bat species, carries a furin cleavage site, a molecular notch that helps viruses enter cells more easily. That feature was once thought limited to Old World bat virus lines.

The letter reviews why the notch matters: it boosts cell entry and spread in related viruses, and removing it weakens them in lab animals. Over 180 bat coronaviruses were already known across the Americas, none with this feature. The authors link the find to habitat damage, which stresses bats and raises shedding. They call for a One Health system joining human testing, virus genome tracking, and animal ecology before spillover, not after.
pmc-13269960:
Wei Wu, Yi Zuo, and Jing Jin published a case report in 2026 on prenatal diagnosis in a Chinese family. Their unborn child carried a small missing piece of chromosome 16, at a site called 16q24.3. Such deletions are rarely reported, so counselors have little guidance when screening finds one. The report sets out the family's diagnostic workup.

Standard chromosome techniques have limited sensitivity for tiny missing or extra pieces. The authors argue that combining ultrasound, standard chromosome testing, and a high-resolution microarray scan raises diagnostic accuracy. Genetic counseling runs through each step, helping the family interpret an uncertain finding. The case is presented as a model for handling similar rare prenatal results.
pmc-13270760:
Chi Mei Sun led a 2026 journal article using Bayesian fine-mapping, a statistical method for narrowing down gene regions, to find candidate genes for production traits in chickens. Birds came from a backcross between a White Layer line and Araucana chickens, and traits covered egg number, egg weight, and body weight.

Genome-wide scans found many regions tied to body weight and egg weight, which were strongly heritable, while egg number looked more spread across many genes. Shared regions on chromosomes 1 and 4 affected both weight traits. The fine-mapping pointed to known growth genes such as NCAPG, LCORL, and IGF2BP1, and also flagged new candidates for egg number.
pmc-13270860:
Radhika Narla led a 2026 survey study of the first year of preference signalling in internal medicine subspecialty fellowship hiring in the United States. Signalling lets applicants mark programmes they especially want, adding a new factor for applicants, mentors, and programmes in the 2025-2026 cycle.

The authors surveyed programme directors in five subspecialties at three West Coast academic centres, and 11 of 15 replied. Ten of the 11 agreed signalling helped spot applicants with genuine interest and sped interview selection, but it did not cut overall review work. Directors struggled most with reading a missing signal and deciding how much weight a signal should carry.
pmc-13271060:
Guanling Chen is lead author of a 2026 pan-cancer analysis, a study across many cancer types, of a depression-related gene signature, a set of 382 genes linked to depression. The team computed a score, called DScore, for over 10,000 tumour samples from 33 cancer types and related it to tumour biology, immune surroundings, and survival.

Higher scores appeared in several gut, brain, kidney, and hormone-related cancers, and linked to older age, later stage, and poorer survival in many cancers, though the survival link reversed in a few. In breast cancer, high scores matched an immune-suppressing tumour setting with fewer killer T cells. One gene, CACNA1H, was checked in breast tissue tests.
pmc-13271360:
Lorenzo Ghelfi is lead author of a 2026 scoping review, a mapping of a young research field, on using artificial intelligence to detect relapse in psychosis. Relapse is common in psychotic disorders, a leading cause of disability worldwide. The authors searched three databases for studies using machine learning or language processing to spot relapse early.

Only ten eligible studies were found. Most collected data through smartphones and smartwatches. They used passive tracking and frequent in-the-moment check-ins. Social media and internet searches were also used. Model accuracy varied widely across studies. Detection rates and overall scores both ranged from weak to fair. Few findings were replicated, the authors conclude.
pmc-13271460:
Laura Holdsworth is lead author of a 2026 qualitative study, one based on deep interviews, of doctors' experiences in Lesotho during the COVID-19 pandemic. Most research on health worker wellbeing in the pandemic comes from Western countries, leaving the strain on staff in African settings poorly documented.

Seven doctors described their wellbeing through the crisis. Five themes emerged: feeling under pressure, unprepared, and out of control; constant uncertainty and threat; isolation alongside connection; coping largely on their own; and new perspectives gained. The challenges spilled beyond work and harmed wellbeing, yet doctors drew support from family, friends, and colleagues, and found lessons in the experience. The authors discuss national and local support needs.
pmc-13272960:
Abdelaal Shamseldin leads a 2026 study of Egyptian soil bacteria that can break down atrazine, a widely used weed killer that pollutes farm soil. Forty-four candidate bacteria were isolated from polluted sites, and 34 could use atrazine as a nitrogen source. Two strains stood out and were tested further.

The best strains, from Klebsiella and Ochrobactrum groups, each broke down about 81 percent of atrazine and carried known degrading genes. Both made the same breakdown product. Using a statistical tuning method, breakdown rose to 94.2 percent and 96.7 percent for the two strains. The authors present this as a bio-safe option for cleaning polluted fields in Egypt.
pmc-13273660:
Bunduki and colleagues argue, in a 2026 comment article, that female genital schistosomiasis belongs inside Africa's cervical cancer agenda. The disease is caused by parasitic worms in water. It damages women's genital tissue and is often missed.

The authors note that cancer prevention in Africa now centers on HPV. Vaccines, screening, and treatment all target that virus. Yet schistosomiasis can cause lesions that mimic other conditions. These lesions may raise risks and confuse diagnosis. The comment urges health programs to test for and treat the parasite alongside HPV services. It also calls for training so clinic staff can spot the disease. Joint action, the authors argue, would protect more women.
pmc-13274160:
Dong Wang and a large team present a 2026 journal article on gut bacteria living inside esophageal tumors that help the cancer resist death. That tag raised two shields against an iron-driven cell death called ferroptosis, and tumors grew faster. Blocking the bacterial product or the tag erased the effect in cells and mice.
pmc-13274760:
Qin-Mei Lin and co-authors present a 2026 longitudinal study of fear of cancer returning in survivors of nasopharyngeal carcinoma, a throat cancer common in East Asia. Fear of progression can shadow life after treatment. The team asked whether health literacy, the skill of finding and using health information, calms that fear over time.

Health literacy stayed moderate while fear stayed stubbornly high, and the two were linked at every visit: more literacy, less fear. Yet once earlier fear was accounted for, literacy no longer predicted later fear, except for one skill, using medical resources, which did protect.
pmc-13276060:

The cargo is rutin, a plant compound that may shield nerve cells but dissolves poorly in water. The team packed it into hybrid nanoparticles, tiny spheres part polymer and part lipid, meaning fat-like material.

One formula loaded the drug well and stayed small. Coating it with a glucosamine and chitosan blend, both sugar-based materials, changed how fast rutin leaked out. In mice with a chemically induced schizophrenia-like condition, the coated carrier worked better than both plain rutin and the uncoated carrier. pmc-13276160:

From the very start of each return, they headed almost straight toward the refuge. Their swimming speeds stayed steady and their paths barely wandered. Final approach distances were tiny compared with the trip length, and fish showed no long searching near home. The authors say the pattern fits goal-directed navigation toward a fixed, remembered target.
pmc-13276560:
Mohamed Abdulkadir Hussein and co-authors wrote a 2026 commentary on a neglected crisis among older Somali refugee returnees. People who fled war, lived displaced for years, and returned home now age amid food insecurity. Their muscle wasting and nutritional frailty, the authors argue, are invisible in health data and aid planning.

Severe food insecurity more than doubles the odds of sarcopenia in older adults in poorer countries. Returnees face chronic protein and micronutrient shortages, the core drivers of muscle loss. Inflammation rises in malnourished older bodies and accelerates the breakdown. pmc-13276760:
Takeshi Yamaguchi and co-authors report a 2026 journal article on daily rhythms in the brain tissue that makes cerebrospinal fluid. The choroid plexus produces this fluid and houses a strong internal clock, hinting that fluid production rises and falls across the day. The molecular basis was unknown.

Staining showed the water channel sitting at the fluid-facing surface at night but nearly gone by day. The authors say protein-level control likely sets daily fluid output.
pmc-13278060:
Pascal P McKeown delivered the 2026 Royal Victoria Hospital Annual Oration in Belfast on October 3, 2025, a tradition dating to 1827. The audience included medical and dental students, trust leaders, colleagues, and family.

The speech traces ideas about the heart across two millennia, from Hippocrates, Aristotle, and Galen onward. Harvey's work is presented as a radical break with centuries of settled belief. McKeown also looks ahead to the future of health care, with detours along the way. A Graham Greene line on stories frames the talk: beginnings and ends are chosen, not given.
pmc-13279660:
Akmez Latona and colleagues report a 2026 study of a blood clot test change in major trauma care. The FIBTEM test, part of a clot check called ROTEM, weighs fibrin based clot build. Fibrin is the mesh protein in clots. Its reagent changed from one platelet blocker to two, for fuller platelet shut down. Platelets are small blood cells that plug wounds. Forecast clot sizes at the key fibrinogen mark were near the same, about eight and about seven and a half millimetres. Test power to spot low fibrinogen was checked as well. pmc-13280460:
Nazanin Alaei Faradonbeh and team report a 2026 case of a rare vein finding in the heart, seen by chance at heart imaging. The coronary sinus is the main vein drain of the heart. It is rarely the site of grave disease. Block of it can cause grave flow effects and high death risk if missed. Their patient was a sixty year old man with type two diabetes on long term dialysis.

He had high filling pressure in the left heart and widespread coronary artery disease. Care held tighter fluid control through stronger dialysis, plus guideline heart failure drugs. His symptoms and flow values then got better. Rare sinus finds may merit more checks in select patients.
pmc-13280660:
Maneeth Mylavarapu and colleagues published a 2026 pooled analysis on heart valve care for people on dialysis. These patients have kidney failure and a narrowed heart valve, a risky mix. Two fixes exist. One threads a new valve in through a tube, and one is open heart surgery. The team pooled ten past studies with more than twenty-eight thousand patients.

Patients who got the tube method were less likely to die in the hospital. They also left the hospital sooner. But they more often needed a pacemaker, a small device that steadies the heartbeat. The authors say the tube method looks safer at first for this frail group. They note that all ten studies looked back at past care.
pmc-13281560:
Gabriela Felix and colleagues profiled loose cancer cells in blood in a 2026 research letter. The patients had advanced colon cancer that had spread. Cells shed by tumors drift in the blood and can seed new growths. Past tests mostly just counted them. Gene damage showed in several cell groups, and male patients had lost the Y chromosome in some cells. Normal blood cells showed fired-up swelling and fuel programs. The team calls the work a first sketch, meant to spark firm tests.
pmc-13281760:
Jiadi Liu and colleagues reviewed a new drug target in stomach cancer in a 2026 paper. The target is a surface protein that seals cells in the stomach lining. Two large trials made a drug against it, paired with chemo, a first-line choice for some patients. The patients' tumors carry the target and lack a second well-known target. Since then the field has grown past plain antibodies. New forms include drug-loaded antibodies, two-headed antibodies, and trained immune cells.

The review centers on how to pick and order these therapies. The target's level varies across a tumor and can shift with care. Each drug form needs a different target level to work and brings its own harms. A biopsy may thus miss the mark or read it wrong. The authors map test reading, patient choice, and what to try after the target has been hit once.
pmc-13281860:
Hasan M Al-Dorzi and colleagues tested a common blood marker in sepsis care in a 2026 study. The marker, called CRP, rises with swelling and infection. Doctors often track it over days to judge risk and guide antibiotics. The team read records of one hundred seventy-one intensive care patients from 2020 to 2023. All had at least three CRP readings in the first week. Deaths within ninety days were the main yardstick.

About one in four patients died in that window. CRP levels on day one barely split those who died from those who lived. Changes across the week split them no better. A rival marker did only slightly better. In full models, day-one CRP carried no link to death. One soft hint stood out: patients whose CRP fell used a key antibiotic for fewer days. The authors say serial CRP should not drive life-or-death calls in sepsis.
pmc-13282260:
Kong Qingfei and Xiao Wen wrote a 2026 letter to the editor on a study of symptom clusters during immune checkpoint inhibitor therapy for cancer. Those drugs free the immune system to attack tumours, but they cause side effects that often arrive together. The original survey asked two hundred thirteen patients in China to report their own symptoms, rather than relying only on clinician notes.

The letter praises that patient-centred angle and the careful statistics used to group symptoms into clusters. It then offers three suggestions for future work. Studies should follow patients over time, not just at one point. They should add blood markers, such as inflammation signals, to test shared causes behind clusters. Samples should also cover more cancer types, since lung cancer dominated the survey, and separate single-drug from combined treatment. The writers call the study high quality and forward looking for supportive cancer care.
pmc-13282360:
Paul Fendley and co-authors present a 2026 theoretical physics paper giving a simpler proof that a quantum spin chain model can be solved exactly. The model, called the XYZ chain, describes interacting spins, tiny magnets, in a line. Its exact solvability was known since the nineteen seventies, but the classic proof is hard, using special functions and a key equation. The new work builds the proof differently.

The authors construct a long sequence of conserved charges, quantities that stay fixed as the system evolves, from a matrix-product operator, a compact way of writing structured operators. Those charges commute with the chain's energy operator, which proves solvability. The result holds for a closed loop and for an arbitrary magnetic field at the boundary. Adding a defect keeps the property, yielding a solvable version of the Kondo problem, where a magnetic impurity interacts with its surroundings.
pmc-13282860:
Jiao Li and co-authors present a 2026 study of gut bacteria imbalance in intensive care patients with acute kidney injury, a sudden loss of kidney function. The gut and kidney influence each other, but the pattern in critical illness was unclear. Rectal swabs were taken within twenty-four hours of admission from one hundred ninety-three patients, one hundred forty-two with kidney injury and fifty-one without, and bacterial DNA was sequenced.

The kidney injury group showed higher species richness on one index, suggesting growth of moderately common bacteria, possibly including opportunists. Community composition differed clearly between groups. The injury pattern featured more opportunistic species and some bacteria normally found outside the gut. Kidney blood markers, creatinine and urea nitrogen, were the only clinical factors significantly shaping the community. The authors say the findings map the gut side of the gut-kidney axis in critical illness.
pmc-13282960:
Kidney stones meet nanotechnology in a wide 2026 survey of new detection and treatment ideas from Jieming Zuo's team. Stones are common, often return, and can harm the kidneys over time. Standard care clears stones well but detects risk late and prevents return poorly.

The review covers how nano-sized materials could improve each care step. Uses include sensing body chemistry, finding urine markers, and sending drugs to exact kidney sites. Other uses include slowing crystal growth and guiding heat-based stone breaking. The authors also discuss pairing these tools with smart software and custom designs. Safety and proof in patients remain key needs before routine use can begin.
pmc-13283160:
Cellulose brewed by bacteria could substitute for patient veins in bypass grafts, the prospect Saeed Sharifpoor Kermani reviews in 2026. Heart bypass surgery still favors a patient vein or artery as the gold standard. Such tissue may be absent, diseased, or used up after past surgery in older patients.

Weak points include poor cell sticking and a mismatch with vein traits. The review covers ways to tune growth, surface traits, and strength of the material. Better control could yield grafts that work when patient vessels cannot be used.
pmc-13283860:
Keeping mood and movement steadier in Huntington disease is the aim behind a 2026 clinic study by Shakaib Khan and colleagues. The illness erodes movement, thinking, and mental health together over time. No cure exists, so care quality shapes daily function and decline.

Charts for 56 patients compared periods before and after a joint specialty clinic opened. Mood symptom paths flattened after clinic care began, versus worsening before it. Roughly two thirds of patients responded after the clinic model started. Before it, only about a third to two fifths responded in records. Motor and thinking scores were tracked with standard rating scales. Team care may slow symptom drift.
pmc-13285360:
Radiation doctors lean in favor of AI risk forecasts for later chronic illness in breast cancer survivors, a 2026 survey by Frederik Voigt Carstensen and co-authors finds. Survivors face higher odds of heart disease, bone loss, lung disease, and weight gain, partly from past treatment. Scans taken for radiation planning already hold clues to those risks.

Heart disease forecasts won the strongest backing for relevance, with bone loss next and body makeup after. Usefulness in daily work drew more mixed views. The authors say clinician buy-in will decide whether such forecasts reach real follow-up care.
pmc-13285560:
Wax moth larvae react to a human throat germ much as mammals do, Corina Abt-Becker and co-authors show in a 2026 protein study. The larvae serve as a cheap, ethics-light stand-in for animal infection work, and their defense system echoes ours. Streptococcus pyogenes causes ills from mild skin sores to grave invasive disease.

The authors say the match backs moth larvae as a way to cut vertebrate use.
pmc-13286960:
Muhammed Fatih Serttas and colleagues question a supposedly fixed pelvic angle after spine surgery in a 2026 retrospective study. pmc-13287360:
Wael Sobhy Darwish and co-authors tested a water extract of carob pods in 2026 in rats with chemically induced liver cancer, alone and beside the chemotherapy drug cisplatin. Forty-two rats were split across seven groups covering healthy, cancer, and treatment combinations.

The authors call the pairing a candidate helper treatment, pending work that can carry animal findings toward patients.
pmc-13287760:
Souvik Halder and co-authors designed a compact flat antenna in 2026 for sending signals through soil, where ordinary antennas at low frequencies grow bulky and weak. pmc-13288160:

The authors read hearing loss as a helper factor that strains communication rather than the main driver.
pmc-13289160:
Maria Consuelo Miranda Montoya and colleagues study risk talk in pregnancy during Zika in 2026. The study spans Brazil, Colombia, and Puerto Rico. It held 98 women at seven sites. All were pregnant during or after Zika spread. Test results then carried deep doubt.

pmc-13289260:

The unit, called the ICU, cares for trauma and emergency surgery patients who may need breathing machines, frequent blood tests, and constant medicines. The writing uses plain language for patients and families.

Doctors then match options to those wishes, even when the best path shifts from cure toward comfort.
pmc-13289360:

pmc-13289660:

pmc-13290560:

pmc-13290760:

pmc-13290960:

pmc-13291060:

pmc-13291560:

pmc-13291660:

pmc-13292260:

pmc-13293260:
Zheng-Wei Chen and colleagues build, in 2026, a machine learning risk score for people who have both diabetes and a stiff-heart form of heart failure. This pairing raises the chance of hospital stays and heart-related death.

Nine routine measures were kept, including age, a heart stress marker, kidney function, and heart size. Over follow-up, 327 patients hit the combined outcome of hospital stay or heart death, a count the authors give. Risk rose step by step as more risk factors stacked up in a patient.
pmc-13293460:

pmc-13293560:

pmc-13293660:

pmc-13293760:

pmc-13293860:

pmc-13294060:

Responsibility and accountability get special weight, keeping humane judgment central as tools automate more tasks. pmc-13294160:

pmc-13294760:
Jingran Li and colleagues ask doctors in Chongqing, China, what they know and think about shock therapy for teens in a 2026 study. The treatment, given in changed form, works well for adults with deep depression. Its use in young people stays rare and much debated.

pmc-13295160:

pmc-13295760:

pmc-13296160:

Linking local barriers to chosen strategies rested mainly on stakeholder experience rather than measured proof. Only a few studies measured outcomes, though all six fully analysed ones reported positive findings. The authors call for tighter reporting.
pmc-13296560:
Mariana Martínez-Noriega and colleagues survey, in 2026, white bacterial mats growing on mangrove sediments in Guadeloupe. Using gene barcoding, they compare mats at protected, natural and town-affected sites to see how human pressure reshapes these sulphur-linked communities.

A shared core set persisted everywhere, while town sites alone hosted rare kinds previously tied to human change. Green sulphur bacteria thrived at protected sites and other sulphur users near town. Measured water chemistry explained little, pointing to finer hidden gradients.
pmc-13296760:
Jürgen Becker and Jörg Wilting nominate, in 2026, two proteins as fresh markers for telling lymph vessels from blood vessels under the microscope. Existing markers all appear elsewhere too, and lymph vessel cells differ by location, so better labels are needed for work on malformations and cancer.

Drawing on their own human data and public databases, the authors find liprin beta-1 across starter vessels, collectors and lymph nodes at both gene and protein level. Synemin looks narrower, favouring starter vessels at protein level. They hope the pair spur antibody tools and sharper vessel mapping.
pmc-13296960:
Zixuan Cao and co-authors propose, in 2026, a synaptic clock account of SYNGAP1-related intellectual disability. Gene rescue works strikingly in newborn animals but weakly in adults, hinting the missing protein runs a timed building programme rather than a steady chemical job.

Once set, the rescue window closes. The authors map phase-matched treatments, from early gene replacement to later drug and stimulation fine-tuning.
pmc-13297060:
Ryan Jak Yang Lim and colleagues mine, in 2026, over ninety-seven hundred breast cancer pathology reports spanning thirty years with text-reading software. Pathologists often note harmless or early changes beside the main tumour in free text, and those background features are rarely studied at scale.

Certain background changes clustered with specific tumour types. Once stage and type were counted, though, the background features did not on their own predict patient outcomes. The authors show automated reading can unlock this neglected layer of reports for registry research, even when its prognostic value proves limited.
pmc-13297360:
Niqin Xiao and co-authors review, in 2026, how low oxygen in inflamed rheumatoid joints rewires energy use and leaves chemical marks that deepen disease. Starved of oxygen, joint tissue leans on sugar burning, whose lactate by-product can tag proteins through lactylation and push damage forward.

The review connects sugar burning to inflammation, lining overgrowth, invasive tissue skirts and bone erosion, then details how lactate tagging promotes each step. Treatments aiming at oxygen sensing, sugar burning and lactate marks are surveyed. The authors offer the linked axis as a map for targeted drug design.
pmc-13298160:
Sports products promise recovery and less fatigue, but many active ingredients dissolve poorly or break down before absorption. Yien Xiang and colleagues review design-first gel delivery systems for these compounds in a 2026 article on sports nutrition.

Hydrogels, microgels, emulsion gels, and protein matrices can protect fragile bioactives through processing and storage, then release them on digestion cues. The authors stress sports-specific constraints: stomach tolerance during exercise, osmotic load, nutrient timing, and how exertion changes digestion itself. They propose a decision framework matching each compound and food format, liquid, solid, or semi-solid, to a fitting gel architecture, while noting scale-up and structure prediction remain weak points.
pmc-13298860:
Warming the air while white tea leaves wither sweetens their aroma, demonstrates Fan Huang and a large team in a 2026 processing study. They compared natural withering against temperature-changing warm-air withering across four tea cultivars, combining trained sensory panels with chemical profiling.

Panels found the warmed method boosted sweet and fruity notes while trimming grassy ones. Instruments catalogued 176 volatile compounds, and the new method raised ketones, esters, and alkenes significantly. Four shared compounds, including 1-octen-3-one and cedrol, accounted for much of the fresher character. The authors offer the findings as a basis for refining white tea manufacture across cultivars.
pmc-13299360:
Liver cancer grows as a team effort among tumor, immune, and vessel cells, show Miguel Ángel Díaz-Campos and Enrique Hernández-Lemus in a 2026 single-cell analysis. They profiled 93,032 cells from human liver tumors and healthy liver to map how the microenvironment is rewired.

Macrophages adopted fat-handling, immune-suppressing states, and vessel cells switched on growth and matrix programs. The healthy communication web centered on antigen presentation gave way to tumor-driven circuits favoring blood vessels, chemokines, and lipids. The authors nominate these shared modules as combination drug targets.
pmc-13303560:
Corentin Le Cacheux leads a 2026 multicenter review of severe problems after autologous stem-cell transplant, where patients receive their own stored cells. The team asked how often intensive care is needed and which patients fare worst.

Eight French university intensive care units contributed cases from 2013 to 2023. Among 6,342 transplant recipients, a small share needed intensive care, usually about two weeks after conditioning and most often for sepsis. Many needed drugs to support blood pressure or a breathing machine. About one in four had died by 90 days, with risk tied to illness severity, low albumin, poor daily function, and lymphoma.
pmc-13304460:
Aiping Chen and co-authors test soil treatments for expansive ground that swells and shrinks with water in a 2026 lab study. Cement helps strength, while a clay-based adsorption modifier may tame swelling more directly.

Compaction, swell-shrink, strength, and wet-dry cycling tests compared cement, the modifier, and both together. The modifier packed soil denser at lower water levels and cut free swelling sharply, dropping one mix out of the expansive class entirely. Cement gave the biggest strength gains but held up poorly under wet-dry cycles. The paired system balanced swelling control, strength, and water durability best.
pmc-13306360:
Leandro Hahn measured how potassium feeding affects two apple varieties over four seasons in a 2026 orchard study. Trees of Royal Gala and Fuji Suprema received yearly doses from 0 to 200 kg K2O per hectare in two orchards.

Variety drove most differences in yield and potassium levels, with season second in the reported analysis. When all years and sites were pooled, yield and leaf or pulp potassium barely moved with dose. Soil threshold for output was 170 mg dm−3 for both varieties in the authors' estimate, giving growers calibrated targets for soil, leaf and fruit checks.
pmc-13306660:
Hani T. Fadel reported gum care without surgery that closed a front-tooth gap in a 2026 case account. Her patient, a healthy 34-year-old woman who had quit smoking, sought help for a space between her upper front teeth.

Records showed localised stage III grade C periodontitis with deep pockets and bone-loss defects around teeth numbered 12 and 11. Cleaning-focused therapy and retreatment of leftover sites improved plaque, bleeding and pocket scores in reported follow-up. The gap closed on its own as teeth shifted back, and bone defects looked filled on later X-rays.
pmc-13306960:
Mikołaj Chromiński reviewed sulfur fluoride exchange chemistry for building blocks of DNA and RNA in a 2026 survey. SuFEx links form strong sulfur-based bonds under mild settings, thanks to a stable yet switchable sulfur and fluorine bond.

Use in chemical biology is broad, yet work on nucleosides, nucleotides and full nucleic acids remains sparse in the authors' account. Barriers include scarce enabling methods and clashes with standard chain-building workflows. Recent cases show workable routes, and the review distils design rules for placing reactive groups on each scaffold level.
pmc-13307860:
Carlos Mario Carceles-Rodríguez and co-authors model in 2026 how the antibiotic cefquinome moves through milking sheep and goats after vein, skin, and long acting skin doses. Mixed effect models and Monte Carlo runs let them compare forms and guess the odds of hitting drug targets in each species.

The long acting form slowed uptake and stretched the time the drug stayed in the body for both species. That longer stay raised the odds of beating lung germs at set dose levels in the model runs. Milk held only trace amounts, below the lab limit for firm counts. Dose advice for small ruminants can now rest on fuller data than before.
pmc-13308760:
Jin Soo Joo and co-authors find in 2026 that mice that lack vanin-1, an enzyme tied to vitamin B5 handling, survive lethal flu far better than normal mice. Virus load, immune response, and tissue harm did not differ, so the edge lay in tolerance, not in germ killing power.

Those mice kept more glutathione and showed less fat damage during infection than normal mice did. Blocking glutathione build wiped out the edge, while feeding it shielded normal mice. Vanin-1 may thus be a drug target for severe viral ills.
pmc-13308960:
Eyad Jamileh, Zuha Akhtar, and Maria Babu report in 2026 stomach outlet block from pseudomyxoma peritonei, a rare mucus filling cancer, in a man aged 76 years. Tumour spread through his belly squeezed the stomach exit shut, which brought pain, sickness, and steady weight loss over time.

Five metal stents in a row gave only brief relief, as squeeze and tumour growth crushed each new stent in turn. A scope made bypass join from stomach to small bowel then gave lasting relief, with vein feeding and a nose drain as backup. Early bypass thought beats stent rounds when mucus disease spreads this wide, the team argues from this hard case.
pmc-13309460:
Wallace S Tavares da Silva and co-authors compare two native goat breeds in dry Brazil in a 2026 study. Dark-coated Canindé goats and light-coated Moxotó goats live under the same hot, dry conditions. The team asked how coat, body heat, blood values, and hormones shift between summer and winter.

Thirty goats of each breed grazed together and were checked in both seasons. The dark breed showed higher coat surface heat, thicker coat change, and wider swings in thyroid hormone and blood sugar across seasons. The light breed stayed steadier on most measures. The authors read the dark breed as more flexible and the light breed as more conservative in coping with heat.
pmc-13309560:
Zakaria Mohamed Alghzzawy and co-authors build a tiny gel carrier for a plant compound with poor water solubility in a 2026 study. The compound, silibinin, shows health promise but dissolves badly, so little reaches the body. A carrier that releases more drug in acid conditions could help target diseased tissue.

Gelatin and a synthetic polymer were joined with a low radiation dose to form the gel, after a first step that spread the drug evenly. Particles stayed under 50 nm in size and trapped 82 percent of the drug load during making. Release in acid ran threefold higher than free drug after six hours. Liver cancer cells in dishes grew less under the loaded gel.
pmc-13310060:
Hamed Tahmasebi and co-authors review machine learning for finding new antimicrobial peptides in a 2026 article. Drug-resistant infections form a rising global threat, with older drugs failing against more germs each year. Peptides that kill microbes offer broad action and attack routes that germs struggle to dodge, but the search space of possible peptides is vast.

Learning models can screen millions of candidates, draft fresh sequences with predicted strength, and tune several traits at once, from killing power to safety and shelf stability. Data banks and scoring methods for this niche are surveyed in depth. Weak data and uneven testing still slow translation to clinics. The authors chart next steps for turning computer finds into real drugs.
pmc-13310660:
Qilong Wang and co-authors link salt habits to single depressive symptoms in a 2026 study. Salt intake may affect mood, but symptom-by-symptom patterns and curve shapes were uncharted. Lumping all depression into one score can hide which feelings actually move with salt.

United States survey data covered 23,753 adults from 2005 to 2023, joined by a separate Chinese clinical group of 700 people for comparison. Adding salt at the table tied to higher odds of eight of nine listed symptoms, with odds ratios from 1.24 to 1.37 across symptoms in the main data. Low self-worth, low mood, and loss of interest led the list. Curve analysis probed non-linear patterns by age, sex, schooling, and blood pressure.
pmc-13310760:
Barbara Choromańska and colleagues track tissue enzymes before and after weight loss surgery in a 2026 study. Severe obesity alters the scaffold that holds tissue together, and enzymes called metalloproteinases cut that scaffold. Their role in obesity and its health harms is still unclear.

Blood enzyme activity was higher in women with severe obesity than in lean controls, with or without metabolic syndrome. Sleeve surgery on the stomach lowered some values, but balance stayed disturbed even 12 months after surgery. Harms lasted longer in women with metabolic syndrome. Long term follow up is needed to judge full recovery of tissue balance.
pmc-13310960:
Ge Yunling and co-authors probe dietary tannins against bone cancer through large scale data in a 2026 study. Osteosarcoma is a harsh bone tumor tied to swelling and cell stress. Plant tannins fight both in lab work, yet their targets in this cancer were unclear, so gene, cell, and tissue maps were joined.

A risk score built from tannin linked genes sorted patients by outlook, with high scores tied to worse survival and fewer killer immune cells. One hub gene, TGFA, marked stem like tumor cells with strong neighbor talk. Cutting TGFA in lab cells slowed growth and spread and raised cell death, while boosting it did the reverse.
pmc-13311960:
Marsha Campbell-Yeo and Lior Goldchtaub comment in a 2025 article on a narrative study of parents talking with their preterm babies in neonatal units. Both mothers' and fathers' voices and touch matter, they argue.

Babies born early face higher risk of speech, language, and social problems. Parental presence, interaction, and voice have been tied to better outcomes on cited evidence. The discussed study asked parents what helps or blocks communication with their infants. Feeling close to the baby builds parents' skill and will to interact. Staff, the commentators say, should teach both parents how much this contact counts.
pmc-13312360:
Zongyu Li's 2026 poem 'Practicing with what you left' follows a mourner rehearsing the small rituals of a household after a death. The speaker picks up the dead person's glasses from the nightstand, folds their arms as the owner would, and puts them away. Then the speaker takes them out again, seven times on the first day.

A grey sweater still holds the shape of elbows but not warmth, and smells of camphor and tobacco that are already fading. The hardest object is a pill bottle labeled in the speaker's own handwriting, holding seven tablets that could not keep the person alive. The speaker returns the pills and screws the cap tight, as if something still needed preserving, and closes not yet ready to touch the bottle again tomorrow.
pmc-13312460:
Atte Tapiola and colleagues examine, in a 2026 study, whether hemoglobin levels within the normal range relate to knee joint findings in young adults. The data come from the Northern Finland Birth Cohort 1986, whose members had knee MRI scans, exams, and questionnaires at age 33, with 275 people included in the final analysis.

Cartilage lesions were somewhat more frequent in the highest hemoglobin third than the lowest. Bony osteophytes at the shin and thigh bones ran the other way, and joint fluid was more common at high hemoglobin. People with higher hemoglobin also had higher body mass index, blood sugar, cholesterol, and blood pressure. Regression models found only small effects. The authors conclude hemoglobin was not consistently tied to MRI findings in this mostly symptom-free group, apart from slightly more small cartilage lesions at higher levels.
pmc-13315760:
Zifan Zhu and a large team engineered in 2026 a single-dose nanoparticle vaccine that guards against two threats at once, Pseudomonas bacteria and tetanus toxin. Wounds from trauma or disaster can admit both at the same time, no licensed Pseudomonas vaccine exists, and multi-dose courses are hard to finish in emergencies.

Built on a lumazine synthase particle, the vaccine displays a fused Pseudomonas antigen and tetanus toxin fragment C together. In mice it raised antigen uptake and dendritic cell activation, and one shot produced fast, strong antibodies plus three kinds of cytokine-making spleen cells. Lung germ counts and inflammatory signals fell after challenge.
pmc-13316160:

Each step in the chain has a clear job to do.
pmc-13316360:
eClinicalMedicine, as issuing journal, published a 2026 editorial warning that drug-resistant infections form a hidden pandemic. Since penicillin arrived in 1928, germs have steadily learned to beat the drugs built to kill them, and the editorial ties that trend to fresh global action.

It cites 1.14 million deaths in 2021 blamed directly on resistance and a forecast of 39 million more deaths between 2025 and 2050 if trends hold. Member states at the 79th World Health Assembly adopted an updated global plan for 2026 to 2036 built on One Health thinking across people, animals, farms, and nature. Prevention, tracking, careful drug use, and steady funding form the core response it urges.
pmc-13316760:

Piezo1 thus helps set fiber build even without heavy loading.
pmc-13317860:
Fariah Mahzabeen and co-authors study, in a 2026 user project, how older adults in Bangladesh take to smartwatches, tools that could ease pressure on clinics as populations age. Most adoption research comes from rich countries, so local, mixed-income voices were missing.

Comfort ratings climbed steeply, with those calling it very comfortable rising from 26 percent early on to 80 percent at the final check in the reported figures. Heart rate checking stayed the favorite feature. Daily use held steady while feature use grew late in the study. Missing health features and clear instructions shaped long-term engagement.
pmc-13318560:
Anna Dávidovics and co-authors describe a 2026 project translating the DREEM questionnaire, a widely used measure of the learning environment, into Hungarian for medical and health professions students. No validated Hungarian version had existed before.

Translation and cultural adaptation followed international guidance, and an online survey at the University of Pécs Medical School drew 529 valid replies from medical, dental, and pharmacy students in late 2024. Consistency was excellent and repeat testing held up well, while checks of the original five-part structure gave only partial support. The average score of 135.0 points suggested students viewed their environment positively overall. The authors back its use for benchmarking, with care around the structure findings.
pmc-13318660:

Each extra index point linked to 6.9 percent lower risk in the same models.
pmc-13318760:
Sandro Vento writes a 2026 commentary on reforming medical training in low- and middle-income countries. In 2019, national health workforces were short at least 6.4 million physicians, he notes. The shortage bites hardest in low-income settings. Schools must adapt to society's needs without dropping core principles.

Public medical schools carry the central mission, Vento argues. Health ministries must plan graduate numbers and guarantee decent jobs and pay. Otherwise trained doctors leave for high-income countries. He warns schools against chasing rankings and graduation metrics. Lowering standards can fake success while graduates learn little. Accreditation paperwork should not replace serious assessment by experienced faculty. The goal is competent, compassionate doctors who serve their own countries.
pmc-13318960:
Isadora Oliveira de Sousa and co-authors describe a 2026 project building and validating a triage protocol for dental emergencies in Brazil. Yellow risk labels led at 50 percent, followed by green at 45 percent in the pilot. Average wait to treatment was one hour and thirty-three minutes. Dropout was only 2.5 percent overall. Ten professionals rated the tool, with 97 percent agreement, and judged it clear and relevant.
pmc-13320260:
Haoming Wu and co-authors review mouth taken gels for lower gut illness in a 2026 article that shifts focus from disease first to microbe first design. Past work aimed gels at calming swelling, repair, or tumor kill and treated microbes as a side note. Newer plans design the gel around microbe needs first, and the review maps that shift plus the trade talks among gel, microbes, and host.
pmc-13320460:

Twelve studies entered the pool, and the shared count put wrong use near two in five hospital patients in the estimate reported, though studies clashed very widely. Wrong reason for the drug and wrong course length were the most common faults. Other illness at the same time stood among the drivers named. The team urges stewardship drives in wards.
pmc-13321260:
Ercha Hu and colleagues survey disease germs in desert rodents and ticks in a 2026 field study from Xinjiang, China. Sampling ran from October 2024 to June 2025 on the southern edge of the Gurbantunggut Desert. Rodents and their parasites can carry germs that pass to people, yet this dry region was little studied.

Teams collected 142 gerbils and 361 ticks and tested them for Rickettsia and Bartonella gene marks. Bartonella was common in rodents, at 40.14 percent, while spotted fever group rickettsiae appeared in only 1.11 percent of tick samples in the study. Gerbils look like key Bartonella hosts, and one tick type carried Rickettsia conorii, which maps local risk.
pmc-13321360:
Mahnaz Ashrafi and co-authors add energy use to brain network maps in a 2026 study. The team built a metabolism-weighted connectome from combined PET and MRI scans in healthy volunteers.

The authors propose a unifying rule: regions most vital for cognition pay the highest energy cost, and that cost may leave them open to degeneration. Energy aware maps could guide future brain research.
pmc-13321560:
Shangwen Lu and co-authors compare ten ways to forecast monthly hepatitis B cases in China in a 2026 study. Monthly reported cases from January 2004 to December 2024 were drawn from public surveillance data.

Models trained on data to 2023 were tested against held back 2024 cases, using 252 monthly observations in all. The mean monthly reported count was 91,901 cases in the data. Classic seasonal models, machine learning models, and hybrid versions were scored on several error measures, and the best were used to project 2025 counts.
pmc-13321760:

The laboratory scored 98 percent overall in the assessment. Every area scored full marks except lab system quality, at 89 percent, held back by a lack of external quality checks for Marburg testing. Mapping of testing sites and response records complete a picture of a fast, well run national response that other centres can learn from.
pmc-13322860:
Xichao Wu and colleagues compare incretin-based drugs for type 2 diabetes in a 2026 network meta-analysis of clinical trials. They covered 15 therapies, from single-action GLP-1 drugs to dual and triple receptor drugs, across 102 trials with 98,693 patients.

All drug classes beat placebo on blood sugar control in their analysis, with tirzepatide, orforglipron and semaglutide among the strongest for that outcome, and retatrutide strongest for weight loss. Gains also appeared for lipids, blood pressure and kidney and insulin measures. Side effects were mainly mild gut symptoms that passed, and low blood sugar stayed uncommon. Higher doses helped more but caused more side effects, so the authors back choices fitted to each patient.
pmc-13323160:
Berg and co-authors test a virtual reality animation for teaching drug absorption in this 2026 study. Students who had finished a basic pharmacology course watched the animation at five international sites.

In total 133 students completed a questionnaire, and about half said the animation changed their understanding of absorption. Thirteen medical students in Bergen also joined focus group interviews. Their comments formed three themes about linking pharmacology to other subjects, balancing engagement against overload, and learning deeply while facing exams. Berg concludes the tool works well and engages students, but it must allow self pacing so learners are not overwhelmed.
pmc-13324460:
Keita Soda and co-authors test a shortcut for counting viruses in water in a 2026 methods study. Standard testing first extracts viral genetic material, a slow step that dirty samples can block.

With pepper mild mottle virus as the model, the best setting was 120 °C for 15 seconds, matching results from normal extraction. Heat above 140 °C damaged the genome and hurt accuracy. Results held up across qPCR and digital PCR and stayed steady in wastewater. The team suggests the approach could speed routine virus checks and suit automated, near real-time monitoring once more virus types are validated.
pmc-13324560:
Samanta Dodino and colleagues use camera traps and AI to track penguin breeding timing across the sub-Antarctic in a 2026 study. When birds breed shapes their fit with the environment, and warming seas may shift those dates.

Rockhoppers arrived on time but left earlier, shrinking their season. Macaronis both arrived and left earlier, a shift rather than a squeeze. Dates tracked winter sea surface temperatures most closely. Breeding success stayed steady in both species, which suggests flexible timing, though hidden costs for populations remain possible.
pmc-13325160:
Karthikeyan Venkatachalam and co-authors compare powders made from tangerine peel of three Thai cultivars in a 2026 food study. The peel, a citrus byproduct, is rich in useful compounds that often go to waste.

Cho Kun, Sai Nam Phueng, and Bang Mod powders all stored well, with water activity below 0.30 in every batch. Cho Kun led on phenolics at 49.98 mg per g and flavonoids at 36.11 mg per g of dry weight. Its antioxidant scores also topped the set, and its vitamin C reached 76.78 mg per 100 g. All powders fought Bacillus cereus, with clear zones from 20.91 to 29.33 mm. D-limonene dominated the scent profile throughout.
pmc-13325360:
Thamires Martinho Prados, Leda Maria Saragiotto Colpini, and Giancarlo Alfonso Lovón-Canchumani assess the life cycle of neodymium-iron-boron magnets in Brazil in a 2026 study. These rare earth magnets drive wind turbines and electric motors, but their supply chain is dirty.

Modeling followed ISO 14040 and 14044 rules with SimaPro software and EcoInvent data. Mining hurt most, above all the roasting step, which burns much energy and emits particles and greenhouse gases. Acid leaching in oxide making added marine and radiation burdens. Machining in magnet making drove warming, ozone, and water impacts. The authors urge tighter rules, recycling loops, and cleaner power to shrink the footprint.
pmc-13325860:
Peter W. Bright and colleagues pair chemical screening with fish toxicity tests on tap water in a 2026 study from western Oregon. Unknown and emerging contaminants slip past routine water checks.

Twelve public tap samples and one bottled water went through high-resolution mass spectrometry workflows. Suspect screening named 52 likely compounds, and 13 were confirmed, including the fungicide propiconazole and a plasticizer. One confirmed find, 18β-glycyrrhetinic acid, had not been reported in drinking water before. Zebrafish embryos showed shape harm from that compound and from a phthalate mix. Behavior shifts followed one single compound and seven mixes. The paired approach widens safety screening.
pmc-13326360:
Xian Yu and a large team study the enzyme cathepsin S in macrophages after brain bleeding in a 2026 paper. Bleeding inside the brain damages white matter, and no therapy yet targets macrophage-led repair of that wiring.

A mouse model of intracerebral hemorrhage was treated with the cathepsin S blocker LY3000328. Single-cell sequencing of tissue near the clot found infiltrating macrophages, above all a fat-handling group, carrying most of the enzyme signal. Blocking the enzyme dampened that lipid program and lowered ApoE, ABCA1, and ABCG1 levels. Culture tests with precursor cells probed whether macrophage fat support for new myelin suffers, with an LXR drug used as rescue.
pmc-13327860:
Bandar S Alharbi, Majed M Aljabri, and Endale Alemayehu Ali map mental routes into diabetes distress in a 2026 survey study from Saudi Arabia. Distress from daily diabetes care affects up to 36 percent of people with type 2 diabetes and worsens outcomes. The team surveyed 438 adults at four primary care centers.

Checked scales measured pain catastrophizing, views of illness, and distress, and modeling traced paths among them. Dwelling on pain and holding emotional views of illness both fed distress directly, and pain rumination also fed distress through the emotional route, with an indirect effect of 0.34 in their model. Grouping methods split patients into burden profiles, pointing to where counseling could help most.
pmc-13328360:
Yu Sun, Qian Liu, and Xiaona Liu study what builds employability in Chinese university students in a 2026 survey.
