Questionnaires covered 735 undergraduates in Hebei Province.

All three factors, career planning, self-concept, and learning attitude, lifted employability directly in the structural model. Learning attitude also sat in the middle, passing part of the benefit of planning and of a healthy self-concept into readiness. Universities should help students draw clear career plans and build a sound self-view, the authors advise, since attitude turns both into action.
pmc-13329660:
Isabela DeJohn and colleagues study whether preventive vancomycin by mouth stops repeat gut infection in young cancer patients in a 2026 report. Clostridioides difficile can return when broad antibiotics are given again. Adult data hint at benefit, but child data are scarce. Records covered primary infections treated from 2017 to 2024.

The starting group held 163 patients. After exclusions, 72 patients received 150 broad antibiotic courses within 6 months of their first infection. Repeat infection arose in 17.9 percent of courses without preventive treatment and 7.4 percent with it in the raw counts given. Matched analysis linked prevention to lower risk. Small size and bias risks mean the finding needs larger tests, the authors caution.
pmc-13330360:
Shiyu Li and co-authors survey low mood in fathers of preterm babies in intensive care in a 2026 study. Fathers in a Gansu hospital unit were surveyed two to three days after admission, between November 2024 and October 2025. In total, 379 fathers completed mood, personality, and family function scales.

With a mood scale cut point of 10 or more, 29.55 percent screened positive for depressive symptoms in the reported results. Higher income band, paternity leave, and mid-range birth weight each linked to lower odds in the models given. Some personality traits raised odds, while outgoing traits lowered them. Weak family function linked to far higher odds. Early support for fathers is warranted, the authors argue.
pmc-13331960:
Ramazan Bayat and colleagues built a near-infrared sensor for dopamine in a 2026 nanotechnology study, using single-walled carbon nanotubes wrapped in a repeating short DNA strand. Dopamine is a key brain messenger, and detecting it selectively among other body chemicals is a standing challenge.

The wrapped nanotubes glow in the near infrared. Their brightness rose as dopamine levels increased across the tested range of 10 to 100 µM, while other biological samples gave no matching response. The detection limit worked out to 4.2 × 10−5 M, with a quantification limit of 13.24 × 10−5 M. Because nanotube glow does not fade or blink like ordinary dyes, the authors see the sensor as a candidate for longer-term dopamine monitoring tasks.
pmc-13333360:
Huimin Huo and co-authors optimized a greener way to pull health-giving polyphenols out of the truffle Tuber formosanum in a 2026 study. The fungus is prized as food and medicine, yet no efficient, low-impact extraction recipe for its polyphenols existed.

Ultrasound-assisted extraction first beat older methods head to head, giving 14.7 percent more yield than hot reflux while using 7.5 times less energy. Statistical screening named power, time, temperature, and alcohol strength as the levers that matter. Surface modeling fixed the best recipe at 95 minutes, 210 W, 70 °C, and 60 percent ethanol, lifting total polyphenol content to 2.72 mg/g, a gain of 16.24 percent. Importance analysis confirmed power as the dominant factor. The optimized extract also scavenged radicals and reduced iron more strongly in standard antioxidant tests. The authors present the recipe plus its explainable modeling as a template for other rare fungi.
pmc-13333460:
Andreea-Emanuela Baciu and colleagues ask whether fluid collecting between a trauma patient's brain hemispheres forecasts later hydrocephalus, in a 2026 retrospective study. Removing part of the skull saves lives after severe head injury, but in half of survivors the injured brain later swells with trapped fluid, sometimes needing a shunt.

The trauma-center review covered 104 patients older than 15 who had decompressive craniectomy for head injury between 2011 and 2025. Half developed radiological hydrocephalus. On multivariable analysis, the thickness of the interhemispheric hygroma, the fluid pocket between the hemispheres, tracked the diagnosis independently, with odds rising 19 percent per millimetre, and it also predicted needing treatment. Discrimination for treatment need was good, with an AUC of 0.81, and a thickness near 8 millimetres marked the practical alert level. The authors propose the simple tape-measure number, taken from routine scans, as a cheap early-warning sign, while asking for outside validation.
pmc-13333760:
Rui Jiang and co-authors tested intermittent theta burst stimulation for leg weakness after stroke in a 2026 randomized study. They tracked recovery with a standard motor scale and with functional near-infrared spectroscopy, which watches cortical activity during tasks.

Sixty-six patients with post-stroke hemiplegia were split evenly between real stimulation plus basic rehabilitation and sham stimulation plus the same rehabilitation. After four weeks the treated group scored better on the Fugl-Meyer lower limb scale. Brain recordings also differed, with stronger task-related activation over the injured side's premotor and primary motor areas and the opposite side's somatosensory area. The combined behavioral and imaging gains suggest this brief magnetic stimulation pattern can aid leg rehabilitation.
pmc-13336360:
Benke Huo and co-authors used entropy to decode what makes a metal alloy form glass in a 2026 materials study. The best glass-forming compositions have traditionally been found by the deep eutectic rule of thumb or by trial and error.

Their entropy engineering strategy starts from eutectic or intermetallic phases whose melting entropies can be measured precisely, favoring those with the lowest values. For copper-zirconium-titanium alloys, glass-forming ability ranked in step with the melting entropies of the starting phases. The optimal composition they designed, Cu59.99Zr28.75Ti11.26, landed essentially on the known champion Cu60Zr30Ti10. The authors claim the first quantitative account of the phase competition behind glass formation, giving alloy designers a measurable target instead of lore.
pmc-13338760:
Ki Young Huh, Gaeun Kang, and Kye Hun Kim assess readiness for remote clinical trials across Korea in a 2026 regional study. Trials cluster heavily in Seoul, limiting access elsewhere. Seventeen regions were scored on specialists, nurses, beds, and equipment per patient.

Data covered 1,924 approved trials and 7,760 trial-center pairs as reported. No province outside Seoul reached 80 percent of Seoul's specialist density in the reported comparison, while bed density varied most widely. Combined readiness scores for four disease areas moved together across regions. Gwangju stood out among provinces, showing where remote trial hubs could grow first.
pmc-13343460:
Haruko Tateyama and co-authors synthesize new uranium complexes in 2026, pairing a bulky imidophosphorane ligand with alkyl, benzyl, and hydride groups on tetravalent uranium. Mixed-ligand uranium alkyls are prized but tricky, since uranium-carbon bonds break down easily, so the team built them step by step from a monoiodide starting material.

The route gave benzyl, neopentyl, and methyl versions cleanly, and no fully substituted homoleptic product formed even with excess ligand salt. Chemical oxidation of the neopentyl complex yielded a cationic product holding an ether molecule rather than a uranium(V) alkyl. Hydrogen gas at low temperature produced a terminal hydride, confirmed by NMR and deuterium labeling, which then broke down quickly on warming.
pmc-13344860:
Yuriy Pya and co-authors document a 2026 case replacing two heart valves by catheter in one session. A 68-year-old woman faced severe aortic stenosis plus a mitral valve choked by heavy calcium. She also had severe obesity, diabetes, kidney disease, past chest surgery, and a pacemaker. Open surgery was out of reach.

Planning leaned on a patient-specific 3D-printed heart model, which set implant depth and prompted a fabric skirt addition to the mitral prosthesis. A self-expanding aortic valve went in through the leg first, anchored partly, then a balloon-expandable mitral valve followed through the heart tip. Both seated with no leak around them, though a moderate outflow gradient remained.
pmc-13347360:
Mei Qiu and colleagues grade mine groundwater quality at the Huafeng coal mine with a combined scoring framework, in a study published in 2026. Mine water must be drained to stop roof flooding, yet its reuse needs sound grading. So the team merged game-theory weighting, fuzzy classing, and ideal-point ranking to balance expert and data-driven weights for sandstone aquifer samples.

Quality looked badly degraded, with every sample past Class V limits for dissolved solids and 77.3 percent past that class for total hardness in the reported checks. Sodium and chloride led the pollutants, and rock-water contact inside a folded, confined structure drove the chemistry, with shallow southern water fed sideways and shaped by mineral breakdown.
pmc-13350260:
Liyang Cai and Yuki Nakanishi wrote a 2026 commentary on natural product nanoengineering for gastrointestinal stromal tumours, cancers that resist lasting control despite targeted drugs. Relapse, spread, and resistance to kinase inhibitors still limit treatment.

Zinc oxide nanoparticles draw interest because they generate reactive oxygen, stress cells, and nudge death pathways. Most studies so far use other tumour types, with few examples in tissue like GIST. A recent extension of the approach into GIST is treated as promising but early. The authors balance that promise against the gap between bench results and a therapy patients can actually receive.
pmc-13350360:
Zhenpeng Jiang and co-authors examined how measuring washout timing in contrast ultrasound changes liver cancer diagnosis in a 2026 study. Contrast ultrasound helps classify liver lumps when CT or MRI leave doubt, and when the contrast fades from a lump is a key sign.

For high-risk patients scanned between 2020 and 2021, the team compared washout time read by eye against software-measured values, all against tissue-proven truth. The two readings shifted standard category assignments and accuracy for hepatocellular carcinoma differently, and the authors derived a best software threshold. Precise timing could reduce reader disagreement on a sign that often decides the diagnosis.
pmc-13351960:
Minmin Hu and Chuanfeng Wu write a 2026 letter refining how GLUT1 should be read in non-small cell lung cancer. Their comment responds to work by Hantzsch-Kuhn and co-authors using a large tissue array cohort. High GLUT1 protein linked to worse tumour traits and poorer survival, and staining was stronger in squamous cancer than in glandular cancer.

GLUT1, though, dropped out as an independent survival factor once other traits were counted. Hu and Wu praise the split analysis by subtype but raise biological and method concerns. Immune cells in the tumour setting can also take up much glucose, which clouds a simple tumour-cell reading. They argue more care is needed before GLUT1 guides prognosis or treatment choice.
pmc-13352160:
Mehaboobathunnisa Sahul Hameed leads a 2026 review of AI methods for judging tumour cellularity in digital pathology. How much of a sample is tumour affects gene test quality and treatment choice. Pathologists now estimate the share by eye, and scores vary between readers.

AI systems read digitised slides and return objective cellularity scores that can show whether enough tumour is present for testing. The review gathers public datasets and benchmark tools, compares automated methods, and lists research and commercial options. Barriers to clinic use are covered too, including the need for clear outputs that match how pathologists reason. The authors frame AI as support for, not replacement of, expert review.
pmc-13355260:
Zhaoxia Li and co-authors report a 2026 case of a 73-year-old man with severe gout plus prostate cancer and kidney disease. He had lived with gout for over 20 years, with large lumps of urate crystals, and standard flare drugs were unsafe for him. The team gave a single shot of firsekibart, a drug that blocks a key swelling signal, plus a short steroid course.

Pain and swelling eased within a day, and swelling markers fell sharply over three months. Urate levels reached target on a second drug, kidney function improved, and no tumor growth, bad infections, or heart events appeared. The authors urge larger studies to confirm long-term safety in such high-risk patients.
pmc-13355760:
Tamar Kinaciyan and co-authors report interim results in 2026 from KONFIDENT-S, a long-term study of oral sebetralstat for swelling attacks in hereditary angioedema. Even on preventive therapy, patients still get breakthrough attacks of painful, sometimes dangerous swelling. Thirty-five patients on one of three preventive drugs treated 382 attacks with the study drug and tracked relief times.

Patients took the drug a median of six minutes after spotting an attack. Relief began at a median of about one hour, severity fell by about four hours, and attacks fully ended at about fifteen hours. Results were much like across all three preventive drugs, and no serious treatment-linked harms appeared.
pmc-13356760:
Eduardo Solís García and co-authors report a 2026 case of a 75-year-old man with a new squamous cell lung cancer inside his left main airway. He was a former heavy smoker who had lost a right lung lobe to the same cancer type twenty years earlier. The new tumor nearly blocked the airway split, causing severe breathlessness and low oxygen, and surgery was ruled out given his prior operation.

He received focused internal radiation, called brachytherapy, in six weekly doses placed inside the airway. The tumor vanished fully on scope checks and stayed gone at six months. The authors present the method as a strong option for selected airway tumors when surgery or external radiation cannot be used.
pmc-13361460:
Rubens Camargo Siqueira reviews light therapy for retinal diseases in a 2026 paper. Photobiomodulation uses red and near-infrared light at gentle levels to nudge sick cells toward health. It needs no surgery and no drugs. The review explains the molecular chain the light sets off inside the retina's cells, starting in the power plants called mitochondria.

A cell enzyme, cytochrome c oxidase, absorbs the light at its metal centers. The catch frees a blocking gas, nitric oxide, so energy flow speeds up and the cell makes more ATP fuel. Brief stress signals then switch on defense genes that raise antioxidant shields. Siqueira lays out how these steps could protect the retina, and what proof is still needed before clinics adopt the method.
pmc-13361760:
İzzet Melih Gürkan and co-authors tested a new blood-clot material for gum stem cells in a 2026 lab study. Platelet-rich fibrin is a membrane made from a patient's own blood, widely used to aid dental healing. How the blood tube is coated may change the membrane's structure and power. The team compared fibrin made in plain glass tubes, titanium tubes, and tubes coated with nano-hydroxyapatite, a bone-like mineral.

Gum tissue and blood came from one healthy male volunteer. Stem cells from the gum were grown with each membrane type. A standard test measured how alive and active the cells stayed. If a mineral coating makes the membrane kinder to stem cells, dentists could gain a better healing aid made chairside from the patient's own blood.
pmc-13362360:
Yerkezhan Tolegenova and colleagues published a 2026 study of how much older adults in Astana, Kazakhstan move each day. They surveyed 608 adults aged 60 and older, most of them women, and measured their daily activity with a standard scale made for older people. They also checked body fat, waist size, muscle mass, and hand grip strength.

Most of the group had a moderate activity level, gained mainly from walking and house tasks. Higher activity went with a bit less deep belly fat and a stronger grip, but all of the links were weak. The authors warn that one survey at one time cannot prove cause, yet the work gives Central Asia a first set of local baseline numbers for later studies on aging and health.
pmc-13362760:
Paschalis Karakasis and a large team wrote a 2026 review on atrial fibrillation in people with diabetes. The two conditions often pair up and together mark high risk for stroke, heart failure, and early death. The review spans how common the pairing is, the body changes that drive it, and how care should run from early risk through established disease.

High blood sugar, insulin resistance, swelling, and fat around the heart can scar and rewire the upper heart chambers. As the authors explain, that makes the erratic rhythm easier to start and harder to stop. Care must go beyond rhythm drugs and blood thinners, they argue, to weight, blood pressure, kidney health, and sleep apnea, with checks tuned to each patient's risk.
pmc-13363060:
Laura Grech and Nikolai Paul Pace offer a 2026 perspective on the role of small biobanks in AI-driven genomic medicine. The field often assumes that more data is the main road to trust, yet the authors push back. Small collections, from national and regional banks to hospital and disease-specific sets, reflect local patients closely and carry tight links to clinic records and clear consent rules.

In their view, these banks serve best as proving grounds: models built on huge datasets should be tested, tuned, and checked for fairness on small local sets before real use. Such tests expose weak spots in rare variant calls, privacy care, and fit to local ancestry. Trust, they argue, is earned in these hard local checks, not by scale alone.
pmc-13363160:
Xiaofang Chen presents a 2026 computer modeling study of chabazite, a zeolite sieve, loaded with alkaline-earth metal ions. Zeolites act as molecular sieves in industry, and swapping in different ions tunes what they catch. Chen modeled dried forms holding beryllium, magnesium, calcium, strontium, or barium ions, predicting their crystal shapes, electron traits, and how strongly each ion grips the frame, all by periodic density functional theory.

The five forms kept near-identical frames with slight twists. As the ions grew heavier, each sat closer to the center of the sieve's eight-ring window, and the energy gap and grip strength shifted in clear trends. The beryllium form stood out with the widest gap and strongest grip. The predictions may guide the design of new sieves.
pmc-13365860:
Zhekang Peng and co-workers sum up in 2026 the role of a cell brake gene, NLRC3, in the late immune crash of sepsis. Sepsis first fires the immune guard too hard, then a long calm can leave folks bare to new germs. This brake gene dips in the first hours, then climbs with time.

Its climb can blunt many guard cell types, they note, which feeds the crash phase. Past work ties the gene to that dip and climb in set cell sets. The team frames the gene as a drug aim to right the immune scale and cut late deaths in sepsis care.
pmc-13366360:
Iddi Mapande and co-workers link in 2026 ten years of malaria counts in Dar es Salaam, Tanzania, to rain and heat shifts. The coast city grows fast, and its germ risk by month was not well mapped. The team splits trend and season, then fits bend math to the counts.

Case rates fell by more than three fourths in the span, yet a set peak still hits each year just after the rains. Rain one to two months back drives the peak most, and warm nights near a set heat aid it. Warn plans should key on past rain, not just the sky now.
pmc-13367160:
Yuting Feng and Mingqi Zhang sum up in 2026 stem cell shed bits as a care path for dry eye ill, a tear film fault that stings and blurs. The bits calm swell, tune immune acts, and aid heal, with no live cells to seed growths. They can drop on the eye with ease.

Tricks to load the bits, mix them, or set them in gels can lift their stay and aim. Cord stem bits look most ripe for clinic use. Gaps stay: eye walls block uptake, make and store rules lack, and safe proof is thin. The pair map the road to trials.
pmc-13367960:
Mennillo and colleagues apply single-cell spatial transcriptomics, a method mapping which genes are active in individual cells at their exact tissue locations, to archived colon biopsies in 2026 gastroenterology research. The biopsies, preserved in paraffin blocks from healthy controls, ulcerative colitis patients, and patients with checkpoint-inhibitor colitis, were arrayed together for comparison. Three datasets tested different commercial imaging panels, asking which combination best resolves the cell networks that organize inflamed gut tissue.

One platform, MERSCOPE, failed on these samples: only 0.17 percent of its cells passed quality control, so it was dropped from the analysis. Custom Xenium panels of 290 and 480 targeted genes, plus an expanded panel of roughly 5,000 genes, performed the core comparisons. The custom panels gave better sensitivity and cell-type resolution on the old paraffin tissue. Mennillo presents the collection as a practical resource for studying colitis cell networks in routine clinical biopsies.
pmc-13369960:
Ordunez and a large regional panel set priorities for joining up heart, kidney, and metabolic care. Their 2026 paper reports Phase 3 of HEARTS 2.0, the Americas adaptation of the World Health Organization's HEARTS initiative. These conditions overlap heavily yet are usually managed separately, and the panel aimed to pick interventions primary care services can actually deliver together.

A multidisciplinary panel appraised 45 candidate interventions using structured evidence reviews, evidence-to-decision frameworks, and anonymous rating rounds. It prioritised 38 for implementation. Hypertension care remains the entry point. The package adds early diabetes and kidney disease detection, lifestyle support, and risk-based combination drug therapy. It also adds task-sharing with non-physician staff and structured long-term follow-up. The authors present the list as the evidence base for updating the HEARTS clinical pathway at scale.
pmc-13370860:
Rainer Fährrolfes and co-workers give in 2026 PegaPlus, a web tool that lets drug pros sort screen hits by drag on a map while a learn tool learns their hand. First sorts of huge screen pools take long hand work. Their map learns from each drag and re sorts the pool in step.

A learn tool on line takes in pro moves and chem traits, then lifts its own sort calls. Tests show the pair route cuts hand steps by half next to pure hand work on several pools. The tool ships free on the web for drug hunt teams.
pmc-13374360:
Assaeed and colleagues survey the plant life of Rawdhat Khuraym, a depression near Riyadh, Saudi Arabia, now part of a protected reserve system, in 2026 desert ecology research. Rawdah meadows collect rainwater and support rich vegetation for the Arabian desert. The team documented the site's floristic composition across seasons and classified plants by life form and family. They related vegetation patterns to soil properties to inform sustainable management of the protected area and its grazing and recreation pressures.

The survey recorded 89 species from 30 families in the protected depression. Annuals made up 57.3 percent of species, finishing their life cycles in wet spells, while perennials formed 42.4 percent of the flora. Four families, Asteraceae, Poaceae, Fabaceae, and Brassicaceae, supplied 50.6 percent of species found. No species appeared on the international threatened list. Assaeed frames the inventory as the reference against which change in the reserve can be judged.
pmc-13380260:
Panagiotis Kousidis and colleagues describe a 2026 proof-of-concept study using printed breast models to help pathologists examine tissue removed at mastectomy. Accurate examination depends on matching the removed tissue to earlier scans, which is hard when there are several tumours or treatment has blurred their edges. A physical model could guide where to cut and sample.

The team printed patient-specific models from two breast scan cases, one with a single tumour and one with several. They marked out the breast outline, the tumours, and landmarks for orientation. The models were made on demand for each case. The study shows the approach is feasible and may reduce sampling errors.
pmc-13382560:
Fei Ying, Xuan Zhao, and Tao Wang wrote a 2026 commentary on a study using genetics to test whether stomach cancer raises the risk of lung cancer, and the reverse. The original study used a method that treats inherited gene variants as natural experiments, comparing European and East Asian populations. The commentators praise its rigour and offer extensions.

Their main suggestion is to split each cancer into its subtypes, since stomach and lung cancers each contain forms with different genetic roots. Subtype-level genetic data would let future studies reveal effects that pooled analyses hide. They also recommend following reporting guidelines for this method. The suggestions are framed as directions for complementary future work, not fixes for the published study.
pmc-13382660:
Claudia Patricia Villamizar Caballero and co-authors report a 2026 study of thin films of bismuth selenide, a material that can turn heat into electricity. The films were made by evaporating tiny sheets of the material, produced by a hot injection chemical method, onto glass in a vacuum. Heating the films afterwards changed their properties.

Films heated with extra selenium became better ordered and conducted electricity far better than untreated films. Their heat-to-voltage response also rose several-fold. Such improvements matter for small generators and cooling devices that use temperature differences. The study links each heating condition to crystal texture and electrical behaviour, giving makers a recipe to tune the films.
pmc-13383160:
Sara Zbair and colleagues report a two-year-old boy whose very high blood calcium revealed acute lymphoblastic leukemia in a 2026 case report. The child had a month of leg weakness, tiredness, and reduced alertness, and early tests pointed away from nerve disease. Blood work showed severe calcium elevation with low parathyroid hormone, ruling out the usual gland cause.

Scans showed many bone lesions, and marrow testing found 27 percent blast cells matching precursor B-cell leukemia. Fluids and bone drugs lowered the calcium before chemotherapy began under a standard protocol. The case warns clinicians that stubborn high calcium in a small child can signal hidden cancer.
pmc-13384960:
Karol Suchowiecki and George Y. Wu update diagnosis of a liver disease variant that lacks its usual antibody marker in a 2026 review. Five to ten percent of primary biliary cholangitis patients test negative for antimitochondrial antibodies. Their illness otherwise looks like the standard form, with itching, tiredness, and cholestasis signs.

Diagnosis then rests on specific nuclear antibody tests, and on liver biopsy when those also come back negative. Imaging first rules out other causes of blocked bile flow. Treatment matches the standard form, led by ursodeoxycholic acid, and works best when started early, the authors note.
pmc-13385460:
Pownall and colleagues review how training for mental health staff takes in the United Nations global goals. Those goals span health, schools, fair work, and the climate. The team screened the field and read forty-seven papers in full. Three broad ways of teaching came out. One used active, sharp thought on hard issues. One used group work across fields. One used hands-on service in real settings.

Use of the goals is growing, but it stays patchy. Few courses line up with each other. Staff who teach get little training for this work. No firm guide links the goals to mental health training. The review sets out steps to close those gaps.
pmc-13385860:
Hua Hou, Tianxiang Tan, and Diancheng Wang improve helmet detection for busy traffic scenes in 2026 work. Missed detections from blocked views and heavy computing costs limit real-world camera systems. Their upgrade of a compact YOLO model adds smarter upsampling, a fused feature block, and a gated multi-scale unit.

The added parts sharpen small object detection while keeping the model light for edge devices. Tests showed accuracy up by 2.4 points on the main metric, with a leaner parameter count than the base model. The authors pitch the system for real-time safety monitoring where computing power is scarce.
pmc-13386460:
Günce Göc and co-authors correct figure assignments in the supporting information for a cryo-EM structure study in a 2026 correction notice. The original article described the periplasmic domain of the FtsH protein and its functional dynamics. The authors report that two supporting figures were swapped in the published supporting information file.

The notice reassigns the resolution figures to their correct numbers, with captions that match the methods text. A second swap between a structure comparison figure and an activity data figure is likewise renumbered in text order. Readers gain a corrected map of which panel supports which claim in the supplement.
pmc-13386860:
Alexander Tishchenko and colleagues identify a second viral protein that silences cell-to-cell messaging in a 2026 study of pseudorabies virus. Gap junctions let neighbors share defense signals, and the virus shuts them down by tagging the channel protein connexin 43. A known viral protein starts the kinase signal, but a partner was missing.

The lipid-tagged protein pUS2 proved required for strong channel tagging and message shutdown, without switching the kinase on itself. Its lipid anchor drags the active kinase to the cell surface where the channel sits. Mutants lacking the anchor failed at every step, which completes a two-step viral strategy.
pmc-13386960:
Dan T. Boghici and colleagues review the copying machinery of alphaviruses in a 2026 minireview. Tools built on these viruses have driven gene studies for nearly four decades. Interest has surged again because self-amplifying mRNA shots promise longer output from smaller doses than standard mRNA vaccines can give.

The review explains how the viral proteins and short conserved RNA parts work as a team to build new RNA and sway host cells. It then traces key steps in the growth of replicon tools and current ways to tune the copying parts and RNA layout. Gaps in basic knowledge that still block smart design close the piece.
pmc-13390860:
Fengwei An and colleagues propose, in 2026, a deep learning method to measure road surface texture, a key factor in skid resistance. Existing ways to judge skid resistance vary widely, and each carries limits in accuracy or scope.

The team trained a U-Net segmentation model on prepared asphalt images to produce clean black-and-white maps of the surface, from which texture distribution values can be calculated precisely. A three-dimensional pavement model supported reverse construction of reference images for training and checking. Highway engineers gain an image-based route to texture measurement that could make skid assessment faster and more consistent across road networks.
pmc-13390960:
Kalyebara Paul Kato and co-authors describe, in 2026, advanced pelvic organ prolapse in young Ugandan women treated at surgical camps. In low-resource settings, prolapse surgery often reaches women only through outreach camps, yet the burden among women under fifty was poorly documented.

Reviewing records of women aged eighteen to forty-nine who had prolapse surgery in urogynecology camps, the team measured how many had advanced-stage disease. They recorded how it presented and which factors were linked to severity. Community health planners gain the data needed for education, screening, and surgical planning. Advanced prolapse in young women signals years of untreated disease. It also signals heavy physical labour.
pmc-13391660:
Bruna de Sousa Gomes leads a 2026 animal study on whether oil from the licuri palm fruit can calm pancreatitis and its lung fallout. Acute pancreatitis triggers intense whole-body inflammation and oxidative stress that can injure distant organs, especially the lungs.

In rats, pancreatitis was induced with L-arginine, and the fixed oil of Syagrus coronata was tested for effects on inflammation, oxidative markers, and lung changes. Natural product researchers gain preclinical evidence on a regional Brazilian plant oil as a candidate adjunct, framed by the systemic nature of severe pancreatitis rather than pancreatic damage alone.
pmc-13391760:
Hafiz Umair Siddiqui leads a 2026 feasibility study on doing donor kidney removal and recipient transplantation back-to-back on one shared robotic platform. Single-port robots enable new approaches to both operations, but scarce robotic access can prevent running donor and recipient surgery simultaneously.

Among forty-five living donor and recipient operations from 2019 to 2025, fifteen pairs used a simultaneous single-port workflow on the same platform, while thirty used laparoscopic donor surgery for comparison. The team judged feasibility, safety, and efficiency. Transplant centres gain a scheduling model that stretches one expensive robot across two linked operations without, in this series, abandoning the approach.
pmc-13392660:
Somchart Tana and seven co-authors mapped how blood measures hang together in beef cows kept by smallholders in northern Thailand, comparing Brahman crosses with Charolais crosses. Ninety-seven healthy breeding cows aged three to six years from three provinces gave blood for automated counts and chemistry. Rather than judging each measure alone, the team used clustering and pattern-finding methods to look for linked groups.

Six tidy modules emerged, covering red cells, platelets, white cells, protein handling, liver enzymes, and kidney function, which supports the idea that blood traits move as coordinated systems. The two breed types overlapped heavily on the main patterns, and breed explained only a sliver of overall variation. The authors suggest farm conditions and daily management shape cow physiology more than breed label in these herds.
pmc-13392960:
Jingyou Zhong and four colleagues pooled randomised trials comparing combined exercise, meaning aerobic work plus resistance training, against aerobic exercise alone in young people carrying excess weight. Twenty-nine trials with close to fourteen hundred participants aged from childhood into mid-adulthood met the entry rules. Body composition, blood pressure, blood fats, and insulin handling were all examined.

Combined training beat aerobic training on lean body mass and on insulin resistance measures, including insulin levels and a standard resistance index. For weight, body mass index, fat share, waist size, systolic pressure, and most blood fats, neither approach pulled clearly ahead, and one healthy cholesterol fraction slightly favoured aerobic work alone. Several pooled results rested on few trials with low certainty, so the authors frame combined training as helpful for chosen goals rather than broadly superior.
pmc-13393260:
Fang Chen and fifteen colleagues report a tiny protein, just one hundred four amino acids long and named MP104, hidden inside a long non-coding RNA and switched up in colorectal cancer. Such microproteins were long overlooked because their parent RNAs were assumed to make nothing. Patients whose tumours carried more MP104 fared worse, which drew the team to test what the protein does in cancer cells.

Laboratory assays showed MP104 driving cell growth, movement, invasion, and spread. Tracing its partners revealed a chain. The protein helps an enzyme tag a metabolic brake for destruction. That frees a growth switch, which stabilises a translation factor. The protein also shields that factor from another disposal route. The net effect is a tumour cell making proteins at full tilt. The authors nominate MP104 as both a warning marker and a drug target.
pmc-13394860:
Eric Williams Jr and co-authors survey, in 2026, the swelling list of scores drawn from glucose sensors in type 1 diabetes. Sensors track sugar every few minutes, far beyond what a single blood test can show. Scores now range from simple time-in-range to blended and research-grade measures. The team read 102 papers and sorted 36 scores into four groups.

Both eyes of a patient stayed in or out together, keeping the analysis honest at the person level. Results help surgeons match lens promises to the daily reading and driving needs patients describe.
pmc-13420960:
Tansha Anand and Neelshan Anand wrote to the editor arguing that laser trials for melasma need objective pigment measures, not just doctors' scores. Melasma is a patchy darkening of facial skin, and the letter responds to a split-face laser trial in Asian women.

The trial graded results with two clinical scales, but both lean on the eye and can miss small pigment shifts. Tools such as light-reflection meters and skin microscopes can measure melanin amount and spread directly, Anand notes. Objective measures would sharpen comparisons between the two lasers, whose gains differed only slightly and never reached significance. They could also flag early pigment return before relapse shows on the skin, the letter adds.
pmc-13421260:
Un and colleagues reviewed in 2026 closing a patent ductus arteriosus in adults by catheter. The ductus is a blood vessel that should close after birth; when it stays open it strains the heart and lungs. Most evidence comes from children, so the authors add data from their multi-centre adult registry.

Adult closure succeeded in about nine in ten to all cases across the reported series. The authors' registry matched that record, with a low rate of complications. Raised pressure in the lung arteries, common in adults with this defect, complicates the choice of who should be closed and how. Adult ducts can also be calcified or oddly shaped, demanding tailored imaging and device choice. The authors call for larger studies to pin down the best approach and long-term outcomes in adults.
pmc-13421360:
Kimberly Zayhowski and six colleagues interview health professionals, in a 2026 study, about checking inherited breast cancer risk before gender-affirming mastectomy. Guidelines clash, so staff fall back on personal judgement, and practice turns uneven. Keen individuals, not set protocols, drive good care. Surgery at a young age tangles the talks, and gaps in the care path put safety at risk. The authors call for standardised routes into surgery.
pmc-13421660:
Heraiz and colleagues tested in 2026 whether a golden barrel cactus and a fungus living inside it can protect nerve cells. The cactus, Echinocactus grusonii, is a Mexican plant known in gardens but little studied chemically. The team profiled extracts from its spines and stem and from its resident fungus, Aspergillus oryzae.

pmc-13423060:
Stefano Mocci and a large Sardinian team use whole-exome sequencing to hunt genetic roots of idiopathic pulmonary fibrosis, a scarring lung disease with no known cause. Studying a founder population with shared ancestry, they reasoned, could surface rare variants that stay hidden in more mixed groups.

A gene-burden test flagged 82 genes rich in damaging variants, among them MUC5B and several genes tied to the tiny hairs that clear airways. Telomere faults and airway-clearing defects, the authors suggest, both feed susceptibility.
pmc-13423160:
Huyen Thi Hoa Nguyen leads a twelve-author qualitative study of family planning among Kinh and Mong communities in Vietnam's Son La province. High fertility is prized locally, yet unsafe abortion is common, and the team set out to learn how cultural and gender norms shape women's control over reproduction.

Participants described husbands and mothers-in-law directing contraceptive choices, and some women refusing intrauterine devices to protect male comfort. Early marriage and the practice called wife snatching were treated as normal tradition. The authors read these accounts as structural and symbolic violence narrowing women's autonomy.
pmc-13423360:
Carnio and colleagues reported in 2026 a late complication in a man burned over sixty percent of his body in a 1989 flame fire. His skin was rebuilt with his own grafts, donor grafts from his father, and cultured sheets of his own skin cells. Calcium built up under the scarred skin, a rare problem that breaks into chronic ulcers and raises cancer risk.

Carnio describes how the first ulcer came in 2004, with lower leg ulcers returning on and off for twenty years. Tissue tests found calcium deposits plus three separate well-differentiated squamous cell cancers growing in the ulcerated areas, the classic pattern of a Marjolin ulcer, cancer arising in a chronic wound. He needed 25 operations to cut out deposits and cancers and rebuild the gaps. The authors urge lifelong watching of large burn scars and quick biopsy of any ulcer that will not heal.
pmc-13424060:
ElNahass and colleagues published a 2026 study on scoring how natural implant gums look. The Pink Esthetic Score grades gum shape around a single front implant. Front-only photos can miss depth, contour, and scarring from other angles. The team built an extended score using front, side, and top photos.

Twenty blinded raters from four dental specialties scored 30 implant cases twice. The extended score added grades for emergence profile and mucosal scarring. The two systems' total scores stayed close on average across cases. Yet scores differed in nearly three of four paired readings overall. Case traits, not rater identity, drove most of the score spread. A fuller view may catch flaws that front photos alone hide.
pmc-13424260:
Woo-Sung Do and four colleagues describe a shoulder operation combining two graft procedures for rotator cuff tears too damaged to repair directly. One method rebuilds the capsule for static stability but can fail or stiffen rotation; the other reroutes the lower trapezius muscle for dynamic power but adds no static support.

The thick graft gives durable top coverage, while a small open extension of one portal eases graft passage and stitch handling. The combined build, shown in an accompanying video, aims for stability and motion while lowering contact pressure in the joint.
pmc-13424360:
Wang and a large team publish an open brainwave dataset in this 2026 resource paper for brain-computer interface research in stroke rehabilitation. Such systems let patients rehearse movements mentally while software reads their intent from scalp electrodes, but progress is limited by scarce, single-task datasets. Their collection adds two imagery tasks and follows patients over time.

Twenty-four stroke patients recorded EEG while imagining movements under two paradigms. One was moving the stroke-affected hand. The other was imagining a sixth finger. That trick comes from robotic extra-limb research and may bypass damaged motor pathways. Recordings span pre-training, post-training, and follow-up stages of rehabilitation, released with clinical information. Standard classifiers distinguished the two imagery tasks at roughly 85 to 86 percent average accuracy in the team's preliminary checks, confirming the data carry usable signal for interface development.
pmc-13424560:
Yerkanat Syrgabek and colleagues review a solvent-free method for capturing coffee's aroma chemicals before lab testing. The method, called solid-phase microextraction, uses a coated fibre that soaks up scent compounds from the sample's air or liquid.

Paired with gas analysis machines and statistics, the fibre method supports aroma profiling, authenticity checks, and sorting coffee samples. Fibre reuse and zero solvent waste stood out as the method's strongest green points.
pmc-13424660:
Puntmann and a large European team report in 2026 the Myoflame-19 trial, testing two repurposed drugs for post-COVID syndrome with heart inflammation. Many patients keep cardiac symptoms long after infection, yet no targeted treatment exists.

The double-blind trial enrolled 279 participants whose heart scans showed inflammatory involvement and assigned them to losartan plus prednisolone or matching placebos for 16 weeks. The main measure, the change in how strongly the heart's main chamber pumps, did not differ meaningfully between groups. Several symptom and imaging measures leaned slightly toward the drug group. Every one of those results remained compatible with no effect, though, so the authors call them leads for future trials rather than findings. Treatment itself proved safe and well tolerated.
pmc-13427060:
Cenkner and colleagues published a 2026 study on a mental fitness app built for US Navy sailors. Sailors face heavy stress from fast work tempos and long deployments. The app teaches clear thinking, calm emotion handling, and problem solving skills. The team tested early versions with 13 first-term sailors aboard a ship.

Sailors in round one gave feedback on a rough draft of one lesson. Their input added a badge game feature and a practice session. Round two used a working draft, with sailors thinking aloud while tapping through. Ratings and talks flagged what felt clear, useful, or clunky to new users. Building with sailors, not just for them, anchors the design approach. The program grew from therapy methods with long clinical track records.
pmc-13427660:
L. Olgiati and co-authors build, in a 2026 study, a language model that predicts which cancer trial patients will quit early. Leaving a trial in the first month, or failing screening, harms patients and slows studies. The team first tuned a French language model on oncology reports from one cancer center, naming it OncoBERT. Consultation notes for trial patients then trained the early-leaving predictor.

On past records covering about a thousand reports, the model caught most early leavers while keeping false alarms moderate. A later, forward-looking test scored lower but still useful marks. Word-level explanations showed the model keyed on signs of worsening general condition, a known risk factor clinicians recognize. The authors suggest pairing such tools with trial-matching software so referrals go to patients likely to stay the course.
pmc-13427960:
Tobias Sjørslev Bodilsen and co-authors audit, in a 2026 Danish study, the side effects of placing several monitoring probes into injured brains. Intensive care teams use combined probes to track skull pressure, brain oxygen, and brain chemistry after severe injury. Records covered 223 patients at one national hospital between 2017 and 2023. Scans after placement were reviewed in 196 of those patients.

About 13 percent of scanned patients had a small bleed at the probe site, and about a third had a probe in a less-than-ideal spot. Air inside the skull and bone fragments also appeared often on scans. Almost none of these findings needed any treatment. Infection was rare, under 1 percent, though probe faults were reported fairly often. Six-month outcomes did not differ for patients with complications, which tempers worry about the technique.
pmc-13428460:
Helena Codes-Méndez and co-authors test whether interferon-related gene activity tracks disease in juvenile dermatomyositis, a childhood disease inflaming muscle and skin. Their 2026 single-centre study relates these gene signatures to standard clinical scores, organ involvement, antibody subgroups, and treatment response.

Seventy-four patients contributed 158 samples. Expression was highest in patients carrying anti-MDA5 and anti-NXP2 antibodies. Over time, gene activity followed disease course and fell in patients reaching inactive disease, including those on the targeted drug baricitinib. The authors propose the signature for monitoring and stratification.
pmc-13429260:
Zimmerer argues in a 2026 commentary that the United States loses lives to addiction partly because most clinicians get little formal training in substance use disorder. Over forty-eight million Americans had the disorder in 2024. Yet more than eighty percent of those needing treatment never received it, and nearly eighty thousand people died of overdoses that year.

Zimmerer, a practicing therapist, describes piloting a training program called Provider's Pathway with psychiatry residents. The training teaches non-judgmental communication, approved medication treatments, and standard screening tools. She argues stigma and knowledge gaps, not lack of empathy, break the clinician-patient relationship on both sides. Because substance use surfaces in primary care and emergency rooms too, she presents the program as a scalable fix beyond addiction specialty settings.
pmc-13430160:
Jian Chen and co-authors feed, in a 2026 study, a plant compound plus a probiotic to laying hens with fatty liver disease. Fatty liver hemorrhagic syndrome plagues caged layers, cutting egg output and sometimes killing birds. Ninety-six hens aged 50 weeks were split into four groups. One group ate normal feed. A second ate an energy-rich, protein-poor diet designed to induce fatty liver. Two more groups ate that diet plus the supplement pair, at low and high doses. The pair joined quercetin, a plant antioxidant, with a Lactobacillus strain.

Supplemented hens kept laying at better rates and carried less liver and belly fat than unsupplemented sick hens. Blood fats also ran lower. Gut microbe mixes shifted away from groups tied to the disease diet, while liver gene activity tilted toward fat burning. Benefits grew with dose. Poultry producers get a feed-based candidate against a costly disorder.
pmc-13431460:
Horrmann and a large team report in 2026 a blood test that uses machine learning, a method that learns patterns from data, to detect early-stage breast cancer from plasma proteins. The test was developed with a company collection of biobanked samples.

The classifier was trained on 845 women and then checked on a separate set of 397 women, of whom 202 had breast cancer and 195 were healthy. In that held-out check it correctly flagged about 93 of every 100 cancers while wrongly flagging fewer than 8 of every 100 healthy women. Accuracy stayed high across cancer stages and subtypes. Simulations suggested the test could catch most cancers that mammography misses when used alongside it.
pmc-13432860:
Guo and colleagues show in 2026 how a pig coronavirus hijacks the cell's waste disposal system to copy itself. Porcine epidemic diarrhea virus kills newborn piglets through severe diarrhea. The team ran a genome-wide knockout screen, disabling one gene at a time in monkey kidney cells, to find host factors the virus needs. Two subunits of the HOPS complex, the machinery that fuses waste sacs with the cell's recycling compartments, stood out.

Deleting either subunit, VPS33A or VPS18, sharply cut virus production and froze disposal midway, with waste sacs formed but never fused. Mapping showed specific regions of each protein are required for both fusion and virus growth. Two viral proteins, nsp3 and nsp4, bind both subunits directly. Each alone starts sac formation, but together they push the process to completion through HOPS. The authors name this fusion step a target for antiviral design.
pmc-13435960:
Aki Gormezano and a large team count new psychosis cases among gay and bisexual men in metro Vancouver in 2026. Health records for 798 men from two cohorts were matched five to one with men from the general pool. Drug use patterns were part of the survey base.

New psychosis ran at 1.74 cases per hundred person years in the cohort. Matched men showed 0.64, so risk sat about 2.7 fold higher. Opioid use, HIV, unstable housing, and anxiety each linked to psychosis within the cohort. The authors point to housing and social support as levers. Care that joins mental health with housing aid may cut new cases.
pmc-13436460:
Aline de Rodrigues de Queiroz and coauthors compare six antioxidants for their grip on a plant heat valve in 2026. The valve, non photochemical quenching, vents excess light as heat to guard photosynthesis. Each antioxidant was dosed across a gradient under matched light and acidity.

Coenzyme M clamped the valve hardest on every gauge. Melatonin and N acetyl cysteine mostly raised its peak or its release. Ascorbate alone sped its opening. Mutant plants show the effects run through the standard valve parts. Two agents push the pigment cycle in opposite directions, which explains their clash. Antioxidant choice in field sprays needs care.
pmc-13436560:
Huo and colleagues compiled a 2026 summary on fall self-awareness in elderly patients after spine fracture surgery. Their fractures came from osteoporosis, a bone-weakening disease, and had been fixed with an operation. Following a ranked evidence model, they searched Chinese and international sources through December 2025 and graded what they found.

Fifteen sources qualified: one clinical decision summary, five guidelines, five expert consensuses, three systematic reviews, and one prior summary. From them the team distilled twenty-eight recommendations in six areas: building a care team from several specialties, fall assessment and screening, health education, osteoporosis self-management, rehabilitation therapy, and follow-up review. They note direct high-quality proof is still thin, and they advise tailoring plans to each patient's fall risk profile and preferences.
pmc-13436660:
Brian Rice and coauthors chart air ambulance care in northwest Alaska from 2020 to 2024 in 2026. Eleven village clinics feed one hub hospital across nearly 36,000 square miles. For many Alaska Native patients the flight is the only link to doctor led emergency care.

The set holds 1,579 flights for 1,119 patients, almost all Alaska Native. Trauma drove about twenty two percent of flights. Median total time ran 262 minutes, far past any golden hour. Decision time, ground wait, and flight time split the total. Each year four to eight percent of the region rides a medevac. Faster decisions may trim total times most.
pmc-13438160:

pmc-13438460: The Frontiers Production Office issued a 2026 correction to a study of hemoglobin and blood movement during dry breath-holding in elite free divers. The notice is a correction only. One percentage in the introduction was printed as twenty percent when it should have read sixty percent. The figure describes the share of a typical man's blood volume held in the muscles and limbs. The corrected passage is reprinted in full, no data or conclusions change, and the original article has been updated.
pmc-13439260:

The stimulant methylphenidate lifts dopamine and noradrenaline, two brain messengers, and aids choice, but which mental step it changes was unknown. Sixty-one adults with the condition and 63 peers without it played a learned cost and gain choice task.

pmc-13441260:

Eight participants dropped out, leaving twenty-seven finishers. Just over half of finishers met the preset acceptance bar, with kidney disease patients accepting at a higher rate than dialysis patients. The authors advise two-way clinician messaging and lighter data entry for the next version.
pmc-13441460:
Fujii reviews preimplantation genomic selection for cattle. Breeding values are estimated from a few cells of an embryo before transfer. So only genetically best animals are produced. Lab-produced embryos implant worse than in-vivo-derived ones, partly through abnormal epigenetic marks and gene expression in culture. Gene expression checks are offered as a hands-on quality check. pmc-13441860:

pmc-13442460:

Lab checks proved plain mature fat with no signs of fat cancer. The authors call the one-stage plan safe and workable for such paired lumps. They also lay out the body maps and cut steps that made the joint fix possible.
pmc-13443560:

Cancer touched 2,782 people, a 4.8 percent share of the pool, with earlier starts than national marks for many types. Wide scans found 132 firm links between cancers and other ills, strongest where the twin ills share a body zone. Gene scans found 39 variant links and 31 gene links, most absent from big gene banks. The authors give the pool as a base for fairer risk tools.
pmc-13445960:

The team trades a slice of fine edge accuracy for speed, pitching the tool as a screen before heavy review.
pmc-13446360:

pmc-13447060:

pmc-13447560:
Viren Sehgal and co-authors report a hybrid fix for a groin artery bulge after a heart valve procedure in a 2026 case study. Bedside injection failed, and both surgery and stenting were judged too risky given the sac's spot near a major branch. pmc-13448060:

Breastbone fractures carry their own associated injury concerns, while diaphragm tears are uncommon yet dangerous when missed, since abdominal organs can slip into the chest. The review organises key findings by injury type for everyday reporting.
pmc-13448460:

pmc-13449060:

pmc-13449660:

It started a week after the twelve-day war and ran over two months.

The headline finding runs against expectation: patients reported lower stress scores than the healthy comparison group. The questionnaire also captured exposure levels, symptom changes such as tremor and slowness, dose adjustments, anxiety medication needs, doctor availability, and interruptions in drug supply. The authors map which symptoms moved with stress in this group, offering rare evidence on how a chronically ill group weathers a national trauma.
pmc-13449860:

pmc-13451560:

pmc-13451860:

Death was scored in the hospital, in the first month home, across the rest of year one, and out to three years.

Past that point, though, both groups died at higher rates in every year checked. The authors say the late gap, not the hospital phase, is where fair care efforts should aim.
pmc-13452160:

pmc-13454460:

pmc-13457360:

pmc-13459460:

pmc-13459960:

pmc-13460160:

pmc-13460860:

pmc-13461960:

pmc-13462060:

pmc-13462360:

pmc-13462560:

pmc-13462960:

pmc-13463860:

pmc-13465460:

pmc-13465560:

pmc-13465760:

pmc-13465960:

pmc-13466660:

pmc-13466960:

pmc-13467060:

pmc-13467360:

pmc-13468060:

pmc-13468160:

pmc-13470260:

pmc-13470360:

pmc-13471660:

pmc-13473160:

pmc-13473960:

pmc-13474760:

pmc-13474860:

pmc-13475660:

pmc-13477060:

pmc-13477360:

pmc-13477760:

pmc-13478060:

pmc-13479460:

The mat measure was repeated in session two to check test-retest reliability, and a survey captured how acceptable and feasible the mat felt as both test and training tool. The authors report whether a single device can credibly serve both measurement and practice roles.
pmc-13479660:
Gerda Marčiūtė, Ignas Lapeikis, and Greta Kasputytė published a 2026 review of virtual reality as an add-on for cutting pain and anxiety during care procedures. Forty papers from 2020 to 2025 were read. Deep distraction works by seizing the focus that pain would claim.

Winning uses spanned shots, blood draws, and vein taps in children, plus work in childbirth, bone surgery, vessel surgery, heart care, and dental care. Across age groups, patients felt less pain and fear during sessions with headsets. Side effects were rare, and spirits rose. The authors conclude virtual reality is safe enough and works well enough to join routine practice, while noting studies vary in task type and depth of the virtual world.
pmc-13480260:
Yaxin Zhao and co-authors present a 2026 study of a pay reform for public hospital staff in China, piloted from 2017. Survey panels covered 102 hospitals and more than 111,000 health workers across fifteen provinces in 2016 and 2017. A matched comparison method split reform effects from wider trends in wages and prices.

After the reform, base pay took a larger slice of total pay, rising by over three points, while merit pay edged up by half a point. Total pay rose slightly, with base pay up by a clear margin and merit pay up less. General hospitals led on base share gains, while specialist hospitals led on merit growth. Contract and short-tenure staff gained performance shares without matching total gains, so the equal-pay aim stayed unmet. The authors urge stronger base pay cover for those groups.
pmc-13483560:
Urechescu and co-authors charted how face and jaw fractures in southwestern Romania changed across the COVID-19 years. Their 2026 study covered 914 patients treated at one major center from late 2017 to late 2025. The team split cases into pre-pandemic, pandemic, and recovery periods and compared fracture patterns, causes, and treatments month by month.

Monthly case numbers dipped while pandemic restrictions held, then climbed back afterward toward earlier levels. Yet the recovery was uneven, and the share of patients with documented related injuries stayed lower after the pandemic than before it. The statistical model explained only part of the month-to-month swing, which the authors flag openly. Urechescu cautions that trauma services should plan for rebounds after lockdowns while keeping better injury records than the pandemic years produced.
pmc-13483860:
Wancheng Liao investigates fat droplets as a hiding strategy that lets colorectal cancer cells sleep through chemotherapy and later return. Published in 2026, the work builds dormant, growing, and relapsed cell states from patient-derived grafts and cell lines, then profiles gene activity and droplet contents. Candidate control genes are tested by silencing, boosting, drug blocking, and mutation.

Sleeping cells carried more lipid droplets than growing or relapsed cells. A partner transcription factor switches ACSL5 on directly. Breaking the chain drained droplets, raised reactive oxygen, and woke the cells, while high ACSL5 in patients tracked with worse outlook. A dormancy maintenance circuit is exposed.
pmc-13486460:
Suwatjanee Naephrai characterizes the venom of a tropical tree ant and finds its main weapon is a doubled peptide with a repeated evolutionary story. The peptide bursts cells, fires mammalian pain neurons, and kills insects.

Similar doubled peptides with similar jobs turn up in other ant lineages that are not close relatives. Independent invention several times over marks the dimer design as a repeatable winning solution rather than a shared inheritance. Ant venoms prove far more inventive at the architecture level than a single-family story would suggest, which matters for anyone mining venoms for drugs or insecticides.
pmc-13486660:
Ruan and team worked out how to calibrate an infrared star-measuring tool whose design defeats ordinary tuning. Its eyepiece is gone, its view is narrow, and its sensor resolution is low. The two-face trick separates the target's true direction from the camera's center-point position, which otherwise trade off against each other hopelessly. With that constraint, the remaining camera settings fall out at the precision sky work demands. Field checks confirmed the tuning held under real watching conditions. Ruan offers the method for other compact infrared tools that share the same tuning headache.
pmc-13487960:
Hernan Andres de la Barra Ortiz and colleagues review high-intensity laser therapy for patellofemoral pain in a 2026 systematic review and meta-analysis. This pain sits around the kneecap and is common in active people. They searched many databases for randomized trials and judged study quality with standard tools. Only four small trials qualified, and every one paired the laser treatment with therapeutic exercise such as strengthening or stretching.

Laser plus exercise reduced pain more than control care right after treatment and at follow-up in pooled results. Function scores did not differ clearly between groups. All trials carried high risk of bias, samples were tiny, and results varied, so confidence in the findings is very low. The authors ask for larger, better trials before firm advice is possible.
pmc-13488160:
Yanwei Lv and co-authors design flower-shaped nanoparticles to treat chronic pancreatitis in a 2026 animal and laboratory study. The disease brings lasting pancreas inflammation, scarring, and loss of function, with few effective drugs. The team first tracked pyroptosis during disease development. Pyroptosis is a fiery form of cell death. They then built particles carrying the drug disulfiram inside a coating that responds to gut conditions. The coating lets release happen near the target.

In a mouse model, the particles eased inflammation and scarring, calmed the cell death pathway, and helped restore pancreas structure and digestive output in the reported tests. Gene activity patterns shifted back toward normal, mainly in secretion pathways. The authors present the platform as a delivery strategy needing further safety work.
pmc-13488560:
Hye-Young Yoon and colleagues survey surface disinfection practice among dental hygienists in South Korea in a 2026 questionnaire study. Germs can survive on clinic surfaces, and standard methods exist for each surface type, yet real-world uptake was little studied. Responses from 182 hygienists were analyzed by surface, patient load, and whether the clinic had a named infection control staff member, after incomplete replies were removed.

Full standard practice was rare everywhere, peaking at under a quarter for the bracket table and falling to near zero for drawer handles in the reported rates. Hygienists seeing forty or more patients daily followed standards more often than those seeing few patients. Clinics with a designated infection control person also did better. The authors call for simpler, better-supported routines.
pmc-13491360:
Ramos and colleagues map in 2026 the literature on X-linked dystonia-parkinsonism, a hereditary movement disorder affecting mostly Filipino men with roots on Panay Island. Research had concentrated on genes and movement while neglecting diagnosis, care, and daily life.

The scoping review included 27 studies. The typical course starts with twisting movements in one body part, spreads widely, and adds parkinsonism within a year or two. Most patients tested carried the disease-causing change in the TAF1 gene, yet diagnosis still takes years. Deep brain stimulation reduced the severity of the dystonia, and medicines brought partial benefit. Qualitative studies surfaced stigma, loss of identity, heavy caregiver burden, and financial hardship alongside coping and resilience. The authors call for care models that add psychosocial support to genetic and clinical services.
pmc-13492460:
Meganathan and co-workers in California unveiled in 2026 a chip that can taste potassium at the scale of one heart cell. Potassium flow sets the heart's rhythm, and early faults in that flow warn of rhythm trouble. Older tools read all ions at once or pierce the cell, which harms long term study. Their platform, named KINESIS, grows a forest of tiny pillars tipped with a membrane that picks out potassium alone.

The team grew heart cells made from human stem cells on the pillars. The cells sat on the tips without their skins being pierced. Drug tests gave clear, split readouts: caffeine and ouabain, two drugs that move potassium in known ways, each shifted the signal as the books predict. The authors pitch the chip for drug safety screens and for modeling a single patient's heart faults in a dish.
pmc-13493360:
Xia and colleagues tested in 2026 a modified curcumin compound against glioblastoma, the most aggressive common brain tumour. The compound, called DMC-GF, derives from demethoxycurcumin, a relative of the turmeric pigment. The team ran lab assays on tumour cells and a mouse model with tumours grown in the brain.

DMC-GF significantly suppressed tumour cell growth, triggered programmed cell death, and strongly slowed tumour growth in the mice. It targeted a growth kinase and interacted with a regulator protein, changing the STAT3/AKT signalling axis, a key survival pathway. That shift triggered the mitochondrial route to cell death. Profiling pointed to mitochondrial energy production as a central event in the response. The authors position DMC-GF as a promising candidate drug for glioblastoma. They note such candidates matter because current glioblastoma treatment options remain poor.
pmc-13495160:
Nattanich Intagun, Wannapa Chinadet, and Pinpinut Wanichsaithong survey, in a 2026 study, how ready dentists in Northern Thailand feel to treat patients who have intellectual or learning disabilities. These patients face steep barriers to dental care and suffer worse oral health. The team sent a tested questionnaire to dentists in public hospitals across seventeen provinces and gathered 306 replies.

Most dentists had treated such patients, yet two thirds saw fewer than ten a year. Talking with patients and managing behavior topped the list of hard parts. Over half felt high stress, and some said stress cut the quality of care. Nearly all judged their undergraduate training too thin. Having enough staff and equipment was the one clear driver of confidence, while stress rose with long experience and further degrees. The authors call for stronger training, better-staffed clinics, and firmer referral paths.
pmc-13495260:
Pin Cao, Peng Liu, Lu Ji, and Chong Qiao hunt, in a 2026 study, for warning signs of massive bleeding during cesarean delivery in a high-risk placenta group. Their patients had complete placenta previa, where the placenta covers the cervix, joined with placenta accreta spectrum, where it grows too deeply into the womb wall. Most research covers women with a past cesarean; this group had none.

The team reviewed 109 such patients at one Chinese hospital over five years. About one in five lost at least two liters of blood in surgery, the study's mark for massive bleeding. Three warning signs stood out on their own: older maternal age, a past scope procedure to cut womb adhesions, and a higher pre-surgery ultrasound risk score. The authors urge teams to weigh the woman's history beside the scan score, since scans alone can understate the danger.
pmc-13495360:
Samangan and colleagues showed in 2026 that acute B-cell lymphoblastic leukemia cells remodel their bone marrow home by shedding large oncosomes, oversized parcels budded from cancer cells. Leukemia is known to coach nearby support cells into aiding its growth and drug resistance, but the parcel traffic behind this coaching in this subtype was unclear. The work traces how the large vesicles condition mesenchymal stromal cells, the marrow's support layer.

Conditioned support cells changed the supply of IGF1, a growth factor the leukemia feeds on, in the marrow space. Earlier work from the group ties a clot-dissolving system to freeing this same factor from the surrounding matrix, and the vesicle route now joins that picture. The authors argue that cutting this parcel traffic could starve the leukemia of local support and soften its resistance to chemotherapy, a strategy worth testing in this aggressive childhood cancer.
pmc-13498460:
Shuji Kubo and colleagues test in 2026 whether stem cells can ferry a cancer-killing virus more effectively to tumours spread across the abdomen. The virus copies itself inside cancer cells and carries a gene that makes those cells kill themselves, yet body fluids can inactivate it before arrival. Stem cells that home toward tumours offered a possible shield and transport route, studied here in mesothelioma, a cancer of the lining tissues.

Stem cells from fat, bone marrow, and cord tissue all moved toward tumour cells and produced the virus in the lab. In mouse models mimicking fluid-filled abdominal spread, stem-cell delivery spread the virus through tumours far better than virus alone. Tumour shrinkage was stronger and survival longer with the combined approach under those fluid conditions.
pmc-13498560:
Ningthoujam and a large Indian team spent three years cataloguing fruit flies in Meghalaya, in the country's northeast, where records were scarce despite the insects' power to ruin harvests. From October 2020 to September 2023 they trapped across forest, orchard, and vegetable plots in Ri-Bhoi district. Fruit flies in this family can cause near-total crop losses.

The survey netted 37 species spread across several genera, with Bactrocera the dominant group in the region. Two species were entirely new to science, both in the genus Zeugodacus and found on Khasi mandarin, a local citrus. Community makeup differed clearly between the three ecosystems, with a core of widespread species persisting everywhere and rarer species tied to single habitats. The authors offer the dataset as the reference point for tracking how the region's fruit fly fauna shifts with land use and climate.
pmc-13498960:
Ayesha Almarzooqi and co-authors present in 2026 a rare injury case involving a blood collection under the cartilage at the rim of a child's nostril. Nasal injuries are common because the nose sticks out, yet blood collections usually form in the central septum and count as emergencies. Collections at the outer rim cartilage are far rarer, with only a handful of published cases, mostly in children.

Their patient was a three-year-old girl seen after facial trauma. Untreated collections of this kind can starve cartilage of blood, leading to tissue death, scarring, or infection that spreads deeper. Prompt recognition, surgical drainage, and antibiotic cover are presented as the safeguards against lasting damage. The warning covers both the look and the function of the nose, aimed at clinicians who may never have seen this site involved.
pmc-13499360:
Ahmed Jamal Chaudhary and co-authors test in 2026 whether two cheap admission blood measures can warn early that sepsis patients will develop organ failure. Sepsis, a dangerous response to infection, kills many patients worldwide, and spotting high-risk cases at arrival guides urgent care. Their cross-sectional study ran at a medical college in Turbat, Pakistan, from January to June 2025, enrolling 384 adults with sepsis by consecutive sampling.

Just over one third of patients developed organ dysfunction, and that group arrived with far higher values for a white-cell ratio and for creatinine, a kidney-related waste marker. Both measures predicted dysfunction well in curve analysis and stayed independent predictors after adjustment for other factors. The authors propose the pair as simple, low-cost tools for early risk sorting where advanced tests are scarce, while noting that neither marker is unique to sepsis.
pmc-13499660:
Ronny Vargas and a large co-author team trace in 2026 the path of nanotechnology, engineering at the scale of billionths of a metre. The field has moved from early liposomes in the 1960s toward today's nucleic acid delivery systems. Carriers built from fats, polymers, and inorganic materials can shield drugs and steer them to diseased tissue. The review sorts these carrier families and gives concrete examples of products already approved for sale.

Development energy now concentrates on cancer, infectious disease, brain disorders, and heart and vessel disease, with fat-based nanoparticles gaining ground in pipelines for gene silencing and gene editing therapies. Barriers to clinic remain practical, covering manufacturing scale, long-term stability, regulatory uncertainty, patent issues, and animal models that poorly mirror human disease. No single carrier suits every use, so progress depends on several platforms each proving its own niche.
pmc-13499960:
Ilgın Arı and co-authors test in 2026 an artificial intelligence model that outlines jaw fractures on cone-beam CT scans, a three-dimensional dental imaging method. Accurate fracture mapping guides surgery for lower jaw breaks, a common facial injury. Scan data from 92 patients covering 142 fracture sites were gathered retrospectively, with two maxillofacial surgeons hand-drawing the reference outlines. A standard self-configuring network was trained on most cases and tested on the rest.

Performance was scored two ways, by whole volume and slice by slice, using overlap and distance measures. Volume-based scores beat slice-based scores on every reported metric, with moderate overlap accuracy overall and smaller surface errors in three dimensions. The authors conclude that judging such tools volumetrically gives a fuller and more reliable picture, even though absolute segmentation accuracy remains limited and needs improvement before clinical trust.
pmc-13500660:
Hui Hou and co-authors report in 2026 a treatment that breaks a longstanding trade-off in glow-after-light materials, where plastics that glow longer usually glow dimmer. Their strategy soaks a phosphor-loaded polymer film in an iodine and boric acid treatment. Iodine's heavy atoms help excited molecules cross into the long-lived triplet states that produce afterglow. The treatment simultaneously knits an exceptionally dense cross-linked network that shields those states from being quenched by vibration and air.

The treated film's afterglow lifetime stretched past a full second, a roughly twenty-eight-fold increase in the reported measurements. Its efficiency climbed to about a third of absorbed energy, a similar fold gain. Durability impressed as much as brightness, with bright emission surviving five days underwater and hours in acid, alkali, and hot water. Multicolour security printing, antibacterial surfaces, and water-resistant labels are the suggested destinations.
pmc-13501160:
Aditi Das Shroddha leads a three-author team with a 2026 cardiology case in which a consumer smartwatch first caught a dangerous heart rhythm. An initial catheter ablation, which burns the faulty circuit inside the heart, seemed to settle the problem, yet the arrhythmia returned.

That inherited condition replaces heart muscle with fat and fibrous tissue and can cause sudden death in young athletes. Because the arrhythmias kept recurring and the scar burden was large, doctors implanted a defibrillator under the skin for protection. The case argues for continued doubt when rhythm problems return after ablation.
pmc-13501660:
Christine W St Laurent leads a ten-author team with a 2026 systematic review of how sleep gets measured in studies that use compositional data analysis. That approach treats the day as a fixed budget of sitting, activity, and sleep. Earlier reviews covered activity and sitting reporting but not sleep. The team searched seven databases plus citation chasing and expert input, keeping studies published since 2015 that paired device-measured sleep with the compositional method. Extraction followed sleep medicine guidance for actigraphy practice.

Seventy studies qualified, 60 cross-sectional and 10 longitudinal. Few reported key details of how sleep was measured or processed. Most, 67 studies, included only one sleep component in the daily composition, and fewer than half, 29 studies, noted any sleep-related limitation. Sixty studies rated good quality and ten poor on the assessment tool used. The authors call for standard sleep processing and fuller reporting.
pmc-13501860:

Stage one built the app, with a Python Flask and SQLite back end and a Flutter front end. The dropout rate was 42.5 percent across the arms. The team expects tailored training to reduce severity and strengthen the doctor-patient relationship. The trial sits in the Iranian registry under code IRCT20200721048162N1.
pmc-13502660:
Jurgen Schulz leads an eight-author team reporting a 2026 advance: light-activated labelling reagents fast enough to watch dilute biomolecules in real time. Reaction switches the fluorescence on, brightening up to 150-fold, which removes the washing problem.
