Because the probes are photo-triggered, users also gain timing control over when labelling starts. The authors expect the reagents to open real-time imaging of scarce targets in complex environments.
pmc-13505060:
Neerod Kumar Jha, Abbas Abdul Hassan, and Mohamed Elmahi review what weighs on families through children's heart surgery, from a Middle Eastern view, in a 2026 paper. In the region, family cohesion, faith, many languages, and uneven access shape the path to recovery. The authors urge team-based care, counseling, funding support, and wise use of technology, backed by insurers, hospitals, and schools pulling together.
pmc-13505160:
Qiang Huang, Guangjie Wang, Lei Hu, and Jiahui Xie tracked how land use shapes the carbon balance of counties across China's Chengdu Plain. The plain matters as both a fast-growing economic region and an ecological shield for the upper Yangtze.

From 2000 onward, construction land grew while farmland, forest, and grassland shrank, a pattern projected to continue toward 2030. Net emissions rose first, peaked in 2020, and then eased in the projection. Built land was the main carbon source and forest the main store, together dominating the budget. Spending levels, urban growth, and population pushed emissions up, while investment slightly held them back. The authors propose different carbon plans for city-centre, industrial, and less developed counties rather than one regional rule.
pmc-13506660:

Drug groups ranged from classic chemotherapy to targeted drugs, immune drugs, and antibody-drug pairs.

Harms touched the eye surface, retina, optic nerve, and inner eye, and patterns varied by drug group. Reports on Asian patients were patchy. The authors offer a symptom-based guide for clinics without an eye doctor on site. Steps stress early spotting, simple supportive care, pausing treatment for lasting symptoms, and fast referral when vision falls.
pmc-13506960:
Lucia Yang and colleagues report in 2026 a gene-silencing strategy against diffuse midline glioma, a deadly childhood brain cancer. Most of these tumors carry a mutation in a histone gene, H3-3A, that poisons the cell's gene-control marks and drives growth.

The team designed short synthetic strands, called antisense oligonucleotides, that force the cell to skip the gene segment holding both the mutation and the start signal. Their lead strand skipped that segment precisely, spared a near-identical sister gene, and restored normal chemical marks in tumor cells grown from patients. In mice bearing patient tumors, it slowed growth and extended survival. The authors present exon skipping as a practical way to switch off a harmful gene.
pmc-13507060:
Hoyin Chu leads a 2026 study of angiosarcoma, a rare cancer of blood vessel lining cells, built with direct patient partnership. Tumors under the skin often showed growth signals tied to certain driver genes, while skin tumors leaned on MYC programs and sun-linked change patterns. People born with a harmful POT1 variant faced a far higher risk, and those with a second hit in tumors fell ill decades earlier. Site-aware biology could guide drug choices for this hard cancer.
pmc-13507160:

Eighteen women who had received chemotherapy for at least six months gave in-depth interviews in February and March 2020. Talks in Tigrigna were transcribed, translated, and coded jointly for shared themes.

Fear about the future weighed heavily, while counseling eased distress over time. Social isolation and treatment costs added strain. Stronger counseling, mental support, and financial aid are urged.
pmc-13508360:
Tianjiao Zhang leads a twelve-author team presenting SINTER3D, a method that rebuilds full three-dimensional gene activity maps from thin tissue slices, in 2026 work. Spatial transcriptomics reads which genes are active while keeping their place in tissue, yet slices leave large gaps when stacked. Older filling methods treat each gene separately and blur the picture. SINTER3D instead learns gene activity as a smooth function of three-dimensional position using a neural model. The team tested the system on adult mouse brain, human cortex, developing human heart, fruit fly embryo, and breast cancer tissue. Across these sets it beat existing methods and rebuilt structures that made biological sense. The tool could help turn stacks of slices into true three-dimensional atlases of organs and tumors.
pmc-13508460:

Such a scan could help clinics triage dryness complaints without jumping straight to invasive gland biopsy, though sharper cutoffs are still needed.
pmc-13512160:
Priyanka Banerjee, Rachel Phillips, Anna G. Holliman, Soren P. Rodning, Wellison J. S. Diniz, and Paul W. Ninety genes differed in activity between the groups, including immune and signaling genes, and nine metabolites differed in the fluid, spanning vitamins, amino acids, and fatty compounds. Network maps in subfertile heifers looked heavily rewired next to fertile ones. Two metabolites, a fatty acid tied to inflammation and a vitamin E form, connected widely to immune genes. Pathway patterns split by group, with sugar and building-block routes marking fertile animals and protein-assembly routes marking subfertile ones.
pmc-13512260:
Aaron Chigona and eight co-authors assess health risks from eating wild foods and soil-like materials gathered along Zimbabwe's Great Dyke, in 2026 work. Rocks in the area carry toxic elements from the ground itself, and the team measured those contaminants against world health limits.

Half of the wild foods studied crossed the tolerable risk levels set by global food bodies. A wild fig and soil materials from the ultramafic Great Dyke ground carried the highest cancer and non-cancer risks. Taking medicinal plants as hot infusions cut contaminant intake a good deal. The authors urge environmental health policies that raise community awareness of the danger while respecting food traditions, plus safer preparation guidance.
pmc-13513360:
Irina Lyapina and eight co-authors study whether excess fat around the heart predicts how heart muscle remodels after mitral valve surgery, in 2026 work. The prospective study screened 148 patients with acquired, non-infectious mitral valve disease set for surgical repair under a heart-lung machine. Crossing that fat threshold multiplied the odds of a low right-heart motion score several times over. A second threshold tied to clustering metabolic risk factors framed another comparison. The authors argue that fat around the heart is not inert padding but a marker, and possibly a driver, of worse remodeling around valve surgery.
pmc-13515660:
Sun and colleagues built new drug candidates against tuberculosis by fusing two known weapons into single molecules, work reported in 2026. Safety tests in mouse immune cells were encouraging: every cycloserine hybrid needed more than 40 micrograms per milliliter to harm half the cells, far gentler than thiolutin alone. Two hybrids, T1-CS and T4-CS, gave the best balance of potency and safety.
pmc-13517660:
Tong Guo and a large team report a mouse study, published in 2026. It asks whether polystyrene microplastics worsen liver harm from cadmium. Cadmium is a toxic metal. Mice received microplastics, cadmium, or both. Exposure lasted six weeks. The team examined liver injury. Gene activity in the liver was examined too.

Mice exposed to both pollutants had the worst liver damage. Their stress and inflammation signals were strongest. Their energy use was most deeply disturbed. The combined exposure disrupted a control pathway. It involves the AMPK and FOXO regulators. The liver cells' mitochondria were impaired. Plastic particles can amplify cadmium's harm in mammals, not just in fish, this suggests.
pmc-13517960:

Overall, 3.87 percent of samples were positive, spread across seventeen administrative regions, and among positives Babesia major made up 31.2 percent, Babesia occultans 29.6 percent, Babesia bigemina 18.0 percent, and the more dangerous Babesia bovis only 7.2 percent of detections. Infection rates varied sharply by region. The authors say molecular monitoring found babesiosis in regions where it had never been recorded.
pmc-13518960:
G Keerthana and R Padmanaban present HOA-OBL in 2026, a hybrid tool for assigning tasks to drone fleets. Opposition-based learning was woven in so the search also probes mirror-image plans, widening the hunt. Tests with 20 drones and 100 tasks cut energy use by roughly 17 to 33 percent versus four rival algorithms. Load spread evened out by about 33 to 50 percent. The pair argue the pairing scales better for real missions.
pmc-13520060:
Antreana Hadjipavlou leads a seven-author narrative review in 2026 on artificial intelligence tools for preserving the parathyroid glands during thyroid removal surgery. Missing or damaging these tiny glands causes lasting low calcium, a common and sometimes dangerous complication. Visual spotting by the surgeon remains standard, yet glands are small and wander in location.

Searching three databases for work from 2015 to 2025 surfaced 368 records, of which 11 studies qualified, covering AI or deep learning identification, often paired with near-infrared autofluorescence imaging. Hadjipavlou and colleagues judge the techniques feasible and promising for accuracy and speed. Evidence is still limited, so they call for high-quality prospective studies before clinical benefit can be claimed.
pmc-13520160:
Yu-yang Du leads an eleven-author review in 2026 on lipophagy, the process by which cells digest their own fat droplets through the lysosome, the cell's recycling compartment. Stuck fat droplets poison cells and feed metabolic, heart, cancer, and brain diseases. How droplets get selected for digestion, and how to tune the process safely, remained unclear.

Effective digestion needs the droplet coat remodeled, nutrient sensors such as the AMPK-mTORC1-TFEB axis coordinating lysosome supply, and contact points where droplets trade lipids with other organelles. Lipophagy protects when it clears excess fat, yet misfiring can fuel inflammation, scarring, or tumors. The reviewers call for better biomarkers and tissue- and stage-specific interventions.
pmc-13520260:
Haiyue Wu leads a thirteen-author genome survey in 2026 of the myosin gene family in the Chinese mitten crab, a farmed freshwater species whose muscles rebuild in bursts at each molt. Gene activity was tracked across three larval stages, from swimming zoea through megalopa to early juvenile, alongside a full catalog of myosin genes.

The crab genome holds 23 myosin genes in 11 subfamilies, with the muscle-heavy Myo2 group expanded to nine members, likely through tandem copying on one chromosome. Comparisons across 42 animal species showed some myosin classes missing from all arthropods, marking lineage losses. Activity of individual genes rose or fell by stage, matching each phase's muscle demands during metamorphosis.
pmc-13520360:
Natalie B. Lister leads a large team that codes in 2026 what sits inside adult weight loss trials. All trials in the set also tracked eating disorder risk. Trials bundle many parts together. Sorting the parts may show which ones raise risk and which ones lower it.

The search found nearly 15,000 records at first pass. A total of 58 trials fit the coding rules. The trial teams checked coding for 26 of those trials. Checked arms used about 24 methods on average. Methods grouped into clusters such as food teaching. The list gives future trial teams shared words for planning safer weight loss care.
pmc-13521160:
Hosaam Nasr, Faisal A. Almudaiheem and Bader S. Alhamdan describe in 2026 limb-saving hybrid treatment for sudden leg artery blockage appearing shortly after knee replacement surgery. Such blockages are uncommon after joint replacement, yet delayed recognition risks limb loss because pain mimics normal post-surgery soreness.

Care combined open surgery to clear the artery behind the knee with catheter-based methods to restore flow down the leg. Trial evidence cited suggests hybrid routes can match limb salvage of either approach alone. The case walks through diagnostic pitfalls and staged revascularisation choices, offering a template for orthopaedic and vascular teams facing the same emergency.
pmc-13522360:
Xiaoxuan Zhu and colleagues published a 2026 community study from the Jidong area of China that sets reference ranges for blood vessel density in the macula, the central part of the retina. Healthy adults provided the reference group, while a separate group was used to test links with body-wide illness. Measurements came from OCT angiography, a scan that maps tiny retinal vessels without dye.

Reference percentiles were built separately by age, sex, and eye length for two layers of small vessels near the fovea. Diabetes stood out in the second group, where people with diabetes tended to have lower density in the deeper layer and more often fell below low percentile cutoffs. Clinicians could use the ranges to judge an individual scan, although testing in other populations and on other devices is still needed.
pmc-13524160:
Pi-Yi Lin, Yu-Tong Yen, Ming-Jen Lu, and Han-Shui Hsu study, in a 2026 cohort, whether meeting early calorie targets helps septic patients in intensive care, grouped by nutritional risk score. Malnutrition is common in critical illness, yet benefit from early feeding was uncertain. The analysis used the modified Nutrition Risk in the Critically Ill score.

The cohort held 258 ventilated adults with sepsis in a surgical intensive care unit during 2021 and 2022. About 63 percent received under half of estimated calorie needs in the first five days, and the rest received at least half. Twenty-eight-day intensive care mortality did not differ significantly between groups. Kidney replacement therapy and longer ventilation predicted death in adjusted analysis. The authors conclude early calorie adequacy alone did not improve survival here.
pmc-13525960:
Cigdem Soydal leads a very large multicenter team in a 2026 study of dose and survival after transarterial radioembolization for a bile duct cancer arising inside the liver. The treatment delivers radioactive yttrium-90 microspheres through liver arteries. Which dose measures predict response and survival, for glass versus resin spheres, was the central question.

The retrospective cohort gathered patients treated between January 2014 and December 2024 across thirteen centers with lobar or segmental approaches. Post-treatment imaging, either SPECT or PET based, was reviewed centrally, and absorbed doses were computed for perfused liver, tumor, and whole liver with specialist software. Response was judged by comparing scans before treatment with scans two to four months later, grouping complete and partial responses together. Liver toxicity was graded on a standard scale.
pmc-13526460:
Bong and colleagues report a 2026 case of a 41-year-old woman who developed a painful left buttock mass years after gluteal fat grafting, known as a Brazilian butt lift. Her swelling appeared five years after a revision surgery, far later than most complications of the procedure.

Surgeons removed a mass measuring about five centimeters across and sent it for testing. The tissue showed fat death, hardening deposits, and a pocket of inflammation, but tests found no bacteria and no cancer. The authors note that such delayed sterile reactions can look like infection or tumors. They urge long-term follow-up after buttock fat grafting so late problems are caught and treated correctly.
pmc-13528060:
Mengjie Chen and three colleagues profile how lupus patients respond to the drug telitacicept in a 2026 exploratory study. The drug blocks two signals that drive antibody-making cells. Ten patients were sampled before and after treatment. Ten healthy controls joined for comparison. The team sequenced gene activity and B-cell receptor repertoires. Clinical scores were tracked for twelve months.

Treatment shrank B-cell clone diversity and lowered plasma cell estimates. Naive B cells partly recovered. Clones using three gene families tied to disease activity largely vanished. Genes in two growth pathways switched down. An unexpected rise in interferon-driven genes appeared after treatment. Patients with that rise improved fast at first, then slipped back. The authors urge bigger studies to test that signal.
pmc-13529860:
Yoshinobu Kanda and six colleagues report a phase three trial of maribavir for cytomegalovirus in Japanese transplant patients in a 2026 study. The virus threatens people whose immunity is suppressed after grafts. Sixty-one patients enrolled at twenty-two sites. Forty-one received the oral drug, twice daily for eight weeks. Most were stem cell transplant recipients.

By week eight about sixty-eight percent had cleared the virus from blood, confirmed by repeat tests. About eighty-eight percent reported some side effect. Nausea led at about twenty-four percent, then anemia, fever, and headache. Two deaths occurred and were judged unrelated to the drug. The authors call the balance of benefit and tolerability acceptable. The group included patients whose infections resisted standard drugs. Maribavir thus fills a real gap in post-transplant care.
pmc-13530160:
Chih-Ping Hu and co-authors simulate in 2026 how chip panels warp and peel during fan-out panel-level packaging. Two build orders receive comparison: wiring first versus molding first. Carrier plates of steel, glass, and ceramic support the work, and two large panel sizes enter the models.

Heat, material shrinkage, and stepwise adding or removing of layers all shape the predicted bending. The wiring-first route matched real results best at an average reference temperature. Stress peaked in the same layers across cases, while the molding-first route warped sharply when panels were released. Close agreement with experiments backed the design guidance.
pmc-13531060:
Ajay P Kerai and co-authors detail a 2026 combined heart-lung transplant for a giant pulmonary artery aneurysm driven by high lung pressure. The 58-year-old woman had longstanding pressure disease of unknown cause, heart strain, and a leaking pulmonic valve. Her aneurysm had grown close to nine centimeters across.

Transplant replaced both organs at once, and graft function stayed excellent afterward. A stroke during recovery caused major lasting harm despite the sound grafts. The authors note aneurysms can keep growing even when pressure readings look stable, so waiting too long can close the transplant window.
pmc-13531760:
Priyadarshini Dutta and co-authors test in 2026 whether vaped cannabidiol relieves nerve pain in rats without harming lungs. Animals with a squeezed sciatic nerve breathed CBD vapor through a custom automated exposure rig that measured dosing precisely. Plain carrier chemicals used in vape liquids were tested alongside.

CBD vapor did ease pain measurably. Lung tissue showed shifts in inflammatory signals and in a danger-sensing pathway that may explain harm. The carrier mix alone sparked a strong inflammatory response, undercutting claims that such additives are harmless. Benefit and lung risk arrived together, urging caution.
pmc-13531960:
O Trent Hall and colleagues survey in 2026 whether pain erodes safer injection habits among people who inject opioids. A total of 130 people recruited at a syringe service program compared their own practices during best and worst pain over the prior week. Everyone had training and free sterile equipment, which isolates pain as the variable.

At worst pain, participants washed hands less, cleaned the injection site less, and waited less often for a clean safe place. Equipment reuse rose, as did injecting faster or at a higher dose. Pain itself emerges as a harm-reduction target beside equipment supply.
pmc-13532760:
Chen and Martinez-Cardoso studied job lock in 2026, the bind of older workers who keep working out of need even though they want to retire. Using a long-running national survey of Americans aged 50 and over, they tracked 5,217 workers for more than six years to see whether feeling locked in predicted later health problems.

Job lock was common, reported by more than three in four workers at the start. Those workers later had higher odds of rating their health as fair or poor, of depressive symptoms, of other psychiatric problems. Of being overweight or obese, even after pay, background, and habits were taken into account. Links grew stronger for people who stayed employed the whole period, and for workers aged 62 and over heart disease joined the list. The authors urge steps that lower the money and insurance barriers to retiring.
pmc-13534660:
Matej Martinc and colleagues benchmark in 2026 machine learning models that map electric polarisation in ferroelectric materials from advanced electron microscope data. Such maps reveal function, yet reading them from four-dimensional diffraction data is hard by hand. Four model types were trained and compared on a niobate material.

Models trained on synthetic patterns scored high on matching synthetic tests, yet the gap to real experiments stayed a major barrier. A prototype training scheme plus classic dimension methods with augmentation looked most promising for closing that gap. Error patterns also matched crystal defects, hinting at defect detection uses.
pmc-13536760:
Clement Munguiko leads a 2026 scoping review mapping models for teaching health trainees at the bedside. Training now demands shared skills worldwide, yet guidance on teaching models stays scattered. Searches in early January 2026 across five databases plus grey sources covered work from 2000 to 2025. From thousands of records, 26 studies qualified and eight distinct teaching models were mapped.

Two models appeared most often, one built around brief focused coaching and one built around learner-led case reasoning. Most studies came from the United States and involved medical students, with none from Africa. No single model fit every setting. Clear structure, active learner roles, reflection, feedback, and role modeling recurred across models. The authors urge faculty training and research in low-resource settings.
pmc-13536860:
Alemayehu Abate and Melkamnesh Azage study bloodstream infections in young children in Bahir Dar, Ethiopia, in a 2026 clinic survey from late 2025. Blood infections with drug-resistant germs threaten children under five years most. A total of 281 febrile children at a specialized hospital gave blood for culture and drug testing, while parents answered structured questions. Models searched for factors tied to positive cultures.

About one in five children had a bloodstream infection, most often from Klebsiella pneumoniae, with gut and related germs making up most isolates. Resistance ran high against many common antibiotics and lowest against two reserve options. Infants, fever lasting over a week, and partial or missing immunization each raised infection odds. The authors urge stronger drug oversight, fuller immunization, and faster diagnosis.
pmc-13538060:
Saadia N. Mirza and colleagues report new enzyme routes to improved polyene antifungals in a 2026 study. Polyenes kill fungi broadly yet harm patients through toxicity and dissolve poorly, while chemical rebuilding is costly and wasteful. The team uncovered pathways to previously unknown polyenes, including unusual enzymes that attach sugars to the core structure. A second enzyme family was also retuned to swap a harmful chemical group for friendlier options.

Adding a second sugar plus swapping the harmful group produced polyenes with stronger fungal killing and lower toxicity in tests. Clean fermentation and enzyme routes reached the new compounds without heavy chemical synthesis. The authors present enzyme tailoring as a practical path to safer, more affordable antifungal drugs as resistance rises.
pmc-13538460:
Hirotake Ishida and colleagues track sensory nerve activity after burn injury in mice in a 2026 study of lingering pain and itch. Burns often leave weeks of itch during healing, yet nerve workings behind the timeline stay unclear. A scald burn on cheek skin produced pain-like wiping and itch-like scratching behaviors on different schedules. Live calcium imaging watched face nerve cluster cells at rest and under chemical probes across recovery days.

Pain behavior peaked on the first day and faded within five days, while itch behavior peaked at one week and lasted up to four weeks. Numbers of spontaneously active nerve cells rose on both checked recovery days. Heat-sensing cell shares held steady, while itch-probe cell shares dipped early and partly recovered. The authors link heightened spontaneous nerve firing to both post-burn pain and itch.
pmc-13538560:
Fangyuan Zheng and colleagues compare light-activated particles for destroying a stubborn drug pollutant in varied waters in a 2026 study. Chloroquine phosphate survives standard wastewater treatment and threatens aquatic life. Five metal oxide particles were tested under ultraviolet light in pure water, drinking water, and synthetic seawater. Particle traits were measured alongside the aggressive oxygen species each produced.

Titanium dioxide performed best, clearing most of the drug in drinking water in line with its top oxygen species output. Zinc and cerium oxides worked moderately, swayed by acidity and salt content. Bismuth and tungsten oxides lagged, especially in complex waters. The authors stress testing cleaners in realistic waters and back titanium dioxide as the sturdiest option.
pmc-13540260:
Zhenrong Zhang and seven colleagues ask, in a 2026 modelling study, whether resting pulse rate helps predict falls among older people with glaucoma. Glaucoma steals side vision, and falls in this group can mean fractures and long hospital stays.

From a national Chinese ageing survey, 249 people with glaucoma who had not fallen at the 2015 baseline were followed to 2018, with a much larger non-glaucoma group for comparison. Several prediction methods, including an XGBoost model, combined health, medicine, vision, and laboratory measures. Interpretable machine learning was used to weigh what the pulse reading added. The authors stress that pulse is a supporting feature, not a stand-alone eye measure.
pmc-13540460:
Xinran Qiu and thirteen colleagues report, in a 2026 study, how dihydroartemisinin, a relative of the malaria drug artemisinin, pushes scar-forming liver cells to die by overloading them with copper. Liver fibrosis, the scarring behind much chronic liver disease, lacks good drug options.

Under copper overload the compound targets a transport protein called RAB1B, keeping copper-bearing vesicles flowing into hepatic stellate cells, the scar makers. Mitochondria then take up copper and trigger a copper-driven death called cuproptosis, followed by iron release and a second death mode, ferroptosis. The team packaged the compound in membrane-coated nanoparticles aimed at these cells and saw matching effects in rodents.
pmc-13542160:
Eiji Kawase and colleagues propose a cutting method in 2026. The field is large-scale optimisation. Huge planning problems grow until direct solving is hopeless. Their method cuts such problems into independent pieces. Ordinary solvers can then finish the pieces in parallel. Routing and scheduling are the target uses.

The method first scores how strongly variables interact. It phrases the cutting task as a maximum-cut problem. An Ising-model solver then makes the cut. Delivery routing tests showed clear gains. Feasible answers came far more often than before. The method reached in one minute what the naive method needed thirty minutes for. It also cut most variables out of the main problem.
pmc-13542760:
J H W de Beus and colleagues published a 2026 randomised trial comparing a one-piece zirconia implant with a two-piece titanium implant for replacing a single upper premolar tooth. Fifty patients were allocated evenly between the ceramic and metal implants, each restored with a lithium disilicate crown three months after placement. The main measure was change in the bone level around the implant over three years of use, alongside survival, gum health, appearance, and patient satisfaction.

Bone level barely changed in either group after three years, with average losses of only a few hundredths of a millimetre and no meaningful difference between materials. One zirconia implant failed to fuse with bone; the rest performed well. Bleeding scores ran slightly higher around ceramic implants, while appearance and patient-reported outcomes leaned slightly toward zirconia, again without firm differences. Both options look viable for this use on three-year evidence.
pmc-13543360:
Helia Mardani and colleagues published a 2026 umbrella review, a summary of meta-analyses, on immunonutrition for cancer patients undergoing surgery. Immunonutrition means feeds enriched with nutrients meant to support immune function, and undernourished surgical patients suffer many complications. The team gathered fifty-four existing meta-analyses from major databases and pooled their results again with a random-effects model covering complications, infections, leaks, deaths, and hospital stay.

Across the pooled evidence, immunonutrition cut overall complications by about a fifth and infectious complications by nearly two-fifths. Surgical-site infections and anastomotic leaks, where joined bowel ends fail, also fell, and patients left hospital roughly 1.75 days sooner. Timing mattered: feeding after surgery outperformed feeding before or around it for cutting complications. The authors support immunonutrition in cancer surgery while noting the stay result varied widely between underlying studies.
pmc-13543760:
Eunsu Song's team compared Xanthium strumarium fruit in 2026, a traditional East Asian medicine, sourced from Korea and from China. Only one origin's material is recognised by current pharmacopeias. The team sequenced chloroplast genomes and profiled selected plant chemicals by two lab methods. They also ran activity tests for antioxidant, skin-enzyme, and antibacterial effects, asking whether origin leaves a measurable fingerprint.

The genomes were near-identical except around one gene region, with the Chinese material carrying more mutations. The origins split clearly on chemistry. Korean fruit held more plant sterols and key phenolic acids, plus a compound called xanthatin found only there, while Chinese fruit carried more total fatty acids. Korean extracts also scored stronger in every activity assay. Five key chemicals drove the split. Origin-based quality standards, the authors argue, would be fairer than treating one country's harvest as the only genuine article.
pmc-13547360:
Zeyno Nuhoğlu and Abdurrahman Aksoy tested in 2026 whether two common anesthetics, propofol and ketamine, can shield lung cells from oxidative damage, a question with relevance for surgery in lung cancer patients. They exposed A549 lung cells to hydrogen peroxide to create the stress, then added each drug or the pair together across a range of doses. Cell survival and a panel of damage and defense markers were measured after a day.

Treated cells showed less of a fat-damage marker and higher levels of antioxidant defenses, including total antioxidant status, superoxide dismutase, and glutathione, than stressed cells left untreated. The combination shifted the markers more than either drug alone. The authors call for further study of a supportive role in lung cancer settings.
pmc-13547560:
Anna Doraczynska-Kowalik and a Polish team counted in 2026 large deletions and duplications, called copy number variants, in the BRCA1 and BRCA2 genes among patients tested at a regional cancer center. These structural variants guide preventive care and eligibility for targeted drugs, yet Polish data were thin because testing for them is not mandatory. Records covered 2,720 people tested between 2021 and 2024, almost all of them breast or ovarian cancer patients.

No BRCA2 copy number variants appeared at all. Pathogenic BRCA1 variants of this type turned up in 23 people from 13 families, under one percent of those tested, with loss of exon 21 the commonest. Affected families showed many related cancers, early onset, and a notable share of aggressive triple-negative breast cancers. The authors recommend routine testing in high-risk families.
pmc-13548560:
Shiwen Wu and colleagues investigate how stem cells from human fat tissue ease diabetic kidney disease, in a 2026 study combining patient tissue data with mouse and cell experiments. The kidney damage is driven by lingering inflammation, and one cleanup job matters greatly: macrophages must eat dead cells before they stir more trouble. Single-cell sequencing of human diabetic kidneys showed that this cleanup machinery was disrupted in the organs' macrophages.

In diabetic mice, the infused stem cells traveled to injured kidneys, improved filtration, and reduced tissue damage. Rather than flipping one inflammation switch, the cells restored the whole cleanup sequence, from finding dead cells to digesting them and settling down afterward. Kidneys showed less oxidative stress and calmer inflammation as a result. The authors identify this restored cleanup program as a main route of benefit.
pmc-13548660:
Sen Yan and colleagues trace how cold weather, gut microbes, and one amino acid conspire to destabilize artery plaques, in a 2026 mouse study. Cold exposure is increasingly tied to worse atherosclerosis, but the pathway was murky. Mice prone to plaques and fed a Western diet were kept cold, then studied with multi-omics tools, stool transplants, and cell experiments.

Cold sped plaque growth and fragility while scrambling gut microbes and raising blood leucine, an amino acid. Transferred microbes reproduced the leucine rise. Extra leucine quieted a gene in macrophages that normally sustains their cleanup of dead cells, so debris piled up, inflammation rose, and plaques weakened. Restoring a gut bacterium that cold had depleted normalized leucine and calmed plaques, while feeding leucine mimicked cold. The authors propose microbial tuning of leucine as a prevention target.
pmc-13549960:
Liu Yang, Chenglin Zhou, and Biao Sang ask whether basketball expertise turns decision making more planful when the task wears basketball clothing, in a 2026 psychology experiment. Reinforcement learning theory separates model-based choices, which use a mental map of how actions lead to outcomes, from model-free habits that simply repeat rewarded moves. Thirty-five national-level players and twenty-seven novices played a two-stage decision game in two skins: abstract symbols and basketball tactical diagrams.

Players leaned model-based in both versions and reported understanding the task better, while novices leaned habitual. Players using the planful style also answered more slowly, though slow answers in novices did not signal planning. The authors conclude expertise helps people fuse feedback with task structure, and they suggest training with sport-specific displays can sharpen decisions without lectures on strategy.
pmc-13551760:
Qianling Li, leading five colleagues, published a 2026 cross-sectional study of how older surgical patients view their own aging. Negative self-stereotypes about aging can slow recovery, yet drivers in patients with several chronic conditions were underexplored. The survey recruited 188 such patients having planned surgery at a Chongqing hospital between July and December 2025, using scales for daily function, illness burden, frailty, and decision preferences.

Average stereotype scores sat near the middle of the reported scale. Regression linked stronger stereotypes to first-time surgery and higher illness burden scores, while patients who preferred active decision-making scored lower in the reported model. The authors aim the findings at spotting high-risk patients early so perioperative support can protect recovery and quality of life.
pmc-13551860:
Sindi Uruci, leading eleven colleagues, published a 2026 case report of a kidney drug used off-label in a man with polycystic kidney disease and suspected IgA nephropathy. The 58-year-old had genetically confirmed PKD2 disease, and protein leaking into his urine climbed over three years despite standard blood pressure treatment. A biopsy was contraindicated, so the team started empagliflozin, an SGLT2 inhibitor proven in other kidney diseases but little studied in polycystic disease.

Urine protein fell steadily within a month and stabilized at a reduction above eighty percent through eighteen months in the reported course. Kidney function stayed stable and no infections or adverse events occurred. The authors present the case as support for the drug class's safety and protein-lowering effect in this combined condition.
pmc-13551960:
Xinyue Chen, with seven colleagues, published a 2026 study of lifestyle and disease in the UK Biobank. The cohort held 148,155 adults free of the studied diseases at the start. Five habits formed a healthy lifestyle score. They were not smoking, modest drinking, regular activity, a healthy diet, and healthy sleep. Outcomes covered eleven heart, metabolic, and related diseases.

Most single habits tied to lower disease risk. The combined score showed a clear step pattern. The healthiest group had much lower risk than the least healthy group. The strongest link was for pulmonary hypertension, a lung vessel disease. Healthy sleep carried the largest weight in the score. Adding lifestyle to standard risk models improved prediction a bit.
pmc-13554160:
Mohammed AlKahtani models a three-tier supply chain that buys recycled inputs while setting prices and sharing ad costs in a 2026 study. Supplier, maker, and retailer each choose how much recycled material to use, within what the recycling market can supply. Demand in his model answers to price, joint advertising, and the average recycled share. Fuzzy cost figures are turned into firm numbers before solving.

Four solving methods raced to lift total chain profit under budget, storage, and supply limits. A step-by-step quadratic method won, giving the highest profit with balanced choices at each tier. Profit proved most sensitive to how much recycled input exists and what it costs. Reward strength helped steadily but less. The model offers firms a planning tool for greener chains.
pmc-13554360:
Pearce replied in 2026 to two commentaries on his article arguing that research ethics oversight should be reshaped around patient choice. Dr Robert Steel raised five reservations about democratising oversight, while Dr Min-Fu Tsan defended current review boards on four grounds.

He argues his framework keeps expert safety boards while letting patients weigh their own risks. Against Tsan, he cites data showing central review approval taking a median of 216 days in one large study. He rejects the claim that a single-board mandate solved delays, noting it covers only some US studies. He also calls the therapeutic misconception charge misapplied, since his framework treats trials as research with uncertain benefit. Pearce concedes sponsors shape protocols, but says review boards still gate consent and design changes.
pmc-13558560:
Fiona Kumnova and ten colleagues profiled in 2026 a molecular alarm system called the NLRP3 inflammasome in human placentas from three stages of pregnancy. Calm, controlled inflammation at the meeting point of mother and fetus is essential, yet how this alarm is tuned across gestation was murky. The team compared tissue from early pregnancies, preterm births, and full-term births, measuring gene activity, protein amounts, enzyme processing, and cytokine levels side by side.

Early placentas carried the highest cytokine levels and the most inflammasome protein despite quiet gene readings. Preterm placentas grouped apart in gene activity and stockpiled alarm parts without switching the key enzyme on. Term placentas raised gene activity while protein and one signature cytokine fell. The authors describe later pregnancy as a primed yet restrained state, loaded but held back, with preterm tissue caught in its own distinct configuration.
pmc-13558760:
Claire Huchthausen and six colleagues showed in 2026 that teaching a lung nodule model with more mature cases only helps when the image statistics are corrected with biology in mind. Radiomic models promise earlier cancer calls on CT scans, yet early nodules in their set numbered barely a hundred and scanners vary. Classifiers trained on those alone performed near chance, so the team added more than two hundred later-stage benign and malignant nodules and tried three ways of harmonising the four acquisition protocols.

Plain harmonisation that ignored biology failed to improve the models consistently. Correcting with a covariate that knows which dataset each nodule came from, or harmonising each dataset separately, lifted test accuracy significantly on both standard measures. The authors call the study a proof of principle on a small single-centre set, with a clear methodological moral for radiomics.
pmc-13559460:
Jingyao Hui and colleagues built a machine learning model to predict bone marrow suppression in lung cancer patients receiving PD-1 inhibitors plus platinum doublet chemotherapy. Their 2026 study drew retrospectively on patients treated at the First Hospital of Lanzhou University between July 2018 and March 2026. Marrow suppression is a serious complication of this common regimen for non-small cell lung cancer.

Three feature-selection methods converged on eight predictors, including age, body mass index, tumor size, and several blood counts. Several learning models were trained and compared, with light gradient boosting performing best. Its accuracy held up reasonably in a held-out test set and in a later, separate patient cohort used for external validation. Explanation analysis showed which factors pushed individual predictions up or down. The authors offer the model as decision support for anticipating marrow toxicity, while noting its roots in a single center's records.
pmc-13563860:
Bakhtiyar Islamzade and two colleagues measure stress, anxiety, and depression among postgraduate dental students, a group carrying patient responsibility on top of study demands. Undergraduate distress is well documented; the postgraduate years are not. Their 2026 study surveyed 192 trainees with a demographic form and the DASS-21 questionnaire, a 21-item distress scale. Scores were doubled to match the severity bands, then related to training factors with correlation and regression models.

The three states moved together tightly, every pairing significant. Stress and anxiety together explained a share of depression scores, with a model value of 0.696 for variance explained. Most trainees landed in the normal band on each subscale. Feeling financially middling, rather than comfortable, hinted at higher distress without holding up in the full model. Year of training, specialty, housing, and smoking showed no differences. The authors advise reading the web of distress as one problem, not three.
pmc-13563960:
Madeline Pan and co-authors examine, in a 2026 retrospective study, vision in 450 patients with intermediate dry age-related macular degeneration at one academic center over a decade. Care records for 759 eyes were split by smoking history and by whether patients took AREDS vitamin supplements, a standard aid for this stage of disease.

Patients taking the supplements started with better vision than those who did not, in both smokers and non-smokers. Vision changes through follow-up were tracked with standard eye-chart measures converted for analysis. The work highlights a baseline gap that can shape how later results are read, and it gives eye clinics a reason to record supplement use and smoking carefully.
pmc-13566460:
Julia A. Ford and Ora Gewurz-Singer write, in a 2026 review for rheumatologists, about kidney disease driven by the antibody IgA, and whether progress in one condition can help another. IgA nephropathy harms only the kidneys, while IgA vasculitis also causes skin, joint, and gut symptoms, yet evidence increasingly links their causes.

Drug trials in nephropathy have recently produced several targeted approvals, while vasculitis still lacks strong randomized trials. The authors compare how the two illnesses appear, explain the shared multi-step disease model, and ask which new drugs might suit vasculitis patients with kidney involvement. Rheumatologists get a bridge between a fast-moving field and their own slower one.
pmc-13570360:
Guanglong Liu and colleagues feed, in a 2026 trial, plant flavonoids from Silphium perfoliatum to 250 young broiler chickens challenged with a bacterial toxin that injures the gut. Five groups compared no treatment, toxin alone, and toxin plus three flavonoid doses in feed, with growth, gut shape, antioxidant enzymes, immune signals, and gut microbes all measured.

Flavonoid-fed birds regained growth, grew taller gut villi, and carried stronger antioxidant defenses with calmer inflammatory signals. Gut barrier genes switched on more strongly, and the cecal microbe mix recovered diversity and helpful species. Poultry producers get a feed additive candidate that protects the gut during inflammatory stress.
pmc-13571260:
Danii L. S. Suijk and colleagues write, in a 2026 letter, about testing losartan, empagliflozin, and both together for lowering blood uric acid in people with type 2 diabetes. High uric acid tracks with heart and kidney disease in this group. Twenty-four participants aged from twenty-five upward entered the comparison of the two familiar drugs.

Each drug is thought to raise uric acid loss in urine through the same kidney transporter. One is a proven diabetes and kidney protector. The other is a blood pressure drug with a known uric acid benefit in a landmark trial. Because the pair is often prescribed together, the study separates their individual and combined effects on uric acid levels and urine clearance. The design answers a practical question for combination prescribing.
pmc-13572360:
Meng Zhang and colleagues review, in a 2026 article, how the fuel choices of macrophages, the immune cells that crowd ovarian tumors, decide whether those cells attack the cancer or shelter it. Sugar burning, oxygen-based energy, and glutamine use each push macrophages toward one of two broad states, inflammatory or suppressive.

Tumor-associated macrophages mostly settle in the suppressive state, helping the cancer escape immunity and resist treatment. The review connects each metabolic pathway to that balance and surveys nanoscale delivery strategies that aim to reprogram macrophage fuel use precisely inside tumors. Ovarian cancer remains highly lethal, and retraining its resident immune cells offers a route that direct tumor drugs have not delivered.
pmc-13572460:
Marianna Piras, with 15 colleagues, reports a 2026 study of blood chemistry shifts tied to weight gain from mental health drugs. Many such drugs add weight and raise heart risk, but the body changes behind the gain are not well mapped. The team used a broad scan of small molecules in blood plasma, not just a few set markers.

The study drew on a cohort of patients who started a weight-linked drug, with 151 follow-up visits from 135 patients. Blood was drawn at the start and again later, and a strict selection method picked 56 features tied to weight change per month. Ten were named, and six were confirmed against standards. Gains in fat-like molecules and in breakdown products of tryptophan tracked with more weight gain. Two compounds tracked the other way. The named set may seed early warning tests.
pmc-13572560:
Lucie Frejlichová, with five colleagues, details a 2026 study of a fungus that may threaten oak seedlings in nurseries. Pedunculate oak anchors European forests, and nursery stock can carry hidden trunk pathogens. The fungus Cadophora luteo-olivacea is known from grapevine disease, but its power to harm oak was unproven.

Inoculated seedlings grew stem lesions that averaged 11.9 centimetres, while controls showed just 0.9 centimetres of wound response. That gap met the classic test for proving a pathogen. In paired dishes, a second fungus, Trichoderma atroviride, cut the pathogen's spread. Protein and chemical scans of the contact zone at days four and eight found 257 shifted proteins by day eight, among them wall-cutting enzymes. Ergosterol, a fungal membrane part, fell. The work feeds nursery risk checks and biocontrol trials.
pmc-13573360:
Yang and colleagues built in 2026 a prediction chart, called a nomogram, for deep vein thrombosis before surgery in patients with broken lower leg bones from injury. Such clots in deep veins are a common and dangerous complication. The team studied 950 surgical patients at their hospital, split into a training group of 665 and a checking group of 285. They tested a blood score called the systemic immune-inflammation index, which blends immune cell counts.

Yang found five independent predictors of clots before surgery: age, fracture site, the inflammation index, a clot breakdown marker called D-dimer, and a clotting time measure. The nomogram built from these factors matched observed outcomes well in both the training and checking groups. The authors say the chart helps clinicians flag high-risk fracture patients early, before surgery, so preventive steps can start in time.
pmc-13573460:
Xiang-yu Zhang, with five colleagues, reports a 2026 study of blood sugar swings in intensive care patients with severe pneumonia. Sugar control often slips in critical illness, and swings, not just high levels, may harm. The team asked whether the path of those swings over the first days splits patients into risk groups.

The study followed 315 patients at one Chinese hospital from 2021 to 2024. A trajectory model found two paths: a small group whose swings started high and stayed high, and a large group with low, steady swings. Early outcomes matched, but after day 14 the high-swing group died more often. On arrival, that group also showed higher infection and long-term sugar markers. Those two markers together flagged the high-swing path well. The authors urge early checks to catch the risky path.
pmc-13574160:
S. Marina Casalino-Matsuda and a large team report a 2026 study of a channel blocker drug in severe viral pneumonia. In bad COVID-19 lung disease, T cells and lung macrophages feed each other's inflammation in a loop. Both cell types use CRAC channels to take in calcium, and the blocker Auxora closes those channels. A prior trial had linked it to far lower 30-day death.

This side study followed a small group of ventilated patients with lab-confirmed disease. Blood levels of two signals, one that calls in fresh immune cells and one growth factor, fell after the drug but not after placebo. Lung wash cell mixes did not shift clearly, and gene changes stayed below firm proof. In lab tests with healthy donor cells, the drug blocked calcium entry in a dose-linked way. The authors frame the work as exploratory mechanism hunting.
pmc-13574760:
Serena Basta, with two colleagues, presents a 2026 proof-of-concept measure for body schema, the brain's working map of the body in action. Few tools can put a number on that map, and lifestyle may shape it over a life. The team used the disorder, or entropy, in the strokes of a self-drawing as the number.

Forty-four adults drew themselves, then a flower as a control, and filled in an activity survey. Body drawings carried lower local entropy than flower drawings once stroke length was counted, which hints the score taps body-specific structure. Leftover entropy fell with age, as if the map settles over time. Activity showed no clear main effect, yet active older adults held their entropy steady. The authors call for balanced follow-up studies to firm the method up.
pmc-13575260:
Hojun Yu leads a 2026 study building a machine learning model that predicts worsening chronic kidney disease in Korean patients. The standard risk equation was built abroad and performs unevenly across ethnic groups. It also misses how a patient's readings change over time.

Records from a Seoul hospital covered 28,209 patients for model building, with a national cohort of 3,960 used for outside checking. Four learning methods were blended into one voting model. Inside the hospital data it scored 0.939 on the standard discrimination measure, clearly above the standard equation. Outside performance was closer to the equation's score. Starting kidney function, its rate of change, albumin, and haemoglobin mattered most. The authors propose the equation for community screening and their model for hospital care.
pmc-13576260:
Weipeng Li and six colleagues study whether the change in a clotting marker around surgery predicts dangerous blood clots in womb cancer patients, in a 2026 cohort study. D-dimer is a protein fragment that rises when clots form and break down. Vein clots after surgery are a severe risk in this cancer.

The study followed 307 surgical patients in Fujian from 2022 to 2024. Each unit rise in D-dimer change lifted clot odds by about 20 percent after wide adjustment. The link was not a straight line: below a change value of 3.78 the risk climbed steeply, while above it the risk eased. Blood thinners, infection, and one lab value explained almost none of the pattern. The authors call the findings early signals that tracking the marker's path, not single values, may sharpen risk checks.
pmc-13578260:
Weiting Shi, Wenkai Shi, Ye He, and Yuwei Wang chart how well art and cultural tourism fit together across China in a 2026 study. They built yearly scores for 31 provinces from 2014 to 2023. The scores ask how smoothly the art side and the travel side adapt to each other. That question grows sharper as the field shifts from growth in size toward growth in quality.

Fit rose over the decade in a wavy climb. Most provinces still sat at low or middle levels, with wide gaps between regions. A machine learning model with an explainer tool ranked what drives the fit. Clean surroundings and public services set the floor. Roads and data links carried the system. Spending on culture and new ideas drove lasting gains. Each driver helped most at certain stages, not in a straight line.
pmc-13578860:
Ingmar Visser leads a thirty laboratory team that retested a famous claim about how babies learn sound rules, in a registered report study. A 1999 study reported that seven month olds learned abstract patterns in syllable strings and applied them to new sounds. The new effort ran a close copy across many labs, testing 839 babies aged five to twelve months, with 650 kept after exclusions.

Babies heard pattern strings, then new strings that matched or broke the pattern, while looking times were timed. Longer looking at the odd ones out would signal learning. No such gap appeared in the pooled results, and a second analysis leaned strongly toward no effect at all. Language mix, age, and test variant changed nothing. Thirty of thirty one lab samples matched the null result, raising hard questions for the field.
pmc-13579760:
Maria Castronuovo and colleagues trace a two way partnership between two proteins that drive chronic lymphocytic leukemia, in a 2026 study. The proteins, called FAK and ROR1, sit in the signal webs that help these white blood cells survive, move, and hide in tissues. Patient cells were prodded with a signal molecule, dosed with a FAK blocker, and sorted into dividing and resting fractions by surface markers.

Triggering ROR1 switched FAK on, while blocking FAK lowered ROR1 in return, proving the loop runs both ways. Dividing cells fresh out of lymph nodes carried the most of both proteins. The FAK blocker teamed with standard targeted drugs to kill far more leukemia cells, even when support cells tried to shield them. The authors pitch the drug pair for hard to treat cases, citing the blocker's clean safety record in solid tumor trials.
pmc-13580060:
Nima Khodakarami and colleagues trace which children keep returning to emergency rooms for asthma, in a 2026 study built on emergency records from three U.S. states. The data hold over four hundred fifty seven thousand asthma visits for children aged two to eighteen. Office care and drug plans often fail these families, pushing them back to hospital doors.

Visit rates ran more than two times higher for children under eleven than for teenagers. Black and Hispanic children and those on public insurance carried heavier burdens, as did children in poorer or non metro areas. Good prior office care cut the return odds by about a fifth, a protective lever the authors highlight. They close with calls for drug access fixes and smarter discharge planning.
pmc-13582360:
Konstantinos Prokopidis and colleagues test how hospital stay length and muscle loss feed each other in older patients, in a 2026 study from Copenhagen. Just over one thousand inpatients aged sixty five and up had muscle mass, grip strength, walking speed, and chair rise power measured within a day of arrival. Sarcopenia, the named syndrome of weak, thin muscle, was scored by European rules.

In patients over eighty, longer stays tied to slower walking and weaker chair rises in both sexes, and to weaker grip in women. In younger men, longer stays tied to weaker grip and chair power and to triple the odds of the full syndrome. Stronger grip and chair power, in turn, tied to shorter stays nearly everywhere. The arrow may run both ways, the authors note, so ward rehab is the lever to test.
pmc-13584460:
Hao Huang and colleagues test a blood-based gene-reading method for finding germs in severe lung infection in this 2026 study. Patients had sepsis, a life-threatening reaction to infection, tied to bad pneumonia. The usual deep test washes out the lungs, which is hard on unstable patients and can flag germs that are not truly to blame. A blood draw is far simpler.

The team compared methods in 122 adults who gave both lung wash and blood samples. Their targeted blood test caught close to two thirds of the cases set by a careful clinical standard, far more than blood culture or a broad blood test. Germs seen only in the lung wash were less often judged the true cause. Patients whose blood and lung results agreed also died less often over the next three months.
pmc-13586660:
Rosamaria Caminiti and a large team review antidepressants for nerve pain caused by chemotherapy. The nerve damage, called CIPN, brings pain, tingling, and numbness that can outlast cancer treatment and shrink quality of life. Searching three databases for recent work, the reviewers kept 11 studies of adults with this pain, with the drug duloxetine studied most and amitriptyline, used in creams, close behind.

Duloxetine cut nerve pain by amounts patients could feel, across several rating scales. Skin-applied amitriptyline also looked promising, though its base of studies is thin. Pairing duloxetine with other pain drugs eased pain further in some reports, but firm proof of an added effect is lacking. Side effects were mostly mild. For prevention, the record stays unclear, and the authors ask for larger, sharper trials.
pmc-13587760:
Alexander Muacevic and colleagues look inside the cheek muscle of patients with oral submucous fibrosis, a scarring mouth disease that slowly locks the jaw. The condition, common where areca nut is chewed, is classed as potentially malignant, yet most study stops at the mouth lining. This descriptive study took small cheek samples from seven patients and three healthy people, deep enough to include the buccinator muscle beneath.

Under light and electron microscopes, every patient sample showed muscle harm: fibers shrunken and split, glassy decay, scar tissue, and narrowed vessels. At the finest level, the contractile threads were lost or broken, energy factories swelled, and collagen replaced muscle. Healthy samples showed none of this. The authors caution that seven patients is a small base, yet the pattern suggests the disease eats into muscle as well as lining.
pmc-13591760:
Jiaqi Liu and seven colleagues examine, in 2026, how age shapes the link between daily oral habits and face pain in jaw disorder patients. Habits such as clenching, gum chewing, or leaning on the jaw can load the jaw joint and muscles. Their clinic sample held 343 adults with painful jaw disorders, each scored for habit load and for pain strength on standard scales.

On a raw look, habit scores showed no tie to pain. Once age, sex, schooling, and diagnosis were factored in, higher habit load did pair with stronger pain. That tie faded as age rose, the team found. Liu and colleagues say age acts as a dial on the habit pain link, which clinics should weigh when advising younger patients.
pmc-13592160:
Mazin Ahmed Subhy Alsheikhly and three colleagues report a rare case of Cushing's syndrome driven by a hormone making liver tumor. A 41 year old woman gained weight fast, showed darkened skin, and ran very low on potassium. Tests proved her body was flooded with cortisol, urged on by high ACTH, a pituitary style hormone. Brain imaging looked clean, yet a body scan lit up one large liver lesion.

Her past held a neuroendocrine tumor near the voice box, and the liver growth proved to be its hormone secreting spread. A cortisol blocking infusion crashed her into shock, delaying surgery until intensive care steadied her. Surgeons then removed part of the liver and stomach, and ACTH fell sharply. The team stresses tight teamwork for such perilous cases.
pmc-13592460:
Carlos Gallardo-García and five colleagues build glucose forecasting models for type 1 diabetes that look past carbohydrate counts alone. Fat and protein also sway how blood sugar rises after a meal, yet most forecasters ignore them. Their models learned from sensor, insulin, and meal records of 351 adults, covering more than 15,000 meals. Forecasts ran up to four hours ahead, with built in tools to show which inputs drove each call.

Adding fat and protein sharpened early forecasts, cutting average error clearly. For later hours, splitting sugars from complex carbohydrates on top of fat and protein worked best. Attribution checks partly matched that split. The team cautions that the gains are modest and non causal, and that outside testing must come first.
pmc-13612860:
Deborah A. Marshall leads a team studying how caring for a child who has juvenile idiopathic arthritis affects the quality of life of the parents who provide that care. This form of arthritis begins in childhood and can bring lasting pain, clinic visits, and daily care work for families. The team drew on baseline data from a Canada-Netherlands study of personalized medicine in childhood arthritis and related diseases.

Parents of children under 18 filled in the CarerQol, a survey that scores the care situation from 0 to 100 and shows which parts of caregiving weigh most heavily. The authors linked those scores with the child's symptoms, disease activity, and family details. Their work helps services see where support for parent caregivers is most needed, rather than treating the child's illness as the only burden.
pmc-13615260:
Ben Rimmer and colleagues review in 2026 the quality-of-life outcomes that people who receive a transplanted organ describe in their own words. The team searched five databases through May 2024. They gathered 40 papers covering 39 interview-based studies. Fourteen dealt with kidney transplants and ten with liver. Eight covered heart, three lung, and four mixed organs. Reporting quality was fair, though the people studied lacked variety in background.

Ninety-three distinct quality-of-life outcomes surfaced, and all fitted within nine broad dimensions the team set in advance. Some themes ran across every organ type, while others belonged to one group alone. For transplant teams, the catalogue shows that life after a new organ is judged by far more than survival or lab numbers. It also points to outcomes worth asking about at every follow-up visit.
pmc-13616360:
Mingxin Feng and colleagues design a plastic composite film that cools surfaces passively, bouncing sunlight away while beaming heat out through the sky's infrared window. Such zero-energy cooling needs two traits at once, high sun reflection and strong heat emission, yet the structures governing each usually interfere. Their composite mixes a three-part block copolymer with a phosphorus compound, arranged so its phases separate at several scales on purpose.

Large-scale separation builds a spongy, connected skeleton that scatters sunlight broadly, reaching 97.2 percent solar reflectivity. The filler settles selectively into one polymer region, tuning the heat-emission side without spoiling the reflection. Splitting the optical jobs between scales gives rooftops and outdoor gear a coating that cools itself under full sun, with no power drawn at all.
pmc-13616760:
Napadol Poomkert, Tawachai Monum, Sukon Prasitwattanaseree, and Pasuk Mahakkanukrauh test in 2026 whether machine learning can estimate sex from the first and second ribs. Their population is northern Thai. The method targets cases where a skeleton lacks the usual pelvis or skull clues. They measured 15 points on the first rib and 14 on the second across 200 right-side and 177 left-side rib sets held at Chiang Mai University, balanced between men and women.

Men's ribs measured larger on nearly every variable. Twelve learning algorithms, trimmed by feature selection and tuned automatically, competed on the data. The best single result came from quadratic discriminant analysis on the right first rib, with 85 percent accuracy on held-out bones. Forensic teams gain a population-specific fallback, with an honest ceiling, for naming unknown remains.
pmc-13616860:
Patricia K. Thomas and four colleagues validate a computer material model of sheep lung tissue for use in impact injury simulations. Finite element models predict chest injury risk, yet they rarely account for lung pressure during breathing or for the stretchy, time-dependent behavior of the tissue. The team translated an existing model into simulation software and tested it against laboratory impact data.

They ran quasi-static runs to check the translation and dynamic runs to test high-velocity loading, at three lung pressures that span the breathing cycle. Force responses matched experiments well, with agreement scores the authors rate as good or excellent. Strain patterns from digital image correlation depended on mesh size, a caution for finer detail. Overall, the validated model gives injury researchers a lung representation that includes pressure and viscoelastic effects.
pmc-13617160:
Cecelia J. Giesen and four colleagues track how an arctic caribou herd adjusts its diet as spring plant growth begins, a brief window that can shape female body condition and reproduction. The team captured one hundred ten females from the Teshekpuk herd in northern Alaska across three June seasons from 2022 to 2024. Droppings, blood samples, and plant growth data at capture sites let them reconstruct diet and body condition.

Diet quality peaked in 2023, when captures followed the start of green-up near the coast, with protein in droppings near twenty percent, against under six percent in 2022 before green-up far inland. Blood markers of protein status matched that pattern, while isotope signatures pointed to lichen-heavy diets in one year and grass-like plants in another. Location during the short green-up window, the authors conclude, strongly shapes the protein gains females can bank for the year.
pmc-13618560:
Thara Chandran and eight colleagues ask whether minerals in drinking water beyond fluoride shape tooth decay, in a cross-sectional ecological study around Mangalore, India. They sampled thirty-one village councils, measured residents' decayed, missing, and filled teeth, and analyzed groundwater from local wells with mass spectroscopy for its mineral content. Fluoride in the area ran below World Health Organization advised levels.

Fluoride itself showed only a weak positive correlation with decay experience, contrary to the usual protective story at adequate levels. Potassium, by contrast, showed a significant negative correlation, suggesting a possible protective association in this low-fluoride setting. The authors conclude that the anticariogenic effect, the defense against cavities, likely comes from the interplay of several minerals rather than any single ion. They call the potassium signal a lead worth following rather than a settled finding.
pmc-13618960:
Qiuhui Tian and six colleagues check whether two cheap blood-based scores can flag which acute pancreatitis patients will turn severe and which severe cases will die within twenty-eight days. The triglyceride-glucose index reflects insulin resistance, while the C-reactive protein-to-albumin ratio captures inflammation against nutritional reserve. In a retrospective cohort of three hundred sixteen patients, they tested both scores with regression, discrimination curves, and bootstrap validation.

Both scores ran higher in patients who progressed to severe disease. Each independently predicted progression after adjustment, with discrimination favoring the inflammation ratio. Validation barely dented results. Predicted risks matched observed outcomes. Among severe cases, high values of either score were associated with higher twenty-eight-day mortality. Survival curves separated above the cutoffs, though mortality estimates carried wide uncertainty. The authors propose the pair as early-warning tools where advanced systems are unavailable.
pmc-13619260:
Cortney C Braund and nine colleagues describe a quality improvement project that sped up care for low-acuity children in a busy pediatric emergency department. Their team redesigned the front end around a physician-led intake model and added an alternate care space for simpler cases. Clearer roles, standard workflows, and staff teaching supported the change, with no extra staff or building work.

Time from rooming to disposition fell by fifteen percent overall, and by nearly half for children needing few interventions. Total stay dropped by thirty percent, and far fewer families left without being seen. Arrival-to-provider time also shrank. The authors argue that reorganizing space and steps a department already has can free capacity for sicker children while moving straightforward cases through much faster.
pmc-13619460:
Sanz-Muñoz and colleagues review in 2026 whether people already carry some immunity to the bird flu virus H5N1, which keeps spreading among birds and mammals and worries pandemic planners. Prior flu infections or vaccines might leave partial protection behind.

The review concentrates on antibody responses that cross-react with H5N1 in people never known to meet the virus. It weighs evidence that seasonal flu infection or vaccination can create such antibodies. The antibodies in question are aimed especially at conserved parts of the virus surface proteins, such as the stalk of hemagglutinin, and at the neuraminidase protein. The authors then assess current and emerging H5N1 vaccines, including adjuvanted and mRNA versions. They close with priorities: watch population immunity, keep surveillance strong, and build broadly protective flu vaccines.
pmc-13619660:
Bruna Leis Endres and eleven colleagues tested whether a treated form of anacardic acid can protect root dentin collagen from decay-like attack. Root caries starts when mineral leaves the dentin and enzymes then chew up the collagen scaffold underneath. The team used cow incisor roots, removed the mineral, soaked samples in the compound called LDT11 or in plain water, and then exposed both sets to a week of caries-like conditions.

Treated samples kept a larger area of dense, well-organized collagen fibers under polarized light. Infrared readings suggested the compound bonds with the collagen and changes its surface chemistry. Heat testing, though, showed no change in total collagen mass, so the protection seems to sit at the surface layer. The authors propose LDT11 as a possible helper for slowing root caries by shielding the exposed matrix.
pmc-13619860:
Sebastian Scheidel and six colleagues built a way to film the lungs emptying during a forced breath out, using MRI, in a 2026 study. Standard breathing tests measure total airflow but cannot show which lung regions lag. Their method uses a spiraling three-dimensional scan path shaped like a Fermat loop, paired with a reconstruction that favors smooth change across space and time.

A purpose-built lung phantom came first: volumes read from its images matched the air actually exchanged almost exactly. Scans in living volunteers then captured the deflation process at a fifth of a second per frame with even five-millimeter detail in every direction. From the segmented volumes the team derived timing measures, such as how long the dynamic phase lasted and how much air left in the first second. The authors present the method as a route to regional lung function testing without radiation.
pmc-13620260:
Xuexia Shan and fourteen colleagues studied why tumors creep back after microwave ablation, a heat treatment that cooks cancer in place. Burning is sometimes incomplete, leaving a rim of living tumor. Single-cell gene sequencing of the lymph nodes draining such tumors showed their scavenger cells, macrophages, had shifted into suppressive types after the incomplete burn.

Those suppressive cells leaned heavily on one growth signal and its receptor, making the receptor a target. The team packaged a chemotherapy drug and a receptor blocker together in a fat-and-protein nanoparticle shaped to reach both lymph nodes and tumor. Across several tumor models the package reawakened immune activity, shrank leftover tumor, and left immune memory strong enough to reject a fresh tumor challenge in cured mice. The authors name the draining lymph nodes as an overlooked treatment site after ablation.
pmc-13623360:
EsmaNur Özen and Fatma Ersin measure what women know about gynaecological cancers and how fatalistic they feel about breast cancer. Fatalism here means believing that fate, not screening or treatment, decides outcomes, a view that can keep women from check-ups. The descriptive study ran from October 2023 to August 2024 in one family health centre district.

The sample held 333 women who completed awareness and fatalism scales. Both scores landed above the middle of their ranges, which the authors read as fairly good awareness paired with moderate fatalism. Schooling, social security cover, learning from health staff, and having had a gynaecological exam together explained part of the awareness spread. Age and schooling shaped fatalism scores. The authors recommend teaching programmes that raise cancer awareness while softening fatalistic beliefs, since health workers proved to be a trusted channel.
pmc-13623960:
Hideto Ueki and colleagues test whether the bare basics of hand movement, captured as three-dimensional positions, can reveal a surgeon's skill on a robotic operating system. Robotic platforms each hoard their own detailed data, which blocks shared standards for judging performance. If plain position data were enough, any robot with tracking could be scored the same way.

Working on Japan's Hinotori robot, the team fed movement features into a machine learning classifier that separated experts from novices with high accuracy. One feature led the pack: how densely the left hand's movements clustered at their peak. A small set of measures still worked when whole surgeons were held out of training, which suggests the signal generalises. Movement patterns also tracked patient outcomes, including blood loss, and experts adapting to the new robot followed visibly different learning paths. The authors propose tailored training based on each surgeon's movement fingerprint.
pmc-13625060:
Harram Najum and colleagues review zero-dimensional anode materials, specks so small they count as dots, across six kinds of rechargeable battery. High-capacity anode hopefuls like silicon, tin, and phosphorus swell badly and fade fast, while wires, sheets, and frames bring their own limits. Dots offer huge surface area, short paths for ions, and room to absorb swelling, so the review weighs them against larger shapes in lithium, sodium, potassium, magnesium, aluminum, and zinc cells.

The verdict is mixed by design. Gains in capacity and speed depend on the chemistry and on how dots are held in a matrix, and first-cycle losses, clumping, and costly synthesis dog every system. Fixing those trade-offs, not chasing capacity alone, is the road to shop-ready cells.
pmc-13625260:
Maisra M El-Bouseary and colleagues grow gold nanoparticles with the help of a soil bacterium, Streptomyces enissocaesilis, and test them on breast cancer cells. Green synthesis swaps harsh chemicals for living microbes, and the ruby-red particles came out small, evenly charged, and crystal-faced. In dish tests on MCF-7 breast cancer cells, the particles slowed growth in step with dose. They halted half the cancer cells at a dose well below the one that harmed normal blood cells.

Treated cancer cells froze almost entirely at the first resting phase of the cell cycle and stopped copying their DNA. Staining and gene tests pointed to programmed cell death switching on, with a cancer-linked growth gene turned down and a guardian gene turned up. The work frames microbe-made gold as a multi-target cancer lead.
pmc-13625660:
Subin Heo and a large team search for warning signs in porto-sinusoidal vascular disorder, a rare liver disease that scars small vessels without cirrhosis. They studied 114 patients, following seventy-four over time for liver-related events, and sequenced RNA from twenty-one liver samples against six healthy ones. A simple imaging ratio, liver size against spleen size, was tested beside fibrosis stage, the tissue scarring grade.

Nearly a third of patients had received a transplant around diagnosis, and fibrosis stage tracked transplant need closely. In follow-up, about one in six patients hit a liver event, and the size ratio past a set cutoff flagged them. Gene readouts shifted with both measures, with vessel lining cells redistributing, scar-forming cells growing, and an inflammation signal rising, which may guide how doctors stage this disease.
pmc-13626360:
Ebrahim Babaee and co-authors mine Iran's national rabies registry, one of the world's largest records of animal bites. Between March 2022 and September 2023 the registry logged 507,404 bite cases, each a visit where exposure and treatment were recorded. Dogs caused about three-quarters of bites and cats a fifth, men made up nearly three-quarters of patients, and northern provinces posted the highest rates per head.

Care looked strong at the front end: wounds were washed in almost every case, and nearly all patients got a first vaccine dose within two days. Cracks showed later, with dose schedules drifting, exposure classes misjudged, and the antibody shot both missed in many bat cases and wasted on trivial ones. The registry, the authors say, is rich enough to steer fixes if its recording sharpens.
pmc-13626660:
Mariëlle L de Goede and colleagues build the first structured interview for moral injury in military veterans. Moral injury can follow acts that clash with a person's deepest values, yet clinics had only questionnaires to map it.
